News.title: Polanski repeatedly refuses to apologise over sick guillotine post – as Farage blasts ‘he must face consequences’
News.content:
ZACK Polanski has repeatedly refused to apologise to Nigel Farage after he reposted an image of an activist wearing a T-shirt calling for the Reform chief’s decapitation.

Mr Farage has now blasted the Green Party leader and said “he must face consequences” for his “appalling decisions”.



The picture – posted on Monday – showed a man in a black top emblazoned with a guillotine and the words “we’re only making plans for Nigel”.

Mr Polanski deleted the image after its contents were “brought to his attention” and insisted he “does not support this type of dangerous message”.



But Mr Polanski said he would not apologise for the “inadvertent mistake” three times when speaking to BBC Newsnight last night.

He said: “Well, if I’d done it deliberately I’d be apologising but because this was a mistake.”

When asked to apologise a second time, the Greens leader claimed Mr Farage had been “fundamentally dishonest” by cropping the image to make it seem like Mr Polanski had posted it himself.

At the third chance, he said: “I think it’s important that I draw a line and don’t play his game… It is important that he’s kept safe, it is important we condemn political violence, but I also recognise this as the political attack that it is.”



The party leader claimed he accepted the collaborative post because he saw people partying at the Green conference.

When he flicked through the images, he only noticed the man was wearing a rainbow hat he added.

Mr Farage said he has reported Mr Polanski to the Metropolitan Police and accused him of incitement to murder.

Mr Polanski said that it would be “odd” for the police to contact him over what he insisted was a mistake.

Writing in the Daily Mail, Mr Farage has slammed the lack of response in the wake of Ann Widdecombe‘s murder.



He said: “No apology, no knock on the door, no wider condemnations, nothing to see here, move along please.”

Mr Farage said he had also reported the post to the London Assembly where Mr Polanski is a member.

“Because when it comes to political double standards and the two-tier policing of our public life, enough is enough,” he added.



He continued: “Now, less than three weeks after Ann’s murder, we have witnessed the grisly spectacle of a party leader posting about how funny it would be to guillotine the leader of the party she supported.

“Sorry but I’m not laughing.”

Mr Farage said: “Polanski must face the consequences of his appalling decisions. Political violence is real. It is serious. It needs dealing with.”

Fellow Reform members have blasted Mr Polanski and branded the leader a hypocrite.

Reform’s Zia Yusuf added: “This is incitement to murder. It should be treated as such by the police.”



And Reform’s Robert Jenrick slammed: “These people are sick.

This went out to hundreds of thousands of followers.

“How ironic, when Zack talks endlessly about being kind and loving to each other.”

The creators of the guillotine T-shirt have since removed it from sale.

Sabcat Printing were selling the £20 top showing the execution method with the words “We’re only making plans for Nigel”.

But the company – part of an “anarchist co-operative” based out of a warehouse in Manchester – claimed it was “satire”.



A Green Party spokesman said: “After attending a public event, Zack accepted a request to collaborate on a post with several images.

“Once this image was brought to his attention he immediately unshared the post.

“He unequivocally does not support this type of dangerous message.”

The Met Police said: “Earlier today – Monday, 27 July – we received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media.

“We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting enquiries into the matter.”



Last week, Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with one count of murder over Widdecombe’s death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Farage has also since revealed he gets 300 threats a month after an Afghan migrant with an AK47 tattoo on his face was jailed for threatening to kill him earlier this month.

The Reform leader has pushed for his party’s politicians to be given beefed-up security.

News.title: Can I trim my neighbour’s roots if they’re growing over my fence? Your legal rights explained
News.content:
TREES have a mind of their own and their branches – and roots – can easily make their way into your property.

But if your neighbour’s pesky plants do cross boundaries, do you have a legal right to trim them?

According to government guidelines, it is perfectly legal to trim branches or roots that cross into your property.



This includes plants that may come from either a neighbour’s home or a public road.



However, you need to be careful about how much you trim.

If you take it too far – and cut roots beyond your property‘s boundary – your neighbour could take you to court for damaging their property.

You may even be caught in a civil matter regarding trespassing, especially if you needed to access their property, or back garden, in order to cut those roots.



The rules also differ depending whether you live in a conservation area, or if the roots you intend to trim are protected by a ‘tree preservation order’.

In this case, you may need to seek permission from your local council, before you begin any garden work.

This can be done either by contacting you council directly, or making a ‘works to trees’ application online, which can be accessed through the government website.

So although you should be within the limits of the law in most cases;



It is always important to double-check the rules, and remember to put down the garden shears if you’re trimming a little too enthusiastically.

News.title: Brit family sleeps on cardboard after evacuation from path of France wildfires due to be fuelled by 42C heat blast TODAY
News.content:
A BRITISH family has been forced to sleep on cardboard boxes on the beach after wildfires turned their French holiday into a nightmare.

After being evacuated from the seaside town of Biscarrosse, the family were left to sleep on cardboard boxes salvaged from a recycling bin and later a tent.



Mum Melissa Sood, 33, was visiting her grandmother with her husband Sunny, 42, their 14-year-old daughter and her brother and sister, when horror wildfires broke out across France.

Firefighters battled to keep the inferno that has destroyed 42,000 hectares under control overnight, amid warnings from Meteo-France that temperatures could peak at 42C today.



Melissa and her family are unable to fly back to their home in Basingstoke because the roads to the nearest airport in Bordeaux are blocked.

They also cannot return to Melissa’s grandma’s house to fetch their house keys due to the evacuation order.



Melissa said her family were on their way back from the beach last Thursday when they first saw large plumes of smoke rising but “didn’t think much of it”.

They were sitting down to dinner at a local restaurant that night when police told them they needed to evacuate.

“We started to run back to the house and there were water planes flying over, and the air was just black,” she said.

The family raced to collect their passports and went to a school being used as an evacuation centre, but they were all turned away except Melissa’s 83-year-old grandma because they were not residents.

With nowhere to go they pulled some cardboard boxes from a bin and tried to get some sleep on the grass near the beach.



“The fire looked like a scene from a disaster movie, it was terrible,” she told Talk to the Press.

“We started to hear explosions, from the gas cannisters in people’s barbecues, it was really eerie.

“My daughter was really scared.

“Our house was evacuated; we had to pull some cardboard boxes out of a recycling bin and use them to try and sleep on the grass.”

Melissa said there were no hotels available to stay at, and all the shops were shut leaving them with just the clothes on their backs.



The family do not know when they will be allowed to return to Melissa’s grandma’s home.

The family have been sleeping in a tent in a friend’s garden in Sanguinet since Friday, but have no blow up mattresses and only a few blankets.

Sunny, a police officer, has contacted the British Embassy, but since they cannot reach it in Paris they are not able to access assistance.

“There’s absolutely no help for people like us, camping in gardens,” Sunny, a police officer said.

“Somebody needs to take ownership, either the insurance company, the British Embassy, or French officials,” he said.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Wildfires have led to the evacuation of about 220,000 people across France, with a fire burning in the Landes area west of Bordeaux razing 42,000 hectares.

French President Emmanuel Macron said France was experiencing “completely unprecedented” wildfires, posing the “toughest since World War Two”.

News.title: Giant 23ft python crushes man, 35, to death and swallows him whole while walking home from party alone
News.content:
GRISLY END Giant 23ft python crushes man, 35, to death and swallows him whole while walking home from party alone

A MAN has been gorged alive by a giant python as he walked home from a party before horrified villagers discovered his body in the reptile’s stomach.

Hasim Lumbessy, 35, who spent the night drinking at a rural bar in North Maluku, Indonesia, walked alone in the early hours of Monday, July 27.



He was walking along a forested path at around 3am when the 23ft monster leapt out of the undergrowth clamping its jaws around his leg.

Hasim was unable to break free from the coiling reptile which eventually crushed him to death.



Relatives had begun to search the route on Monday afternoon after he failed to return home, according to Handres, Sula Islands Police Chief.

Handres said: “In the middle of the journey, they saw blood on the ground and then found the victim’s belongings, including a backpack, sling bag and sandals.

“The witnesses became concerned and documented the items. They decided to return to the village to inform the other locals. They then conducted a wider search.”

The search party focused on the woodland near Fatliwangka Road after following a trail of flattened grass leading into the forest and found a distortedly swollen snake.

Gruesome footage shows the locals slicing the belly of the beast open and finding Hasim’s body inside.

The villagers returned his body to his family for religious rites.



Sula Islands police has issued a warning to those working in their gardens or walking alone in the forest.

“This area remains a wildlife habitat,” Police Chief Handres said. “Therefore, we urge the public to be careful when going to their gardens; if possible, they should go to the forest in pairs rather than alone, to minimise the risk of similar incidents.”

It follows a similar incident in the exact same province just a a month ago when motorcycle rider Lifas, 25, was reportedly attacked by a 22ft python when he stopped on the side of a dirt road in North Maluku.

Meanwhile another incident saw Elisabet Yamalau, 44, killed by a 25ft python when she was tending her cattle.

She was only discovered when her husband found her partially inside the snake’s mouth.



The reticulated pythons can be found all throughout Southeast Asia and their diet ranges from cats, dogs, birds, humans and even other snakes.

They are the largest snake species in the world, which means they can squeeze humans to death.

Indonesia’s tropical climate and the rich food resources in the forests allows their population to balloon.

Ron Lilley, the “Snake Whisperer”, lives in Bali, Indonesia, and is a founding member of the Indonesian Herpetological Society.

He told The Sun: “Pythons are ambush predators, waiting in the undergrowth besides tails where animals and people walk by.”



They can strike and immediately wrap themselves around a human, he said, and constricting them until they can no longer breath.

“No crushing of bones is needed”

Ron had some survival tips if you ever are in danger zone with pythons.

“It may be possible to quickly raise one’s arm to prevent the snake wrapping itself only around one’s neck and face.”

Ron recalled one time he was attacked by this deadly reptile in an enclosure in the UK.



“I was on my own. It bit me on the shoulder but I managed to hit it on the nose with a scrubbing brush before it had a chance to wrap its coils around me.. Fortunately it let go immediately and I retired to the other end of the cage.”

“It’s teeth went through four layers of clothing and caused deep wounds.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“[My advice is] never walk alone in python country,. A few drops of alcohol may cause a python to release its bite if poured into the side of its mouth.”

News.title: Burnham warns of ‘difficult decisions’ on tax for social care… as PM says failing to fix system is ‘dereliction of duty’
News.content:
ANDY Burnham today braced taxpayers for “difficult decisions” to fund adult social care – saying he “could not forgive myself” if he failed to fix the broken system.

The new PM said he would first try to drive reform “within existing budgets” but would be “honest with people” if more cash was needed.



Social care in Britain is wildly expensive and often sees those in need of support forced to sell their homes to stump up costs.

Mr Burnham, whose own father suffers with dementia, said the failure of successive governments has been a “major dereliction of public duty”.



He said: “It’s shameful, to be honest, that politicians have put point scoring before fixing this issue, but that’s what’s happened.

“It’s created a feeling in Westminster that this is too difficult, and if you take it on, you’re taking on too big a political risk.”



Grilled if he would hike taxes to fund a new model, Mr Burnham said: “I think firstly, you have to do more with what you’ve got.

“But… some of what we’d want to do in the fullest sense will require difficult decisions.

“But we will be honest with people about those, we will put them before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people’s consent…”

Mr Burnham vowed to stick to Labour’s manifesto pledge not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.



It opens the door to other options including a widely-touted hike to inheritance tax.

While light on details, Mr Burnham said he wanted a “national conversation” on how to fix social care.

He has expedited a review by Baroness Louise Casey to report back next year.

He has also invited Kemi Badenoch and Sir Ed Davey to cross-party talks to find “common ground” on the issue.

Nigel Farage has slammed Mr Burnham for cutting Reform out of the roundtable.



He fumed: “If Andy Burnham is serious about putting politics aside to solve Britain’s biggest problems, it’s remarkable that he’s chosen to ignore Reform.

“He is conspiring behind closed doors with the failed political establishment to foist further tax rises on the country.

“The fact Ed Davey and Kemi Badenoch are going along with this tells you all you need to know. This is the uniparty in action.”

News.title: Brit woman’s body found stuffed in suitcase in abandoned building in Athens by homeless man sparking Interpol probe
News.content:
BODY CASE MYSTERY Brit woman’s body found stuffed in suitcase in abandoned building in Athens by homeless man sparking Interpol probe

A BRITISH woman has mysteriously been found dead inside a suitcase dumped in an abandoned building in Greece.

The 38-year-old woman’s remains were discovered by a homeless man in Athens with the grim find sparking an Interpol probe.

The Brit’s body was found on Evelpidon Street in the neighbourhood of Kypseli on July 18, shortly after 1pm.



A homeless man who found the case said he followed a foul smell inside the building which had been deserted for at least two years.



He entered a room inside and found the suitcase on the ground with a human limb visible from the outside.

It is estimated that the Brit had been dead for at least six days before she was found.

Police rushed to the scene but couldn’t identify the woman as she reportedly had no tattoos or identification on her.

They announced she was aged around 30, approximately 5ft 4in with reddish hair tied in a bun and wearing black shorts and a T-shirt.

Her shorts reportedly had French university insignia on them which led investigators to believe she wasn’t a local Greek resident.

There were no clear signs of a struggle or any visible wounds on the woman.

An autopsy is expected to be carried out in the coming days to determine how she died.



The mysterious nature of her death sparked an instant probe by Greek officials who called on Interpol and US investigators to help.

Interpol informed the Hellenic Police on Monday that the body belonged to a British woman based on DNA testing.

Investigators are still yet to name the woman but say she had travelled to Greece on a plane via Cyprus after coming from the US.

They are now trying to piece together her final days including speaking to anyone who may have been with her before her death.

Police are yet to identify a suspect.



Interpol typically get involved in such cases when a national police force requests international cooperation for cross-border crimes.

News.title: Travellers are more likely to get a train between cities than fly despite longer travel times, new poll finds
News.content:
TRAVELLERS are more likely to get a train between cities than fly – despite expecting it to cost more and take longer.

A poll of 2,000 adults found 60 per cent would consider going by rail for journeys such as London to Glasgow and Aberdeen to Manchester.



In comparison, only 13 per cent would opt for flying between cities.

While 54 per cent think wheels on tracks offer more choice and flexibility than wings, and 61 per cent consider it to be better for the environment.



This is also supported by the Steer report, which found nearly four in 10 (37 per cent) believe train journeys are more reliable for longer domestic journeys than flights.

While 33 per cent find it more relaxing than other modes of transport, according to the General Public Tracker.



The research was published by transport consultancy Steer and commissioned by Rail Delivery Group as part of the wider ‘Clearing the Air’ report which compared rail and domestic air travel across seven key GB routes.

When comparing data from the rail industry’s Latest Earnings Networked Nationally Overnight (LENNON) system with air fare data from the Official Airline Guide (OAG), it found that despite travellers expecting a train journey between London and Manchester to cost £88, this trip set passengers back an average of £45 in 2025.



While OAG figures show a flight between the two cities cost £115, before extras such as seats or luggage – more than the £82.55 travellers expected it to cost.

Jacqueline Starr, executive chair and chief executive officer at Rail Delivery Group, said: “This research highlights the benefits rail can offer passengers, from lower costs and lower carbon emissions to more time that can be spent relaxing or staying productive.

“With frequent services connecting cities across Britain, rail offers a convenient, flexible and attractive way to travel”.

The research also found across the routes studied, passengers saved an average of £147 per journey by travelling via tracks instead of in the sky.

After the additional costs of the journey are included such as baggage, transfers and airport charges, this means travelling by plane costs 71 per cent more on average than travelling by train.

While those travelling between London and Newcastle can save an average of an hour going by train instead of flying.



For a business traveller making the London–Newcastle journey once a week, that adds up to the equivalent of a full working day every month.

The report also claims an estimated 93 per cent of a rail journey can be spent working, reading, relaxing or staying connected compared with just 33 per cent of a domestic flight journey once checking in, security and boarding time are taken into account.

As a result, passengers travelling by train gain an average of three hours more usable time per journey than those who fly.

The research comes as the Government rolls out its Great British Summer Savings scheme, with a temporary VAT reduction on eligible family attractions and days out helping households get more value from leisure trips across Great Britain this summer.

Andrew Stokes, director at VisitEngland, added: “There’s something special about visiting the treasures of our nations and regions by train.



“Whether it’s a cultural city break, a set jetting stay or a trip to one of our picturesque coastal or rural destinations, travelling by rail offers an easy, efficient and environmentally friendly way to explore more and enjoy spectacular scenery along the way.”

News.title: When is the next bank holiday? Date for final summer bank holiday of 2026 confirmed
News.content:
AS the summer holidays roll on, millions of hardworking Brits are already looking ahead to their next well-deserved long weekend.

Whether you are planning a late summer barbecue, a quick seaside getaway, or simply fancy a relaxing extra day on the sofa, the summer bank holiday is the perfect opportunity to recharge.



But if you feel like you have been waiting a remarkably long time since our last public holiday back in May, you aren’t imagining things.

When is the next bank holiday?

For those living in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the next bank holiday will take place on Monday, August 31, 2026.



If that feels exceptionally late in the season, that is because it is.

By law, the summer bank holiday in these nations always falls on the final Monday of August.



Because the month of August began on a Saturday this year, the last Monday falls on the 31st – the absolute latest possible date the bank holiday can legally occur.

This quirk of the calendar means there is an unusually long 14-week gap between the Spring Bank Holiday, which took place at the end of May, and this upcoming long weekend.

It also means that for many families, the bank holiday will land just days before children are due to return to school for the autumn term in early September.

After this date passes, the next nationwide public holidays won’t arrive until Christmas Day and Boxing Day in December.



When is the summer bank holiday in Scotland?

If you live north of the border, you will not have to wait nearly as long for your extra day off.

In Scotland, the summer bank holiday takes place almost a full month earlier, falling on Monday, August 3, 2026.

The reason for this split dates back over half a century.

Originally, the Bank Holidays Act of 1871 created a uniform summer bank holiday on the first Monday of August for the entire UK.

But by the late 1960s, politicians in Westminster realised that moving the English and Welsh holiday to the end of the month would create a better spread of days off across the year.



Following trials, it was officially enshrined into law by the Bank and Financial Dealings Act in 1971, but Scotland decided to keep the original tradition alive.

Because Scottish schools typically break up for their summer holidays earlier than those in England and Wales, an early August holiday remains a much better fit for their traditional academic calendar.

Does my employer have to give me the day off?

It’s a common misconception that all workers are legally entitled to take bank holidays off.

The reality is that there is no automatic statutory right to paid leave on public holidays.

Whether you get the day off entirely depends on the terms of your employment contract.



Full-time workers in the UK are legally entitled to 28 days of paid annual leave.

Many employers choose to structure this as 20 days of regular flexible leave, plus the eight standard bank holidays.

If your contract clearly states this is the case, you should have the Monday off.

But if you work in sectors such as retail, healthcare, hospitality, or the emergency services, bank holidays are often treated as standard working days.

Your contract might simply state you have 28 days of flexible annual leave, meaning you could easily be rostered to work on August 31.



If you are required to work on a bank holiday, there is also no legal requirement for your employer to pay you a higher rate, such as “time-and-a-half” or double pay.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

While many companies still offer this extra cash as a welcome perk, it’s entirely at the employer’s discretion.

Always check your contract or speak to your HR department if you are unsure of your rights.

News.title: Manchester live: Man 'trapped by tram' suffers possible life-changing injuries
News.content:
A tram is halted within the police cordon on Market Street

The incident happened on Market Street, one of Manchester city centre's busiest shopping areas, with police and paramedics spotted at the scene

Man suffers possible life-changing injuries in Manchester as he's 'trapped by tram'

A huge cordon was in place in Manchester city centre as emergency services responded to a major "police incident".

The incident happened in Market Street, one of Manchester's main shopping areas, as a man in his 50s was taken to hospital with "possibly life-changing injuries" after reportedly being trapped between a tram and the platform.

News.title: France wildfires live: Astonishing arrests as 42C heatwave threatens Bordeaux
News.content:
A handful of people have been arrested for allegedly taking advantage of those affected by wildfires in south-west France, which have forced more than 220,000 people to flee

Astonishing arrests have been made as firefighters continue to battle wildfires that have ravaged 42,000 hectares of south-west France and spread into parts of the Bordeaux metropolitan area.

More than 220,000 people in the Gironde region have been evacuated over the past week in what has been France's largest peacetime evacuation.

But while many have sought refuge in evacuation centres, a handful of people have instead found themselves in police custody. A man was arrested after allegedly "posing" as a psychologist offering support to those affected by the fires in exchange for payment, local police told Sky News.

Two men were arrested several days ago on suspicion of "stealing food and supplies" intended for those affected by the wildfires, the broadcaster reported. Officers have been standing outside evacuation centres and fire-ravaged areas to keep people safe and ensure restricted zones are protected.

Although the regional prefecture said the wildfires remain "stabilised", with "several flare-ups" brought under control overnight, officials said weather conditions remain "unfavourable" today. Temperatures could climb to a scorching 42C in Bordeaux, national weather service Météo-France said.

News.title: Andy Burnham speech live: Emotional PM makes THREE key pledges to finally fix social care crisis
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is outlining how he will fix the creaking social care sector in a major speech this morning, and even invited Kemi Badenoch and Ed Davey into cross-party talks

Andy Burnham promised to fix the crisis-hit social care sector in a major speech this morning, and a new dementia tsar would be appointed.

The new Prime Minister outlined three key parts to his strategy:

Bringing forward the deadline for a review into social care Reviewing pay and career progression for care workers Working cross-party to try and find some kind of consensus

He warned the creaking system can no longer be used as a political football while the NHS and families looking after loved ones count the cost.

He invited Tory chief Kemi Badenoch and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey to urgent talks later today to discuss the problem governments have kicked into the long-grass for decades.

Ahead of his speech, Mr Burnham said: “Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue and to do that, we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward.”

News.title: Anyone with Sky, Tesco Mobile, EE, Vodafone and 02 mobile new warning over 'direct call'
News.content:
Anyone with Sky, Tesco Mobile, EE, Vodafone and 02 mobile new warning over 'direct call'

Massive rise in QR code scams where they gain access to accounts and order expensive items

View Image New scams are seeing criminals impersonate mobile phone companies (Image: Getty)

Anyone with a mobile phone deal is being warned about new scams which are hitting in 2026 - where scammers contact a person directly. BBC Radio 4 show You and Yours was told that people are being targeted with a direct call - and end up having expensive phones sent to their home ‘by accident’ which they then send back, but to the scammers.

‌



All UK mobile phone companies like Sky, Tesco Mobile, EE, Vodafone and 02 have been hit by the scams. Presenter Winifred Robinson said: “Thousands of people are receiving top of the range phones they didn’t order after being contacted by people they thought were from their phone company but who were in fact criminals. What happens is that the phone arrives and the criminals instruct their victims to put their phones in a bag and post it onto them.

‌



“Your phone company, meanwhile, thinks that it was you who ordered these phones and adds them to your bill. It’s a large-scale fraud - nearly 30,000 expensive phones were stolen in this way last year alone. Many people didn’t realise they’d been scammed until the phone bill arrived."

‌



One user told the show she had just been on the phone to Sky adjusting her phone bill when she got another call purporting to be from the provider. She said: “He was very helpful on the phone - he got the bill down. Then about three days later, I was on some step ladders on the wall, taking some ivy down. I answered my phone, the woman on the phone said it was Sky offering me 20 per cent off your bill.”

The victim said she was offered a free smartphone and was asked to give her email address and date of birth - and that was the end of the conversation. A few days later a brand new Samsung phone arrived in the post and earphones. The phone was worth £1,200 and the earbuds £200.

She added: “Later that day, a frantic phone call from the same woman - I recognised the voice and it was the same number on my phone. She said, ‘I’m so sorry, there’s been a problem at the depot. The phone and the earbuds were meant for another customer. I’m going to send you a QR code. Please can you take them down to the post office and send them back. And to say sorry we will send to £300 of Tesco vouchers.’”

‌



The victim took it to the post office, it was scanned and the label was printed out and the items sent. The QR code came from a WhatsApp account called ‘Sky Return’. Then another parcel arrived with the same phone and earbuds - another call came and the victim sent it back again.

She then had another call from the woman: “She was screaming down the phone, saying I hadn’t returned any of the phones, they were going to take all the money from my account and I’d stolen the phones.” The next day she called Sky, who said no one had called her from the company apart from the very original negotiations about her bill.

One user told the Mirror: “I had a call from Sky saying they wanted to cut my bill as so many customers had changed. They asked for my email address then said they’d sent me a pin code which I gave them. I then realised they hadn’t really given me any proof - so I immediately rang off and changed my posswords straight away. They’d got access through my stupidity, but I cut them off.”

‌



In some cases the criminals even turn up at the person’s front door as a courier saying they need to take the phones away, You and Yours reported - but this different method involves the QR codes. The QR code from the above scam went to a terraced house in South Liverpool.

A similar case involved Tesco Mobile, where the victim said 3G was being switched off and they need new Sim cards. They offered a deal on an Apple iPhone and watch - which the person declined, and soon they both arrived. Soon the QR code was sent.

She drove to a Tesco Mobile shop which told her they’d had hundreds of these scams. Victim Jenny took product ID codes before sending them off - so they were able to stop them being used in the UK.

Article continues below

Both Sky and Tesco Mobile accepted the pair had been victims of fraud. Reporter Catherine Earlam said: “If you’re interested in an offer, put down the phone, and call back your genuine provider to check and beware of QR codes on items you didn’t order."

News.title: Two Brits plunge 20ft to their deaths as Lanzarote hotel handrail collapses
News.content:
Two Brits plunge 20ft to their deaths as Lanzarote hotel handrail collapses

Darren Silcox, 56, and Nicholas Thomas, 54, both from Cwmbran, Wales, died after falling from a balcony at the Galeon Playa Apartments in the resort town of Costa Teguise in Lanzarote

View 2 Images Darren Silcox and Nicholas Thomas died after falling from a balcony at the Galeon Playa Apartments in Lanzarote (Image: Google)

Two Brits died after the handrail on their hotel balcony gave way in Lanzarote, an inquest heard.

‌



Darren Silcox, 56, and Nicholas Thomas, 54, both from Cwmbran, Wales, fell from a balcony at a Canary Islands flat.

‌



In October 2025, shop owner Darren and friend Nicholas tumbled from the balcony in the early hours of the morning while on holiday at the Galeon Playa Apartments.

‌



The pair plunged into the atrium stairwell in the resort town of Costa Teguise at 1.30am following a night out.

Dad-of-two Darren passed away two hours after the fall while Nicholas was flown back to Britain for treatment. He was later moved to University Hospital in Llandough but sadly died nearly 10 months later on July 10.

View 2 Images Spain's Civil Guard has initiated an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident (file photo) (Image: Getty Images)

‌



An investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fall has been launched by Spain’s Civil Guard, Wales Online reports.

Investigators are said to be looking at whether poor upkeep or insufficient safety measures contributed to the fatal accident.

Emergency crews rushed to the holiday apartments at around 1.30am after the two men fell. Medical teams who arrived at the location confirmed that the 56 year old man had succumbed to his injuries sustained in the fall.

‌



Opening an inquest into Mr Thomas' death, Gwent coroner Rose Farmer told the hearing he fell between 15ft and 22ft after a wooden bannister collapsed.

He was taken to Doctor Jose Molina Orosa Hospital on the island for initial treatment before he was flown back to the UK at the end of November.

A previous inquest into Mr Silcox's death revealed that he died from a traumatic brain injury, skull fractures and skull lacerations.

Article continues below

The proceedings have been postponed until April 14 next year when a joint inquest is anticipated to take place.

News.title: B&M £25 compact gadget dries laundry, prevents mould and improves air at home
News.content:
B&M £25 compact gadget dries laundry, prevents mould and improves air at home

How to enhance your home's air quality and avoid mould and damp with an affordable B&M device

View 3 Images Shoppers can get 16% off the item in stores (Image: Getty)

B&M is selling a compact gadget designed to address common household issues, including mould and damp. The budget high street store regularly impresses shoppers with its range of affordable homeware and electronics.

‌



Available to view online and buy in stores, shoppers can get the Blaupunkt Compact Dehumidifier 1L at B&M for £25. The device was originally on sale for £30, but thanks to a 16% off discount, customers can get it for less as part of its 'Air Care' department.

‌



B&M says that the "mains powered" Blaupunkt Compact Dehumidifier "removes excess moisture from the air, combatting damp, condensation, mildew and musty odours". It extracts up to 300ml of excess moisture per day.

‌



It comes with a one-litre water tank that features an in-built automatic shut-off when it gets full. For an extra touch, the gadget has several colour LED mood lights, including purple, blue, red, yellow and green, which can all change or remain constant.

B&M is also selling a Blaupunkt Digital Air Purifier for £39. In the product description, the store says: "The Blaupunkt Air Purifier removes up to 99% of airborne allergens as small as 0.3 microns, including grass pollen, ragweed pollen, household dust, dust mite debris, pet dander, smoke and odours through its three-stage filtration system: sponge filter, HEPA filter and activated carbon filter.

View 3 Images B&M's Blaupunkt Compact Dehumidifier 1L (Image: B&M)

‌



"To further assist the air purification process, the Blaupunkt Air Purifier also includes an ioniser feature, which works by creating a static charge around the airborne contaminants. Once charged with static, these particles (dust, allergens, pet dander etc,) fall from the air."

How can dehumidifiers dry laundry, prevent mould, and improve air quality?

A dehumidifier can help dry laundry by pulling moisture from the air and speeding up the evaporation of water from wet clothes. It also helps prevent indoor areas from getting damp, prevents unpleasant odours, and is more energy-efficient than a regular tumble dryer.

Dehumidifiers enhance the quality of indoor air by removing excess moisture, which prevents the growth of mould, mildew, and dust mites. Although they help decrease these allergens, they don't filter out airborne pollutants such as dust, smoke, or VOCs. To achieve a thorough air cleaning, many homes use a dehumidifier in conjunction with a specific air purifier.

Article continues below

View 3 Images B&M is also selling the Blaupunkt Digital Air Purifier (Image: B&M)

Dust mites and mould spores thrive in high-humidity conditions. By lowering the moisture levels, you effectively starve them.

Getting rid of damp, humid air also helps to eliminate the musty odours often found in poorly ventilated areas like basements or bathrooms. Reducing humidity not only makes the air feel cooler but can also make it easier for people with asthma or respiratory problems to breathe.

News.title: Geoff Hurst finally finds out how he was spotted as England potential by Alf Ramsey 60 years later
News.content:
1966 legend Geoff Hurst has just learnt for the very first time how he was spotted as a potential England player by manager Sir Alf Ramsey.

Incredibly, it was in a League Cup second round game for West Ham against Division Three minnows Mansfield Town on October 13, 1965 in front of just 11,590 people. Hurst said he was “completely unaware” that Ramsey was even at the game.

The match was played five months before Hurst made his England debut and, of course, later that year he became the first man to ever score a hat-trick in a World Cup final - exactly 60 years ago.

View 7 Images Eton Manor legend Graham Phillips (right) with respected author and historian Grant Bage (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



England icon was left penniless and forced to sell jumpers from his 1-bed flat READ MORE :

The extraordinary revelation was uncovered by Ramsey’s biographer Grant Bage in a series of new interviews. Ramsey told one of his closest friends, respected amateur team manager Charlie Phillips how he was impressed by how Hurst handled long balls from Bobby Moore that night.

Two of Hurst’s goals at Wembley in the 4-2 win over West Germany came from long passes from Moore. Now Bage, who spent six years researching and writing his biography The Unseen Sir Alf, has informed Hurst who had no idea Ramsey was even at that particular match.

Hurst replied: “I was completely unaware that this happened, which completely changed not only my football life, but my life. October 13th was obviously a very lucky day as I got married on that day 64 years ago. Thank you again.”

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst in his West Ham days (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

‌



Bage said: “Even sixty years on, we keep unearthing new information about Sir Alf Ramsey and the 1966 World Cup. It’s incredible that these ‘nuggets’ are coming out so many years later. It’s amazing that, on an October night at Upton Park at a League cup match against Mansfield, that Alf formulated his thoughts and plans for the World Cup.

“Football was rarely filmed in the 1960s, so the England manager slogged his way round watching hundreds of games, just to work out who the best English players were. And Hurst wasn’t even the player he was going to watch. But now we know that what he saw that night sowed the seeds of World Cup glory.

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst gave Mirrorman Andy Lines exclusive interview before World Cup (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



"Alf Ramsey conquered world football through hard work and attention to detail. Just imagine if he hadn’t bothered to go to that game. Geoff Hurst didn’t even know about it which makes it all the remarkable.”

Bage found the new information after meeting Graham Phillips - son of Charlie Phillips the manager of East London non-league side Eton Manor. Hurst, who played 499 games for West Ham, has little memory of the match which was played almost 61 years ago. Ramsey was coaching them at the time and Charlie became a great friend and trusted confidante.

Bage said: “I can’t thank Graham enough for coming forward with all this detailed extra information. It helps us learn more about how Alf slotted together the only England team to ever win the World Cup."

View 7 Images Eton Manor legend and stalwart Graham Phillips (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



Graham said: “Alf and my dad Charlie had two long telephone conversations, both instigated by Alf, in the immediate aftermath of the 1966 triumph. It was in these telephone discussions that Alf conveyed stories about the World Cup to Charlie.

“There were other conversations, but these were the main ones. But you have to understand that Charlie didn't sit us down after his chats with Alf and brief us on what had been said. The information came out from him gradually, on different occasions, like when we were sitting watching TV, or some relevant story had been in the paper.

“What I recall above all else is my father describing how Alf had, under the Upton Park floodlights, told me that he had witnessed ‘the second coming of Tommy Taylor’. That was a deeply significant comparison, which needs explaining for a modern audience.

“In March 1953 Tommy Taylor had signed for Manchester United, aged just 21. His 112 league goals, in a total of 166 league appearances, helped United win successive league championships in 1955-56, and 1956-57. In 19 senior appearances for England, he also scored 16 goals. Tragically, Tommy Taylor was then one of eight Manchester United players killed in the Munich air disaster of February 6, 1958, his 26th birthday having been reached the week before he died.

‌



View 7 Images Eton Manor legend Graham Phillips with respected author and historian Grant Bage (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

“Alf Ramsey was not prone to hyperbole, so for him to compare Geoff Hurst to Tommy Taylor was amazing: especially as Hurst was not even the main reason Ramsey had gone to watch this particular game. Alf told Charlie that Ronnie Boyce was the ‘intended’ prime target, and perhaps to take another look at Johnny Byrne.

“What must also be remembered by modern football fans, to make sense of this, is that in the mid-1960s there was very little filming of football. Most league games were also played either at 3pm on a Saturday, or on Tuesday or Wednesday evenings early in the season, before cup competitions had got going.

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst scores England's controversial third goal (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“Consequently, if Alf Ramsey wanted to review any promising English player, he needed to attend hundreds of games himself: which is why the England manager undertook this particular scouting mission to West Ham’s unpromising midweek, early-stage league cup game against lower-league opposition.

“Alf told his friend Charlie that, as it happened, Alf had phoned West Ham out of courtesy to tell them he would be attending. Unfortunately, he did not manage to speak to their manager, Ron Greenwood, so did not know whether his message had got through. “Ironically, HAD Ramsey talked to Greenwood, he may not even have made the trip! As things turned out, neither Ronnie Boyce nor Johnny Byrne would play that night, against Third Division Mansfield Town, in round three of the League Cup. Luckily though, Alf went anyway.”

News.title: OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies
News.content:
OpenAI has revealed a cyber-attack carried out by rogue ChatGPT agents went further than just one company.

Hugging Face was thought to be the only victim of the unprecedented hack - but OpenAI now admits its bot attacked several "publicly-available services".

The out-of-control AI found four logins online which allowed it to access four separate, unnamed services.

Meanwhile, in an emergency briefing with hundreds of cyber security professionals, Hugging Face has described what it was like to be on the receiving end of the world's first fully autonomous AI hack.

The firm described how the AI worked at superhuman speed but also made strange decisions and mistakes that no human hacker would have made.

Hugging Face, which is like an app store for AI tools, said the hacking agents worked relentlessly with thousands of different methods trialled simultaneously.

The company first revealed that it had been hacked, external by someone using powerful autonomous AI on 16 July and reported it to police.

Nearly a week later, OpenAI admitted it was its AI that had escaped a closed environment and attacked Hugging Face on its own during a test.

It was trying to find the answers to a hacking exam it had been set by OpenAI, and targeted Hugging Face.

On Wednesday OpenAI updated its statement to include the extra detail that the hack went further than first thought.

"The models identified and used publicly exposed credentials at the account-level on other publicly-available services. This includes four accounts on four services as part of the Hugging Face incident," the company said.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for clarity on whether "publicly-available services" means companies.

News.title: The evidence that shows today's 20-somethings really do have it worse than previous generations
News.content:
Young people in their 20s are facing a tougher start to adulthood than any generation in almost half a century, according to analysis of UK data on housing, employment and wealth, carried out for the BBC.

More than 40% of 25-year-olds are now living with their parents, their wages have stagnated and employment has fallen, show the figures which compare key metrics for different generations at age 25 stretching back to the early 1980s.

The findings are underscored by the experiences of young people themselves who, along with parents, have contacted BBC Your Voice about their circumstances, with many saying they were frustrated about being accused by older generations of not trying hard enough.

We asked the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) to gather and analyse government data, external, for the first time, to see if this generation really does have it worse.

The biggest change it found was where those in their 20s are living.

News.title: Data centres could pay hundreds of millions in deposits for power demands
News.content:
Ofgem has proposed new measures which could see developers of data centres made to pay hundreds of millions of pounds up front.

The British energy regulator said a refundable fee should be charged for projects that want to connect to the network, amid mounting demand for connections to the electricity grid.

It is proposing developers pay a deposit between Â£237,500 to Â£712,500 per megawatt - meaning data centres seeking 1 gigawatt (GW) of power would have to pay hundreds of millions up front, paid back if the project was completed.

The proposal follows growing opposition in parts of the country to plans for new data centres, which are needed to power the artificial intelligence boom.

Data centres are large buildings which house computer servers used to store and process data and run the digital services which power the internet.

Ofgem has started a consultation on its proposals, which will run until 16 September.

It said the amount of electricity capacity being requested by projects seeking to connect to the grid had risen from 41 GW to 125 GW in the past year, reflecting a sharp increase in demand.

This is significantly more than double 2025's peak electricity demand in Britain of around 46 GW.

The regulator said the projects would have to hit key milestones to keep their place in the grid connection queue, which has seen a surge in demand.

An increasing number of centres have been built around the world in recent years to provide the computing power needed to train and run AI systems.

But they are controversial, especially for people who live near them.

Residents have raised concerns about noise, electricity demand and the large amounts of water sometimes used to cool the high-performance chips that generate vast amounts of heat.

News.title: Brits urged to avoid dangerous plug adaptors this summer - what to watch out for
News.content:
Brits going on holiday abroad this summer have been warned to watch out for dangerous travel adaptors, after an investigation suggested thousands may be for sale online.

Consumer safety group Electrical Safety First (ESF) tested 14 products from AliExpress, Amazon Marketplace, eBay and TikTok Shop - and found they all failed to meet UK safety requirements.

It said in some instances the devices could expose users to risk of serious electric shock or electrocution.

AliExpress, Amazon, eBay and TikTok all said they had removed the products ESF flagged from sale, and that they treated product safety as a top priority.

But Giuseppe Capanna, ESF product safety engineer, urged those "heading abroad this summer to think before they buy".

"What looks like a bargain could come at a much higher cost," he warned.

Capanna also said shoppers should buy travel adaptors from trusted retailers "so they can travel with confidence".

ESF tested six regular travel adaptors and eight universal adaptors it suspected could pose safety concerns.

To be sold in the UK, adaptors must not have accessible live parts and only one set of pins should come out at a time.

But the charity found multiple sets could be exposed simultaneously in six out of eight of the universal adaptors it tested.

None of the eight met the required dimensions and mechanical strength, while some pins snapped off under force during tests.

ESF said anyone who tried to remove a broken pin from a socket would be at risk of electric shock.

News.title: Amber heat health alerts in force as heatwave reaches 35C peak
News.content:
Amber and yellow heat health alerts are in force as parts of the UK endure the fourth widespread heatwave of the year so far.

Temperatures are forecast to peak on Wednesday with readings as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest places.

Though the heatwave will come to a quick end for many on Thursday, well above-average temperatures in the mid- to high 20s Celsius will persist into the weekend.

The hot weather, paired with a significant lack of rainfall, will exacerbate conditions in many of the driest areas.

News.title: Matcha and protein pivot pays off for Greggs as profits rise
News.content:
Greggs's pivot towards healthier products and trending drinks has helped it boost sales, with the bakery chain reporting a 20% rise in profit over the first half of the year.

Greggs, the UK's largest fast-food chain, has launched a range of new products this year, many of which latch onto trends such as high-protein salads and matcha.

Greggs's chief executive Roisin Currie previously told BBC News the rise of weight-loss drugs has led customers to to look for "smaller portions", which could affect its bottom line.

Total sales for the bakery topped Â£1.1 billion for the 26 weeks to the end of June - 7.2% higher than the same period a year ago.

Pre-tax profit for the first half of the year was Â£76.0m - up from Â£63.5m for the first six months of 2025.

Currie said the company was "broadening and innovating our menu in line with changing tastes and trends".

The company relaunched its salad range in May, "adding protein and increased choice for customers".

It is also trying to appeal to "new and younger customers" through its new iced matcha lattes, and to health-conscious consumers by making nutritional information on its labels clearer.

Greggs, which has more UK outlets than McDonald's, opened 34 stores in the first half of 2026. That brings the total to 2,773, taking into account 31 store closures.

More than half of the new openings were in areas with no Greggs stores within a mile. A similar proportion opened away from the High Street in locations including petrol forecourts, supermarkets, retail parks, hospitals and university campuses, it said.

Currie said Greggs is monitoring customer behaviour to ensure new stores boost visits "without cannibalising existing shop sales".

She also said Greggs had no price rises planned after its breakfast, lunch and "big" deals went up in May, following multiple hikes last year.

"Our prices are in a good place and we will now be working hard to protect the consumer and making sure that we can offer that value throughout the rest of the year," she said.

News.title: BTS withdraw from Grammys, a month after Asian pop prize introduced
News.content:
Korean pop group BTS have announced they will not submit their music for consideration at the 2027 Grammy Awards.

The news came in a co-ordinated Instagram post, with all seven members of the band uploading an identical statement.

"We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year," a translation of the message read. "I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language."

The band were widely expected to be in competition for some of the Grammys' major categories, including album of the year, after their comeback record, Arirang, became one of the year's biggest-sellers.

The lead single Swim, a US number one, was also predicted to be in contention for song of the year.

But the English-language lyrics would have excluded it from the new best Asian pop music performance prize, which was announced last month.

Under Grammy rules, songs nominated for the category must contain "meaningful use" of an Asian language. More than 80% of the lyrics on Arirang are sung in English.

The introduction of the new award met with mixed reception in K-Pop spaces online. Many fans complained that, instead of celebrating Asian artists, the Grammys had pigeonholed them.

By choosing to mention both region and language in their statement, the members of BTS - RM, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook, Jin and J-Hope - appeared to reflect that concern.

They ended their statement with a message to their fans, known as the BTS Army.

"Thank you to Army and everyone who is always with us," the group said.

The Recording Academy, which organises the ceremony, has yet to respond. BBC News has contacted them for a statement.

News.title: I turned down Love Island and won silver at the Commonwealth Games
News.content:
In another reality, swimmer Katie Shanahan might have been looking for love on her favourite TV show - but instead made a decision that would lead her to a silver medal at the Commonwealth Games.

The 22-year-old told BBC Scotland News she was offered the chance to appear on Love Island last year, the reality dating show where singletons are placed in a Spanish villa.

However Glasgow-born Shanahan turned down the offer of sunshine in Mallorca, choosing instead to focus on her sport at the Tollcross swimming centre.

Last Friday she claimed silver in the 200m breaststroke on the opening night of the Games.

News.title: Unauthorised airport car park grows  despite stop notice
News.content:
Jane Fuller, from Hadleigh, Suffolk, said her daughter's car had been left unlocked for 22 hours in April.

"My daughter has an app on her phone and she managed to lock it from Croatia," she said.

"When we eventually got back to the car park, we had to hunt for it in the dark. We found it parked on top of rubble. It was a shocking experience," she added.

Deb Jordan, from Ely, Cambridgeshire, said the transport to the car park from the airport in May with her family had been "an absolute hazard".

She said passengers had been left stranded at Stansted Airport for more than three hours after landing.

"They piled two busloads of angry people onto one small transit minibus," she said.

"Luggage was piled on top of passengers. I had a pushchair wedged over my head."

On arrival at the car park, Jordan said the family had been given the keys to someone else's car.

Several customers said they had been charged an additional Â£20 on arrival at the car park to pay for transport to the Radisson Blu Hotel at Stansted Airport, from where they then had to walk to the airport.

They were also told to meet at the location at the airport on their return after ringing drivers at New Farm once they had landed.

News.title: Ticket prices set to rise by 15p as Heathrow able to recover runway project money
News.content:
Heathrow Airport will be allowed to charge airlines more for its services to recover money spent on the early stages of its third runway project.

The aviation regulator is permitting the airport to claw back up to Â£320m through higher airport charges to airlines for each passenger. This is likely to end up adding 15p to ticket prices in 2028, rising to 30p in later years.

A bidder which unsuccessfully put forward a rival design involving a shorter runway, Arora Group's Heathrow West, will also be allowed to recover Â£4.1m pounds in costs.

The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) and Heathrow said safeguards would be put in place to protect consumers from unjustified costs.

At this stage, the costs being recovered are only for the early planning and design of the runway during 2025 and 2026.

How much the cost of actually building the runway will add to ticket prices won't be clear for some time.

Tim Johnson, the CAA's director of consumers and markets, told the BBC: "We've announced that the first tranche of costs, which is to help with the planning of this, can be recovered from passengers. That's up to a maximum of Â£320m."

Heathrow airport will also be able to collect Heathrow West's costs up to November last year by adding to its airport charges.

The CAA said allowing these costs to be recouped will result in the maximum airport charge per passenger increasing by around 15 pence in 2028, rising to an estimated 30 pence in the following years.

A Heathrow spokesperson said: "This project is about making travel more affordable and giving passengers more choice, while providing a real economic boost to every region and nation of the country."

"We are carefully considering the CAA proposals and will make investment decisions accordingly," the spokesperson added.

In November, the government announced it preferred the Â£33bn scheme put forward by the airport over Arora's alternative plan.

At the time, the Department for Transport said Heathrow's own proposal offered the most deliverable option, and the "greatest likelihood" of getting a decision on planning approval within this parliament.

The CAA's director of consumers and markets, Tim Johnson, said today's decision "strikes a balance between supporting the delivery of benefits to consumers through timely progress on Heathrow expansion, whilst also protecting them from undue increases in costs".

The regulator said "safeguards" designed to monitor cost efficiency would include transparency and cost reporting requirements, and assurance by independent experts.

Airlines often complain that Heathrow is the world's most most expensive hub airport, and have repeatedly voiced concern that the airport's expansion plans will make it pricier.

The government hopes for a planning decision by 2029.

Plans for a third runway stretch back decades, with the government backing the plans in 2003.

However, the idea has also long faced opposition from climate campaigners, many local residents, and several politicians.

They worry an additional runway will increase air pollution, noise pollution, and breach the government's legally binding climate commitments.

News.title: Polanski says guillotine re-post was mistake but refuses to apologise
News.content:
Zack Polanski has refused three times to apologise to Nigel Farage for re-posting a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said the image showed a "photo of man calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage", which he said could be an "incitement to murder".

The Green Party of England and Wales leader was reported to the Met over the photo, which he then deleted, but told the BBC he had not been contacted by police.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said he would not apologise for an "inadvertent mistake" that he said Farage had amplified in a "fundamentally dishonest way".

The row kicked off on Monday evening when Polanski shared the photo, which he said was the fifth image in a series of 20 from a party, having accepted a request to collaborate with the Instagram account of a photographer at the event.

Posting a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."

Asked if he wanted to apologise to Farage, Polanski said: "Well, if I'd done it deliberately I'd be apologising but because this was a mistake I think the important thing is that I point out this was a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence, and also crucially I make a commitment to be better on social media."

Asked for a second time whether he would apologise, Polanski refused because he said Farage had cropped the image to make it look like he had posted it himself, which he said was "fundamentally dishonest" and only amplified the problem.

Saying he had received a death threat earlier on Tuesday, Polanski added: "The ramping up of the language to say 'this is incitement to murder me' feels like that's also putting me in a dangerous spot."

Given a third chance to apologise, Polanski doubled down and said: "You know as well as I do that as soon as I do that Nigel Farage would run all over social media saying he was correct about incitement to murder and this would all ramp up again.

"I think it's important that I draw a line and don't play his game... It is important that he's kept safe, it is important we condemn political violence, but I also recognise this as the political attack that it is."

"If Nigel Farage wants to apologise for all the times that he's put other people in danger then I will be happy to make an apology," Polanski added.

The Green leader explained he had not read the slogan on the T-shirt when he accepted the collaboration because "what I was seeing was people partying" and he only noticed the man was wearing a rainbow hat as he flicked through.

"It feels quite surreal to be having this conversation," he said, adding: "I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it's quite obvious I've not done anything wrong other than make an inadvertent mistake."

The Metropolitan Police said there was no update on the complaint they had received on Monday.

On Tuesday, Reform asked the monitoring officer from the Greater London Authority, where Polanski is an elected member, to investigate whether he had breached the code of conduct.

Keith Prince, a Reform London Assembly Member, said: "To say that he was unaware of what he was promoting is frankly risible."

A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: "It's truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won't apologise for inciting murder.

"He admits it was wrong. He admits it's dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party."

Asked about the row on Tuesday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there was a "duty on all politicians to be careful about what they post", especially in light of the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe earlier this month.

News.title: 'I'm fortunate I survived a stage 4 diagnosis when so many didn't make it'
News.content:
It's been a decade of treatments, trials and many tears for Lynette McHendry â but also hope and resilience.

Diagnosed with an aggressive form of breast cancer 10 years ago, aged 37, she has defied the odds to face down a disease that made her feel "invisible", while also fighting for access to the treatment that ultimately saved her life, but was not available to her in Northern Ireland.

Ten years ago, a stage four cancer diagnosis may have felt like a "death sentence," but Lynette's story also points towards the advancements in treatment and drugs, which she believes will allow more women to live longer with the disease.

"I am fortunate to have survived a stage four diagnosis when so many of my friends and patients I met along the way didn't make it," she said.

One of those friends was Julie Ann Lillis, who died in 2023.

She, Lynette and Anne McBrien were part of a group called Beaconbridge which called for a special audit of how many women in Northern Ireland were living with stage four breast cancer.

News.title: Woman found dead was murdered, police say, as man's death still 'unexplained'
News.content:
Police are treating the death of a woman in Renfrewshire, who was found alongside the body of a man, as murder.

Stacy Mair, 35, was found near Corsliehill Road in Houston at about 07:50 on Monday after police received a report of concern for a person.

The death of the 43-year-old man is still being treated as unexplained pending the results of a post-mortem examination - however police have said there is nothing to suggest anyone else was involved.

Police Scotland's major investigation team and local officers are carrying out "extensive" inquiries to establish the full circumstances.

News.title: Report on Jewish diaspora finds biggest rise in antisemitism in UK
News.content:
The UK recorded the biggest rise in antisemitic incidents last year of any country with a major Jewish population outside Israel, according to a new report.

The report, published by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism, external, also found that 2025 had been the deadliest year for Jews living outside Israel in more than three decades.

The task force is a group of organisations representing the seven largest Jewish diaspora communities.

It found that antisemitism in Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the UK and the US â which together are home to more than 90% of the world's Jewish population outside Israel â remained at record levels.

Reported antisemitic incidents across the seven countries have risen by 136% since 2022, the year before the Hamas attacks on southern Israel and the start of the war in Gaza, while violent incidents have risen by 97%.

The UK was one of only three countries where reported antisemitic incidents increased in 2025, alongside Argentina and Germany. Incidents recorded in the UK rose by 5% compared with the previous year â the largest increase among the seven countries.

Although reported incidents fell in 2025 in the US, Australia, Canada and France compared with 2024, every country remained significantly above levels before 7 October 2023.

In 2025, 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks, the highest annual death toll since the bombing of a Jewish community centre in the Argentinian capital Buenos Aires in 1994.

News.title: Burnham has no scope to increase borrowing, think tank warns
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet his pledges on defence and the cost of living, a major think tank has said.

Burnham has announced a series of new measures since assuming office last week, including cuts to electricity bills and bringing the bus fare cap in most parts of England back down to Â£2.

But the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) warned the public finances will continue to be squeezed by more persistent inflation as a result of the Iran war.

It questioned whether Burnham had "fully thought through" how his promises would be paid for, but said the prime minister will have to raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere.

Stephen Millard, Niesr's deputy director for macroeconomics, said: "There's clearly no scope for increasing borrowing, so it is about choices."

Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people - including income tax, VAT and national insurance contributions - which Burnham has said he will uphold.

Millard said Niesr was advocating for cost-of-living measures to be funded through higher taxes â "which could involve tax reform rather than higher marginal rates" â or spending cuts.

He said: "People have talked a lot about the welfare bill â that is an obvious place to look.

"The triple lock on pensions, that is very, very expensive, and will get more expensive as we age."

He also pointed to potentially reforming council tax to move towards a land value tax system, or scrapping some VAT exemptions.

"Once you've done all of that, then I'm afraid I would break the manifesto promise and would be looking at the income tax rate."

Niesr also said on Wednesday it expects inflation to keep rising until February 2027, peaking at 3.8% before falling back to the Bank of England's 2% target.

The think tank said in its latest economic outlook that it does not believe the central bank will cut interest rates until 2028.

Its Director David Aikman said that "treading water is not enough" to prevent the national debt from rising.

"Every major shock this century has ratcheted the debt ratio higher, and none of that increase has been reversed," he said.

The Treasury said the government will stick to its fiscal rules while investing in "the public services people rely on".

"Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security," a spokesperson said.

News.title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' mid interview
News.content:
A French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.

Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.

Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".

The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.

Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises.

"It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."

Ukraine launched a wave of overnight drone strikes deep into Russia early Wednesday, hitting a major logistics hub belonging to e-commerce Wildberries in the Ryazan region.

At least nine Wildberries facilities have been targeted in the past two weeks as Kyiv steps up attacks on warehouses, after accusing the firm of helping to bolster Vladimir Putin’s war machine.

According to Data Insight analyst Sergei Semko, goods destroyed by strikes on Wildberries warehouses in Moscow and Tambov regions alone were worth up to an estimated $2.9 billion.

open image in gallery Smoke rises from a Wildberries warehouse near Saint Petersburg after being hit by Ukrainian drones on July 24 ( AFP/Getty )

What is Wildberries?

Wildberries is Russia's largest online marketplace. It has been called the country's equivalent of Amazon, as its business model resembles a mix of Amazon Marketplace, eBay, and Temu.

Founded in 2004 by Tatyana Kim, who is now Russia's richest woman, the company has since become the dominant e-commerce platform in Russia and several neighbouring countries.

Hosting millions of third-party sellers, the platform sells almost everything, from electronics to groceries.

It operates a vast network of warehouses, sorting centres, and logistics hubs across Russia.

Now, its facilities are being deliberately targeted by Ukrainian drones.

Why is Ukraine attacking Wildberries?

Kyiv’s reasons for attacking Wildberries appear to be two-fold.

Ukrainian officials say that the company's warehouses and transport network is actively involved in storing or transport goods that ultimately support the Russian military, a claim Moscow denies.

Because Kyiv alleges that the company is part of Russia's wartime logistics and economic infrastructure, they insist Wildberries’ infrastructure is a legitimate target.

However, the attacks also appear to be part of an attempt to increase economic pressure on Russia.

An ‌executive at Ukraine’s leading arms producer, ​Fire Point, emphasised that Wildberries is being targeted partly because of ​its partnership with state-controlled bank VTB.

open image in gallery The four-year war in Ukraine continues to slow the Russian economy ( (Iryna Rybakova/Ukraine’s 93rd Mechanized Brigade via AP) )

In an interview posted on Monday, Denys Shtilerman, Fire Point’s co-founder and chief designer, described Wildberries as the largest borrower in Russia and said its demise would lead to the collapse of a large number of banks, including VTB.

Described as the “backbone” of what the Kremlin calls the Russian “platform economy,” Wildberries has been considered central to plans for economic growth after the government purchased a 5 per cent stake in the company earlier this year.

Together, Wildberries and competitor Ozon, account for economic activity worth around 8.5% of Russia's GDP.

They support around 4 million jobs, or more than 5% of Russia's workforce.

As the country continues to face a steadily-weakening rouble, and a steadily-increasing inflation rate, the central bank has cut its key interest rate to 14 per cent, highlighting the growing strain on Russia's wartime economy.

Continued Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries are set to further add to this pressure.

How has Russia responded?

For Russia, the attacks on Wildberries mark another severe economic blow amidst the increasing cost of sustaining its war in Ukraine.

The Kremlin has acknowledged it may have to financially prop up Wildberries, which has lost 10 per cent of its warehousing capacity and a huge amounts of stock as a result of Ukrainian attacks.

Meanwhile, the US Senate took the first steps toward passage of a sweeping Russian sanctions bill on Tuesday.

open image in gallery Zelensky met with congress on Tuesday to discuss further sanctions on Russian oil ( AFP/Getty )

After meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky, the bipartisan procedural vote secured an 86-12 majority.

The bill is set to penalise countries that continue to buy Russian oil, gas and other exports.

Every prime minister who enters Downing Street wants to ensure that by the time they go, they have left some sort of legacy – a mark of their premiership that has changed the country or the world for the better.

Andy Burnham has been clear from day one that he wants his legacy issue to be fixing the ongoing social care crisis in this country, but for him this is far more than just a matter of legacy – it is personal.

Just before he took over from Sir Keir Starmer, Mr Burnham gave an interview where he spoke movingly about the plight of his father who has Alzheimer’s disease. Heartbreakingly, he admitted that his father, who would have been so proud, does not even know his son has become prime minister.

As he opened an emotional speech to launch this latest push to solve local care issues, he was close to tears and speaking without notes as he talked movingly about how the experience with his father meant he and his family have the “experience of being on the inside” of this crisis.

It means that Mr Burnham himself has had first-hand experience of the postcode lottery that is social care for the elderly and the fact that those with money stand a much better chance of getting the care they need than those without.

Of course, as things stand, often the provision of much-needed care for the elderly in particular means that they have to sell their homes and use their savings to receive the level of support they deserve.

But beyond his tragic story of his father, this is personal for the new prime minister on another level.

Back in 2009, when he was health secretary in Gordon Brown’s government, Mr Burnham made an attempt to finally fix this problem with cross-party consensus.

He invited the then-Tory shadow health secretary Andrew Lansley for talks to discuss his idea for a levy when people die to help pay for social care.

Lansley came out of those talks and immediately went to the press with a full attack on Mr Burnham’s plans for a “death tax”.

Andy Burnham is willing to invest personal political capital in this issue ( Reuters )

It became a major political issue which helped bring about the defeat of Mr Brown’s government in 2010 and leave Labour in the wilderness for 14 years.

But, of course, the problem went unresolved and in the time that followed has just got worse.

As health secretary Yvette Cooper and Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey have both pointed out, since 1997 there have been 22 failed attempts to solve this problem.

Both these politicians also have personal stories – Ms Cooper with her mother’s dementia and Sir Ed with his disabled son – which show this problem touches people across parties and the whole country.

This is why Mr Burnham has gone out of his way to ask for an end of “political point scoring”, not only in this subject but in other areas too.

In bringing the Tories and Lib Dems on board again – despite the betrayal 17 years ago – he is effectively asking for a war time effort in resolving this crisis.

Mr Burnham is willing to invest personal political capital in this issue not just because he wants to be remembered as a great prime minister but because he knows from personal experience that this crisis cannot continue.

If it does then, as he himself warns, the NHS will collapse under the pressure.

News.title: Will there be a World Cup boycott? Infantino’s deal with Trump empire pushes football to the brink
News.content:
