Sports.title: Welbeck to have medical as Chelsea set to pay first fee for over-26 since 2022
Sports.content:
Chelsea have agreed an undisclosed fee with Brighton for Danny Welbeck.

The 35-year-old has been given permission to undergo a medical in the next 24 hours ahead of his imminent move to Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea have turned to Welbeck as they look to add experience to manager Xabi Alonso's squad.

The last time the west London club paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 was four years ago, when they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona.

Image: Welbeck is set for a medical ahead of a move to Chelsea

It has been two years since Chelsea selected a player over the age of 30 in any game.

Sky Sports News reported earlier this week that initial positive talks had been held regarding a move for Welbeck who has one-year left on his contract at Brighton.

Welbeck has continued to be a reliable goalscorer in the Premier League at 35 years old. Last season he scored 13 times, after scoring 10 in the previous campaign.

His potential arrival would be another example of Chelsea prioritising physically imposing players with Premier League experience this summer.

They have already signed Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117m - a record fee for a British player - and are close to bringing in Crystal Palace defender Maxence Lacroix.

It would also place further doubt on the futures of strikers Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap and Marc Guiu.

Chelsea have signed several players from Brighton in recent seasons including their main striker Joao Pedro, plus Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Robert Sanchez.

A number of Brighton staff members have also moved to Stamford Bridge over the past four years, including sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Sam Jewell.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jay Bothroyd discusses why Jordan Henderson and Welbeck would be good signings for Chelsea and will add the experience the team has been needing

BlueCo's drastic change in transfer policy

Analysis from Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

The BlueCo era at Chelsea has been defined by hoarding some of the best young talent on the planet and developing them in-house. That method has had some successes, but overall, it has not panned out.

Image: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was the last player over the age of 26 who Chelsea paid a transfer fee for

There is clearly some recognition and accountability from the top brass about that. In bringing in Alonso as manager, they know they have lucked out in getting one of the most highly-sought-after tacticians in the game. The Spaniard has clearly identified the need for experience and the club are following his lead.

The interest in Granit Xhaka earlier in the summer was among the first signs of the shift. Even making a move for Lacroix is evidence of a change in approach.

The Welbeck move is surprising, but there is some logic that can be applied to it. Is he going to start every week? No. However, Chelsea's four senior strikers have an average age of just 23. Combined, they have made 269 Premier League appearances and scored 74 goals.

Image: Thiago Silva was the last player over the age of 30 to play for Chelsea

The Brighton veteran has 400 appearances and 90 goals on his own. To have that as your back-up to the young guns you want to develop makes sense.

Jordan Henderson? That's a complete 180 degree turn. Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez are two of the more experienced players Alonso has. If you had to pick anywhere Chelsea needed a wise head, you would not say midfield.

Yet, they wanted Xhaka. They now want Henderson. Alonso may have been the man to oversee the blossoming of players like Florian Wirtz at Bayer Leverkusen. However, he clearly sees the values of opposite characters and knows Chelsea, and perhaps more importantly, he needs people ready now.

Sports.title: Harrington picked as Europe's third vice-captain for 2027 Ryder Cup
Sports.content:
Luke Donald has named Irishman Padraig Harrington as his third vice-captain for the 2027 Ryder Cup which will be played at Adare Manor in Ireland in September next year.

Harrington joins the Molinari brothers, Edoardo and Francesco, in Donald's backroom team for next year's contest, as Team Europe seek a third consecutive Ryder Cup victory following wins at Marco Simone in 2023 and Bethpage Black in 2025.

The three-time major champion, one of Ireland's most decorated and popular sporting heroes, was a player in the only previous Ryder Cup to be played in his home country in 2006.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at Harrington's heroics en route to his Open title defence in 2008

He represented Europe six times in total as a player - including being part of four triumphs - and was previously a vice-captain on three occasions before becoming captain for the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits.

"Luke and I arranged to meet up at The Open and chatted about it, and we felt we could strike up a good team again," said Harrington.

"Obviously, he was my vice-captain in 2021, and we have worked together as vice-captains in the past. And certainly, I feel I've something to give.

"Luke has a very strong team around him already and he felt that we would work well together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports Jamie Weir explains why Luke Donald has been chosen as captain of Europe Ryder Cup team for a third time.

"It's something I didn't expect. I honestly didn't think I'd ever wear the European Ryder Cup logo again. So I'm very happy to be part of it.

"The Ryder Cup has been a special part of my life. Representing Europe has always been one of the highlights of my golfing career, and to be able to do it again in this situation, especially in Ireland, is special.

"You wouldn't want to miss out with it being in Ireland, so I'm very pleased.

"I think it will be a spectacular occasion and one of the great sporting events to be played in the country. The whole of Ireland will be behind it, watching it, enjoying it and living it.

"The fans are going to be fantastic, and I think the atmosphere will be second to none."

Donald said: "Padraig is someone I thought about quite a lot, especially with it being in Adare.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Donald expresses his gratitude to his fans, family and team-mates after being recognised in the King's Birthday Honours list with an OBE for his success with Team Europe.

"I've been around Padraig in many Ryder Cup team rooms, as a player, as a vice-captain to his captaincy, and he's been a vice-captain before in the past as well.

"So he brings a wealth of experience, and I do love the fact that there's a connection. He understands the Irish crowds and all that goes with having a Ryder Cup in Ireland. I think it's going to be very special for him.

"He's loved in Ireland with what he's achieved in the game, and that will only bring more energy to our team. We'll get the fans even more behind us, and you know I think that can only be a good thing. I'm very excited to have his expertise."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ryder Cup captain Jim Furyk is hopeful Tiger Woods will be able to play a role in the team in 2027.

Harrington made his Ryder Cup debut at The Country Club in Brookline in 1999 and was ever-present for the next five editions, helping Europe to victory in 2002, 2004, 2006 and 2010. He contributed a total of 10½ points to the European Team during that period.

He was named as vice-captain for the first time by fellow Dubliner Paul McGinley for the victory at Gleneagles in 2014, a role he returned to in 2016 at Hazeltine National under Darren Clarke and in 2018 for the victory at Le Golf National in Paris under Denmark's Thomas Bjorn.

Harrington then led Team Europe at the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits, which was postponed by 12 months due to the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Sports.title: Liverpool set to open talks with PSG over Barcola signing
Sports.content:
Liverpool are set to open talks with PSG over a potential deal for Bradley Barcola.

After preliminary talks with his representatives, Liverpool have prepared an opening offer and are set to formalise their interest with an official approach.

Signing a winger has been a priority since the departure of Mo Salah, and Barcola has been on Liverpool's radar for a number of years.

The 23-year-old has two years left on his PSG contract and has indicated he will not be signing a new one amid frustrations at a lack of game time. The opportunity to join Liverpool is said to appeal to the player.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Christian Karembeu assesses potential destinations for Barcola

The key to getting any deal moving will be PSG's willingness to reduce the price tag on the man they bought for around £40m back in 2023.

Valuations of top-level players this summer have been high. Sky Sports News reported on Tuesday that PSG value the France international as high as £145m (€170m), however other sources have now indicated it could be around £128.5m (€150m).

The success of Andoni Iraola's teams at Bournemouth and Rayo Vallecano centred around the pace, energy and work-rate from his wingers, so Barcola could be a key piece of the Spaniard's new Liverpool jigsaw.

The fact that Barcola has won nine major trophies in the last two years, including two Champions League titles, shows the calibre of player they are trying to bring to Anfield.

Arsenal also hold an interest in Barcola.

Sky Sports' Adam Bate:

Bradley Barcola could be the most expensive transfer of this summer window with Liverpool and Arsenal among the clubs chasing the Paris Saint-Germain forward. But why is he so prized? He has achieved plenty already. But there is more to come.

The 23-year-old France international has just won the Champions League with PSG back-to-back but had to be content with coming off the bench in both finals. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia's arrival from Napoli in January of 2025 established him as first choice on the left.

But just because Barcola is not a guaranteed starter in Paris does not mean that he is not a guaranteed star. This is a player with pace, physicality and intelligence, someone whose skills have been honed under Luis Enrique. With Barcola, the potential is as vast as the fee.

Read Adam Bate's feature on Bradley Barcola here...

Could Arsenal come in for Barcola amid Vinicius Jr blow?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Dharmesh Sheth suggests Arsenal might now target Barcola after Vinicius Junior opted to remain at Real Madrid beyond this summer

Vinicius Junior will be staying at Real Madrid beyond this summer, Sky Sports News has been told.

The Spanish club have no intention of selling him and are confident he will agree a new contract. This is despite the interest of Arsenal, who are monitoring his situation closely with a year remaining on his current deal.

Sky Sports News' Dharmesh Sheth said this week: "Arsenal will continue to keep an eye on Vinicius Jr's situation still. He hasn't signed that new contract yet. As it stands, he has a year left on his contract. That's why they are exploring the conditions of a possible deal.

"How Andrea Berta does his business at Arsenal is very clear. It's not about one target and then the risk of that target not coming.

"They try to get their ducks in a row with three or four deals, get as far down the line as they can with as many targets as possible, and then decide which player they are going to go for.

"One of those players is Bradley Barcola. He's intimated to PSG that he's not going to sign a new contract. That's primarily because in the biggest games last season, he was on the bench.

"He doesn't want to go through that again. It looks like he could become available for a transfer."

Sports.title: F1 Driver Ratings: Our verdict on 2026's stars so far
Sports.content:
Formula 1 in 2026 is shaping up to give us a fascinating second half of the season as Kimi Antonelli looks to become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.

Antonelli is 50 points ahead of Lewis Hamilton and 59 points in front of George Russell in the Drivers' Championship in a season that has provided plenty of drama, so it is a good time to look at which drivers have starred and who is struggling before we resume racing with a Sprint weekend at the Dutch Grand Prix on August 21-23, live on Sky Sports F1.

So running through the field in current Drivers' Championship order, we have...

Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes - 9/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 7-4 / Points vs team-mate: 219-160

Without doubt Antonelli has been the best driver so far this season and deserves to have a solid lead in the championship after five wins on the spin, followed by a sixth in Belgium.

We should not forget he's only in his second F1 campaign at 19 years old and he has shown incredible speed, with very few mistakes.

His performance at the Monaco Grand Prix in particular was outstanding.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli jumps in Monaco harbour, celebrating his fifth consecutive win of the 2026 Formula 1 season

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari - 8/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 5-6 / Points vs team-mate: 169-138

Hamilton will be frustrated with his below-par execution in the races prior to the summer break as he should be much closer to Antonelli in the title race.

Nevertheless, the seven-time world champion has impressively overturned his big pace deficit to team-mate Charles Leclerc from last year into a small, consistent advantage.

Cut out the errors and don't rule out a serious challenge for a record-breaking eighth world title.

George Russell, Mercedes - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 4-7 / Points vs team-mate: 160-219

Russell has endured plenty of bad luck this season but so has Antonelli and the reality is the British driver has lacked overall pace to his team-mate.

Whether that's down to driving style that affects the power unit, the tyres, or something else, Russell has generally been on the backfoot in terms of pace since the third round of the season in Japan.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell spun out at the Belgian Grand Prix

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari - 7.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 6-5 / Points vs team-mate: 138-169

Leclerc has not hit the heights of previous years this season after a brake issue caused a dip in performance from Miami to Monaco but even after that, it has been very close between the Ferrari duo in the run-up to the summer break.

Although he was fortunate to win at Silverstone, Leclerc drove tremendously to take advantage of Antonelli's misfortune and was there again in Belgium to make the Mercedes driver work for victory.

Lando Norris, McLaren - 8.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 5-6 / Points vs team-mate: 128-92

Norris is driving just as well as he did in the backend of last year on his way to becoming world champion. The difference is the car, prior to Hungary, has not been capable of winning.

Aside from Austria, Norris has been the stronger of the McLaren drivers since the fourth round in Miami and his performances have perhaps gone under the radar.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the moment that Lando Norris claims victory at the Hungarian Grand Prix!

Max Verstappen, Red Bull - 8.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 8-3 / Points vs team-mate: 109-68

Verstappen may not have won a race but is still driving the wheels off his Red Bull and is still seen by many as the best driver in Formula 1.

He has not been faultless but to only have one less podium than both Ferrari drivers is some feat, particularly as the RB22 barely wanted to get off the start line earlier this year.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 6-5 / Points vs team-mate: 92-128

Piastri is in a similar boat to Russell where the new 2026 car and power unit may not suit him and he's finding it difficult to match his team-mate.

The pace advantage Norris had in Hungary over Piastri was significant and that was not the first race where the Australian has been a few tenths slower per lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Home hero Oscar Piastri crashes on way to Australian GP grid in his McLaren

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 3-8 / Points vs team-mate: 68-109

Red Bull finally have a driver who is close enough to Verstappen, so big credit to Isack Hadjar, who will surely keep the seat for 2027.

Hadjar's qualifying pace has been particularly strong, outqualifying Verstappen at Suzuka and Silverstone, but his race pace deficit is bigger and the area to work on the most.

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 6-5 / Points vs team-mate: 43-23

Lawson has enjoyed a breakthrough this year and is proving Racing Bulls were right to retain him for this season.

Eight points finishes, including a great spell through Canada, Monaco and Barcelona when he maximised the performance of his car, is a very good showing from Lawson, who has often been best of the rest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player See what a typical day looks like for Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson living in Monaco

Pierre Gasly, Alpine - 7.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 9-2 / Points vs team-mate: 42-19

Gasly has continued his great form from recent years into 2026 and continues to lead the Alpine team.

Gasly is the only driver outside of the top four teams to claim a podium this season after he was awarded third at the Monaco Grand Prix following Alpine's protest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Pierre Gasly welcomed his Monaco Grand Prix trophy home to Alpine headquarters, discussing his career thus far and what the future holds.

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 5-6 / Points vs team-mate: 23-43

Lindblad is enjoying a great rookie campaign and has been pretty even on outright pace compared to Lawson, despite having less experience.

Lindblad has been keen to get his elbows out which caused some feisty moments in Austria, Belgium and Hungary between the Racing Bulls duo and they will probably continue to find themselves fighting for the same piece of track after the summer break.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Naomi Schiff visits Arvid Lindblad to reminisce about where the Formula 1 dream began for the rookie driver

Franco Colapinto, Alpine - 6/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 2-9 / Points vs team-mate: 19-42

Colapinto had a couple of great weekends in Miami and Canada, where he scored his best career result of sixth, but has still been trailing Gasly on outright pace over the season.

He's definitely close enough though for Alpine to not need to think about changing their line-up, unless a bigger name comes calling.

Oliver Bearman, Haas - 7.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 8-3 / Points vs team-mate: 18-3

Bearman is quietly having an impressive season at Haas - he just does not have the points to show for it.

His advantage over team-mate Esteban Ocon has been substantial and the 21-year-old has also cut out the errors from his first full season last year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oliver Bearman is reduced to tears after driving Ayrton Senna's 1985 Lotus 97T, the car Senna drove to his first-ever Formula 1 victory.

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi - 6.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 5-6 / Points vs team-mate: 10-0

Bortoleto has remarkably finished in the top 11 in the last six races but only has two points finishes.

Bortoleto, in his second season, perhaps has not kicked on as much as we hoped but is still doing a solid job at Audi.

Carlos Sainz, Williams - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 9-2 / Points vs team-mate: 6-5

Sainz will hope he does not have the same long pain Fernando Alonso faced for much of his career - driving well but not getting many rewards for it.

Sainz has been consistently faster than team-mate Alex Albon and six points do not justify the campaign he's having.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Formula 1 has added Malaysia to its 2026 schedule to host the Bahrain Grand Prix that was postponed earlier in the season

Alexander Albon, Williams - 5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 2-9 / Points vs team-mate: 5-6

Albon started to raise his game just before the summer break against Sainz, so perhaps something has clicked, but it was tough going before the Belgian Grand Prix.

The British-Thai driver has been vocal on the radio about the car's performance but, similarly to Russell at Mercedes and Piastri at McLaren, he could be getting more out of it himself.

Esteban Ocon, Haas - 5.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 3-8 / Points vs team-mate: 3-18

It is the same tune at Haas where Ocon has been around three tenths slower than Bearman in Qualifying this year but appeared to improve in the last few race weekends before the break.

Ocon is perhaps the driver most under pressure to keep his seat at the moment with Haas understood to be looking at signing Formula 2 star Rafael Camara or reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli for 2027.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Esteban Ocon crashed his Haas into the wall heavily during opening practice in Canada

Nico Hulkenberg, Audi - 6.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 6-5 / Points vs team-mate: 2-10

Hulkenberg's singular points finish is not a fair reflection of his decent year as he's been very close to Bortoleto on pace and he's perhaps been the most unfortunate of the midfield drivers too.

In Spain, for example, he was on course for points until a piece of gravel kicked up by Lawson struck the emergency safety switch on Hulkenberg's car, shutting the system down.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin - 7/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 9-2 / Points vs team-mate: 1-0

It's very difficult to judge the two teams at the back of the field but Fernando Alonso continues to have the upper hand on team-mate Lance Stroll at Aston Martin.

In the upgraded Aston Martin in Hungary, you could see Alonso visibly hustling his car around to extract everything from it, so he's still got plenty of speed in him.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the onboard of Fernando Alonso as he's forced to let go of the steering wheel as vibrations continue to cause him discomfort

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin - 5.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 2-9 / Points vs team-mate: 0-1

It is a continuation of their previous three years together where Stroll trails Alonso on pace and hasn't had too much to shout about.

Things have not helped Stroll when he's retired from more races than he's seen the chequered flag.

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac - 5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 5-6 / Points vs team-mate: 0-0

Bottas might be ahead of Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez in the Drivers' Championship but it has not been a great returning season for the Finn.

Bottas has shown less pace compared to Perez in qualifying and the race.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Valtteri Bottas crawls back into the pit after his front bib catches fire due to heat in Austria

Sergio Perez, Cadillac - 6.5/10

Qualifying vs team-mate: 6-5 / Points vs team-mate: 0-0

Perez has done very well considering how many challenges Cadillac have had in their first season, getting more out of the car than Bottas.

The one-lap speed advantage Perez is a particular surprise given Bottas was a very strong qualifier at Mercedes.

Sports.title: Who needs late Solheim Cup push for Europe at AIG Women's Open?
Sports.content:
The race to feature for Team Europe in the Solheim Cup reaches a climax this week at the AIG Women’s Open, leaving one last chance for players to force their way into Anna Nordqvist’s selection plans.

The qualification campaign ends after the final women's major of the year, with the top two players in the European Solheim Cup points list and the next six available via the Rolex Women's World Golf Rankings securing their automatic spots.

Double points are on offer for the majors on the European Solheim Cup points, while additional world rankings are available compared to a regular event, meaning jeopardy remains on both lists heading into the final qualification event.

Nordqvist has ruled out naming herself as one of the four captain's picks when she finalises her squad on Monday, live from 3pm on Sky Sports News, but who has their place secured and who needs to impress at Royal Lytham & St Annes?

We look at Team Europe as things stand and which players still could force their way into consideration for either a late qualification spot or a potential last-minute pick…

Who is currently in the qualification spots?

Charley Hull tops the Ladies European Tour points list and is guaranteed a spot via those rankings, while Chiara Tamburlini currently narrowly holds onto second spot ahead of Helen Briem.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking ahead of the AIG Women's Open, Charley Hull claims she doesn't see Nelly Korda as her rival due to the fact she's yet to lift a major title

Lottie Woad (world No 5) is guaranteed a Solheim Cup debut at Bernardus Golf via the Rolex World Rankings, with Maja Stark (world No 25) and Celine Boutier (world No 30) also in via those standings.

Esther Henseleit's fourth-place finish at the ISPS Handa Women's Scottish Open last week lifted her to world No 43 and all-but secured a Solheim Cup return, while Carlota Ciganda (world No 47) and Linn Grant (world No 50) hold the other spots as things stand.

Who can still qualify via the Solheim Cup points list?

Tamburlini enters the AIG Women's Open with 133.1 points just a 1.1-point lead over Briem, with Agathe Laisne (111 points) and England's Cara Gainer (104.63 points) completing the top five in those standings.

Only the top 20 on the leaderboard come Sunday evening earn points via that ranking, meaning Briem needs at least a top-20 finish, Laisne 12th or better and Gainer ninth or better to have any chance of qualifying.

Image: Could Helen Briem make her Solheim Cup debut for Team Europe?

The winner will receive 100 points and the runner-up 75 points, with 50 points for third. Stark (sixth), Ciganda (seventh) and Woad (eighth) are all likely qualifiers via the world ranking, with anyone below that trio in the points list needing a top two finish to have a chance of overtaking Tamburlini.

Fourth gets 45 points and fifth earns 40 points, with spots six to 20th then decreasing in multiples of 2.5. If Tamburlini finishes outside the top 20 and Briem finishes inside, then Briem will overtake her in the Solheim race.

What about the Rolex Women's World Golf Rankings?

Ranking points are given to everyone who makes the cut in a major, with 100 are available to the winner, although it is likely to require a big finish for anyone to break into the world's top 50 and qualify via that method.

Nanna Koerstz Madsen (No 63) and Leona Maguire (No 79) are the next two in the rankings outside of the current automatic qualification spots, having both made their Solheim Cup debuts as rookies in the 2021 victory on American soil.

Image: Leona Maguire is chasing a fourth consecutive Solheim Cup appearance

Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez (84th), Nastasia Nadaud (86th), Dewi Weber (87th), Madelene Sagstrom (88th), Ingrid Lindbland (91st), Mimi Rhodes (92nd), Briem (94th) and Tamburlini (100th) are the only other Europeans in the world's top 100.

Nordqvist sits world No 124 and followed a tied-seventh finish at the Evian Championship with a share of 28th at last week's ISPS Handa Women's Scottish Open, although is adamant that she will not pick herself - regardless of her performance at this week's major.

Image: Nordqvist has featured in the last nine Solheim Cups for Team Europe

"Thank you to everyone who believes in me and wanting me to pick myself for Solheim Cup," Nordqvist posted on Instagram. "I'm humbled and it's been great to play alongside the European girls in this journey. I signed up to be the captain and I am very proud to be, so I will not be picking myself for the team."

Other members of the 2024 Solheim Cup team currently relying on a captain's pick include Emily Kristine Pedersen, who failed to qualify for the AIG Women's Open, 2018 Women's Open champion Georgia Hall - part of the last five teams - and Albane Valenzuela.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the final day from the 2024 Solheim Cup as Team USA secured a 15.5-12.5 victory over Europe in Virginia

And what about Team USA?

Team USA's qualification campaign doesn't end until after the CPKC Women's Open on August 23, when the top seven players in the Solheim Cup points standings and the next two players in the Rolex Women's World Golf Rankings will have earned their spots.

Nelly Korda, Angel Yin, Jennifer Kupcho, Auston Kim, Allisen Corpuz, Yealimi Noh and Lauren Coughlin are currently the top seven in the Solheim list, with Andrea Lee (world No 34) and Lindy Duncan (56th) the two in via the world rankings as things stand.

Jenny Bae (59th) and Alison Lee (61st) are the next two in the world rankings, with Team USA's automatic qualifiers likely to change before Angela Stanford names her three remaining captain's picks in late August.

Sports.title: Next darting superstar? Coates, 20, wins maiden PDC title
Sports.content:
Henry Coates sensationally won his maiden title at Players Championship 25 at Hildesheim in Germany.

The 20-year-old Englishman does not hold a PDC Tour card and came into the tournament as a top-up player from the Challenge Tour, but secured a sensational tournament win, beating Australian Damon Heta 8-4 with a 104.88 average in the 12-leg final.

"This probably won't sink in until next week," said Coates, who became the fifth player ever to win a PDC ranking title without a Tour card.

"Hopefully this is just the start. I've played for so many years and now the hard work and practice is paying off.

"Last time I played Damon it was my second ProTour event, just after I had won my first ProTour game, and I think he taught me a lesson beating me 6-0!

"I'm only a Challenge Tour player, but I'll take what I've got!"

Image: Gian van Veen lost in Jim Long in the round of 64

High-ranking Van Veen, however, was the victim of a 6-3 round of 64 shock defeat to Canadian Jim Long, with Long winning the last three legs to put out the World No 3 after the Dutchman handily beat Tom Sykes 6-3 in the opening round.

His countryman, Michael Van Gerwen, was able to make it through his opening matches, beating Adam Warner 6-0 and Darius Labanauskas 6-3 in the first and second rounds respectively, but Jeffrey De Graaf won five legs on the bounce to secure a brilliant last 16 victory.

Image: Michael Van Gerwen was knocked out of the round of 16 by Jeffrey De Graaf in Hildesheim

Elsewhere, Beau Greaves made a strong run to the round of 16 in her first tournament since winning the Women's World Matchplay in Blackpool, but fell 6-3 to German semi-finalist Niko Springer.

Sports.title: FA joins criticism of Fifa plan to sell off World Cup stakes to private investors
Sports.content:
The Football Association has joined Uefa in condemning Fifa’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

In a statement released on Wednesday morning the FA said they have yet to see any details of the controversial proposals, and expressed grave concerns over Fifa’a governance.

The FA chair, Debbie Hewitt, is one of eight Fifa vice-presidents and watched many World Cup matches alongside the president, Gianni Infantino, yet appears to have been shut out of any discussions over plans that are at an advanced stage.

Fifa has given their 211 member associations a deadline of 19 September to decide whether to apply for an initial payment of $20m (£15m) for the proceeds of a 20% sale of a new commercial entity – Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) – that has been valued at $20bn (£15bn).

The FA’s statement is significant as it is the first time the governing body has criticised Fifa under Infantino, having stayed quiet throughout the Folarin Balalogun affair during the World Cup and endorsed the award of the 2034 tournament to Saudi Arabia.

The FA is understood to have held talks with Uefa and other European associations, who are determined to kill the plan with all options, including a boycott of Fifa tournaments and a potential breakaway thought to be on the table.

“We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached,” said the FA in a statement. “Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved. When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further.”

The FA’s statement followed a similarly strong release from Concacaf, which is particularly significant given that the North American confederation has just delivered the most lucrative World Cup in history for Fifa that produced revenues of $15bn.

The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, was instrumental in winning the joint US, Mexico and Canadian bid for 2026, but was also kept in the dark over Fifa’s plans.

View image in fullscreen FA chair Debbie Hewitt (right), with Gianni Infantino (centre), at the World Cup semi-final between England and Argentina. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

“Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release,” Concacaf said in a statement released to the Guardian. “We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

“We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.

“As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, Fifa, the Confederations and every Member Association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.

“This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the Fifa family will act in the same manner.”

Fifa’s work with the US bank JP Morgan to set up a new company called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would be partially sold off to “raise up to $4.2bn” to fund global football development projects later this year, has left other stakeholders stunned and reignited divisions within the world game.

Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation were already bracing themselves to fight Fifa’s plans to expand the World Cup to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament, and there are fears that inviting private investors will make further expansion inevitable, as well as leading to pressure to stage the World Cup more regularly given its huge commercial value.

Uefa accused Fifa of attempting to sell football’s soul and will hold emergency talks on Wednesday to plan a coordinated response that could involve legal action.

“This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” they said. “Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

“The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa’s to sell.”

Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, joined critics of the plan last night, saying on social media that the sport does not belong to investors.

“The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell,” Burnham wrote on X. “Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”

Sports.title: Where all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the season
Sports.content:
Arsenal: central midfielder

Declan Rice was worked to the bone by Arsenal last season, playing 4,456 minutes in all competitions. This showed at points during the World Cup, when the midfielder’s body looked on the verge of breaking down. Arsenal need high-quality reinforcements in the centre of the pitch so Rice can occasionally have a rest. Christian Nørgaard struggled to get on to the park last season, with Mikel Arteta seemingly not trusting in the former Brentford captain. An extra midfield option could prove crucial to Arsenal retaining their crown.

Aston Villa: left-back

Aston Villa have finished in the top seven for the last four seasons and they won the Europa League last season. They need more depth in the squad to establish themselves among the Premier League’s elite permanently, but may lose left-back Lucas Digne to Paris Saint-Germain. Ian Maatsen is a fine player but he cannot play every week in a season that includes a Champions League campaign, hence Villa’s interest in signing Pervis Estupiñán from Milan.

Bournemouth: right-back

Adam Smith is a Bournemouth legend who has made more than 400 appearances for the club but he is 35 years old. Max Aarons and Julián Araujo were signed to replace him but, for one reason or another, things have not worked out for them. And Álex Jiménez has gone out on loan to Fiorentina. Marco Rose needs to make a statement signing at right-back so Smith can finally rest.

View image in fullscreen Adam Smith puts in some work in the gym during Bournemouth’s pre-season testing. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

Brentford: left-back

Brentford have already addressed their biggest weaknesses, but they could do with an upgrade at left-back. Rico Henry has struggled for fitness and form since suffering a horrific injury three years ago. He played 30 games in all competitions last season but made four errors leading to shots – the joint most of any Brentford player. Reinforcing the left flank would also free up Keane Lewis-Potter to play further forward if Keith Andrews wants to utilise him more on the wing.

Brighton: central midfielder

Brighton will have been planning for James Milner’s retirement and Pascal Gross’s ageing legs for a long time. Only six midfielders over the age of 34 played in the Premier League last season, and two of them played for Brighton. They are thin in the middle of the park and there’s also the possibility of more departures. Carlos Baleba is frequently linked with a move and Yasin Ayari’s impressive performances at the World Cup may have caught someone’s eye. Nobody scored more goals from outside the penalty area at the tournament than the Sweden midfielder. Brighton could do with someone else in there even if Baleba and Ayari stay.

Chelsea: goalkeeper

Chelsea have spent more than £200m this summer – £117m of it on Morgan Rogers – but still have several problem positions. They seem keen to sign a centre-back, and should add depth in central midfield and on the left wing, but a goalkeeper is where the most urgent attention is needed. Robert Sánchez has never truly convinced. Since he joined in August 2023, he ranks second in the Premier League for both errors leading to shots (17) and errors leading to goals (seven). Of the worst 10 culprits in both metrics, Sánchez has made the fewest appearances and played the fewest minutes. Mike Penders has arrived from Strasbourg but, at 20, he is one for the future. Xabi Alonso does not want to start his tenure worrying about the reliability of his first-choice goalkeeper.

Coventry: goalkeeper

There are a lot of unknowns for Coventry as they return to the Premier League for the first time in 25 years, not least how well centre-forwards Haji Wright and Ellis Simms will take to leading the line against the best defences in England. But the biggest unknown of all is who will be between the sticks, because Coventry do not have a first-choice goalkeeper. They want to make Carl Rushworth’s loan deal permanent, but have not been able to agree a fee with Brighton. Only Bristol City keeper Radek Vitek (+8.5) prevented more goals with his saves in the Championship last season than Rushworth (+8.2). Without him, there’s a big hole that needs filling.

Crystal Palace: centre-back

Pierre Sage used a back three in all of Lens’ league games last season, so it’s likely that Crystal Palace will continue to employ the 3-4-2-1 formation that served them so well under Oliver Glasner. They will need more depth at centre-back, though. Having lost Marc Guéhi to Manchester City in January, their Premier League win rate last season dropped from 35% with the England international starting to 22.2% without him. Jaydee Canvot is an adequate replacement, but Palace are still short on numbers at the back. If Maxence Lacroix also leaves the club, their need for another centre-back will become even starker.

Everton: right-back

Séamus Coleman’s 17-year stay at Everton has come to an end and Nathan Patterson is also expected to depart, meaning Jake O’Brien is likely to be their only remaining recognised right-back. Well, we say “recognised right-back”, but the consensus among Everton fans is that the hulking Republic of Ireland international is not dynamic or technical enough to be a full-back. James Garner has also filled in there from time to time. It has been a problem position for a while now.

Fulham: centre-forward

Fulham need more players who can score goals. Raúl Jiménez (nine) and Harry Wilson (10) accounted for 19 of their 43 Premier League goals (excluding own goals) last season and they have both left on free transfers. No one else scored more than four league goals last season. More will be expected from Rodrigo Muniz (one goal), Samuel Chukwueze (three goals) and Kevin (one goal), but Fulham clearly need greater depth in attack. New manager Álvaro Arbeloa is keen to sign Gonzalo García from Real Madrid but Fulham need at least two new faces.

Hull City: wide forward

Hull City desperately need to add a few splashes of quality to their attack. Oli McBurnie has the physicality to lead the line, but the 30-year-old needs players to run off him to be effective. Hull have sold Kyle Joseph to Middlesbrough and have not tried to re-sign Joe Gelhardt after his loan, meaning they are light in attack.

Ipswich Town: striker

Most promoted sides are let down by a lack of precision in both boxes. By signing Issa Diop, Ipswich have secured a proven defender to play alongside Dara O’Shea. But they need more firepower up front. George Hirst has only reached double figures for goals in a season twice in his career, and £24m signing Emersonn has never scored more than six league goals in a single campaign (though he is only 22 years old). Daizen Maeda is a much-needed addition from Celtic.

View image in fullscreen The signing of Daizen Maeda is a boost to Ipswich’s attack. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

Leeds: goalkeeper

Leeds signed Lucas Perri from Lyon last summer for £15.6m in the hope he would solve what had become a problem position. He didn’t. Karl Darlow, originally acquired as backup to Illan Meslier in 2023, ended up playing more games in the league last season. But Darlow then left on a free transfer, ultimately joining Manchester United. Leeds also opted to let Meslier’s contract expire. Their remaining goalkeeper options are Perri, who underwhelmed in his first season, and 33-year-old Alex Cairns, whose most recent competitive appearance was for Salford City in the 2023-24 season. They need another keeper.

Liverpool: right wing

Mohamed Salah’s final season at Liverpool was his most underwhelming, but he still had a hand in 22 goals across all competitions. In terms of what he achieved in nine years at Anfield, Salah is one of the greatest players in Liverpool’s history and close to irreplaceable. His output last season is not irreplaceable, though. A dynamic wide attacker who provides goals and creativity – such as Bradley Barcola – is on the agenda, and Andoni Iraola has a good track record developing such players.

Manchester City: winger

Enzo Maresca has addressed one hole in the Manchester City squad by signing Elliot Anderson, but he could do with another option on the flanks to give City more attacking variety. At the tail end of last season, City lacked strength in depth on the wing. Antoine Semenyo struggled during the run-in and City did not have a quality replacement to turn to on the bench. Savinho regressed in his second season in England, only starting seven league games and scoring just one goal, and players such as Phil Foden and Rayan Cherki are better in the middle.

Manchester United: central midfielder

Michael Carrick’s central midfield options have been enhanced by Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. It’s a pretty good start, but they need more. If we categorise Bruno Fernandes and Mason Mount as No 10s, Manchester United only had three senior central midfielders last season: Kobbie Mainoo, Casemiro and Manuel Ugarte. Casemiro has joined Inter Miami and Ugarte would probably have left too had he not suffered an ACL injury at the World Cup that will keep him out for most of the season. United still need an athletic, ball-winning midfielder.

Newcastle United: full-back

We could have picked a few positions for Newcastle but have chosen full-back as they need one for each flank or, failing that, someone who can play on both sides of the defence. Tino Livramento and Lewis Hall are two of the best full-backs in the Premier League, but they have had injury problems and Newcastle lack depth now that Kieran Trippier, Emil Krafth and Matt Targett have departed. Dan Burn can fill in at left-back but that is not ideal; they have Leo Shahar at right-back but he is an unproven teenager; and Alex Murphy can fill in at left-back but he is more of a central defender.

Nottingham Forest: centre-back

Let’s assume replacing Anderson is a given for Nottingham Forest. The other area they need reinforcements is centre-back. New coach Glasner swears by a back three; he lined up with three or five at the back in every game during his two seasons at Crystal Palace. Forest have several centre-backs already – Nikola Milenkovic, Murillo, Morato and Jair Cunha, plus a couple of prospects – but bringing in at least one more defender with experience of playing in a back three would not go amiss.

Tottenham: winger

When Mohammed Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski are fit again, Tottenham will have a couple of good options on the right flank. However, they are not on the club’s pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia, and may not be available for the start of the season. On the left, Spurs only have Mathys Tel and Wilson Odobert, neither of whom can be relied upon for consistent output. Between them, Tel and Odobert racked up just four goals and three assists in a combined 55 league appearances last season. Odobert is also recovering from a serious knee injury and will miss at least the first few months of the season. That leaves Tottenham with almost no options out wide. They need at least one winger.

Sunderland: creative midfielder

After a very busy transfer market last summer and an extremely successful first season back in the top flight, Sunderland have been quieter this time around. That is understandable but, with a first European campaign since 1973 coming up, they need more depth, and that could mean reinforcement across the pitch. They could really do with a little more creativity, having generated just 23.2 expected goals in open play in 38 league games last season – only relegated Burnley and Wolves fared worse.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Abusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data reveals
Sports.content:
Abusive chanting against immigrants has become a feature of football matches in England, according to new data from Kick It Out.

Last season 39 reports of anti-immigrant chanting were made to the anti-discrimination charity, more than the previous two seasons combined. Phrases such as “stop the boats” and “send them back” were reported as being heard “at all levels of the game”, Kick It Out said.

The growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, at matches and online. Kick It Out received 1,744 reports of discriminatory behaviour in total during the 2025-26 season, a record and a 25% increase on the previous campaign.

The number of reported incidents increased across every type of discrimination to new highs. Reports of racism remained the most common, rising 19% year-on-year, the 792 reports making up 45% of the total. Complaints of sexist behaviour rose 12% to 216, homophobia rose 46% to 203, antisemitism rose 43% to 93, ableism rose 20% to 89, and Islamophobia rose 88% to 60. Kick it Out said all six areas had seen their biggest totals in five years.

Reports of abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year, up by 33% in 2025-26 to a record 248 reports. Equally, the 98 reports of abuse against match officials was the same as the past three seasons combined.

Samuel Okafor, chief executive at Kick It Out, said such behaviour at matches and in online spaces was matched by a rise in hateful rhetoric elsewhere in British society, but he praised the willingness of supporters – and players – to speak out.

“These figures show that discrimination remains deeply embedded across the game at a time when we’re also seeing rises in hate crime and divisive political rhetoric in Britain,” he said. “But they also show that people are more willing to stand up to abuse when they see it, and it’s encouraging to see professional players set that example last season.”

For example, in March, a 60-year-old man was given a suspended sentence for sending offensive messages to the England Women defender Jess Carter, who went public over the attacks during the European Championship last year. In the men’s game, Antoine Semenyo drew attention to the racist abuse he had received over the course of the season, with a charge of racially aggravated behaviour against one man scheduled to go to trial in September.

Kick It Out’s findings concur with those reported by the UK Football Policing Unit last week. The police said that some of the increase could be explained by improved reporting mechanisms, with misogynist abuse only introduced as a separate category of discrimination at the start of last season. Both police and Kick It Out have called on online platforms to do more to stop abuse.

Okafor said: “We will continue to work with football authorities, clubs, leagues, regulators and government to ensure we match the courage shown to report abuse with clear and consistent action so that football is welcoming to everyone.”

Sports.title: Retaining Rodri is key to Manchester City success under Enzo Maresca
Sports.content:
“Welcome home,” was Khaldoon al-Mubarak’s warm greeting to Enzo Maresca on his appointment last month as Manchester City manager. Now, after two previous spells at the club, the Italian’s task is to keep the chair content, and ensure a three-year contract does not end early. To achieve that, Maresca’s tenure must continue Pep Guardiola’s glittering legacy of 20 trophies across a decade of excellence.

The key to the 46-year-old, who was Guardiola’s assistant during the 2022-23 treble season and City’s elite development squad leader two years before that, being successful can be summed up in two words: “Keep Rodri”. Yet with Real Madrid almost certain to launch a bid for the peerless No 6, and him seemingly wanting to play for the Spanish giants, a move away from City may become inevitable.

Maresca’s best hope of avoiding “doing a David Moyes” – who succeeded Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in May 2013 and lasted a mere 34 Premier League games – and thriving as the man who follows the man is to retain Rodri, who has just captained Spain to World Cup glory, winning the Golden Ball as best player in the process. The 30-year-old is contracted until June. City’s stance is that they have no wish to sell and remain intent on persuading him to sign the new terms that have been on offer for a while.

Saying City will definitely be contenders for the biggest prizes next season if they retain Rodri may sound simplistic until you examine his CV and are reminded of the pivotal role he has played for the club. Rodri was key to City’s treble glory, including scoring the winner in the Champions League final against Inter. Then there was the 74-game unbeaten sequence with him in the colours that ran from February 2023 to May 2024. “He’s unbelievable, irreplaceable,” said Guardiola. “The best midfielder in the world by far.”

The World Cup triumph also came after Rodri had been part of Spain’s Euro 2024 glory and City’s 2023 Club World Cup success, again winning the player of the tournament in each. In the two seasons before the World Cup, injury plagued him, however. The result: no Premier League titles in either year for City, halting a record four-in-a-row run for Guardiola’s garlanded team.

Rodri’s ability to mould and control contests was reiterated by his World Cup displays. Exhibit A: the chokehold imposed on France in the semi-finals. At domestic and international level, this is a priceless quality. So if Maresca can field Rodri, City will be feared in the league and on the continent. The back injury for which Rodri underwent surgery on Monday is minor, but the desire to broaden his club horizons – primarily in Spain – remains, meaning there is no certainty he will stay put. Particularly so given the initial resistance of Real Madrid’s president, Florentino Pérez, to acquiring Rodri has shifted, due, surely, to his resurgence at the World Cup and maybe José Mourinho, returning as head coach, expressing a need for the player’s calm and elan.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca worked under Pep Guardiola as Manchester City won the treble in 2023. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

City have invested £116m on Elliot Anderson this summer, an England first-choice midfielder who may be joined by another midfielder in Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old who also impressed at the World Cup for Morocco, and would cost around £85m. However, neither of them or Tijjani Reijnders, Mateo Kovacic nor Nico González can claim to be in the class of Rodri, who may well be in line to claim a second Ballon d’Or following his World Cup exploits.

Maresca won the Championship with Leicester in 2024 and the following season led Chelsea to fourth in the Premier League and to a Conference League triumph, following that up with glory at the expanded Club World Cup, which featured the 3-0 demolition of Paris Saint-Germain in the final. All of this convinced al-Mubarak and his chief executive, Ferran Soriano, that Maresca is the one who can thrive after the era-defining Guardiola.

Quick Guide Gvardiol says 'great things' will happen under Maresca Show Joško Gvardiol has signed a new five-year contract with Manchester City, the defender stating that “great things” can be achieved with Enzo Maresca, the new manager. While the terms include an option of a further 12-months, the Croatian is confident that the Italian’s first season will be successful. “I remember when he was at Chelsea [2024-26] it was difficult to play against them – especially away. We struggled. He’s here and I think we can achieve some great things together,” Gvardiol said. The 24-year-old has made 122 appearances and claimed six trophies with City since joining from RB Leipzig in 2023 for £77m and was voted the club’s 2024-5 player of the season. Gvardiol said: “I remember my first season when I arrived – back then I was kind of still young. In these three years I’ve learned a lot of things from all my team-mates, my friends in the dressing room and on the pitch in the last three years. "I still think there are a lot of things to improve and learn but I’m only 24, I have enough time.” Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

However, as Maresca made clear with his “after Sir Alex [Ferguson]” reference in his unveiling on Friday, directly following greatness can be treacherous. The comparison between him and Moyes is hardly precise, though. Moyes arrived at United trophyless and with no experience of the pressures of an elite club. Maresca’s résumé shows a season and a half in the Chelsea hothouse and, with his prior experience of City, he is versed in the organisation where he now plays a crucial role.

City have five weeks of the market remaining to try to persuade Rodri his future is at the club. Guardiola’s stance was never to stop any player exiting who wished to do so. The logic is understandable: what is the point in retaining an unhappy employee? In this case it would also be one who wants to return to his native city. “Having played for Atlético [Madrid] before would not prevent me from playing for Real Madrid,” Rodri said in March. “There are other players who have done that before. Maybe not direct transfers, but eventually. You can’t turn down one of the world’s best clubs.”

Even Real Madrid boycotting Rodri’s Ballon d’Or-crowning ceremony in November 2024 in protest at Vinícius Júnior’s failure to win the vote has clearly not dissuaded the midfielder that the Bernabéu can be the home al-Mubarak characterises City as for Maresca.

Sports.title: Is Kazuyoshi Miura the oldest goalscorer in competitive football history? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Kazuyoshi Miura recently scored in the Emperor’s Cup at the tender age of 59 – is he the oldest goalscorer in football history?” asks Terry Winter.

If we were picking an all-time Knowledge XI, ‘King Kazu’ would be in the mix for a place. He’s appeared in various age-related queries over the years, and tales of his exploits always give us hope as we wheeze through middle-age. On Saturday, Miura scored his first competitive goal ⁠in nearly four years as ⁠Fukushima ​United thrashed Iwaki Furukawa 7-0 in the Emperor’s Cup.

Miura’s goal extended his record for the oldest goalscorer in professional football. These are the oldest goalscorers we could find, but drop us a line if you can beat them.

59 years 149 days, Kazuyoshi Miura: Fukushima United 7-0 Iwaku Furukawa, Emperor’s Cup, 25 July 2026

51 years 5 days, Innocent Benza: Herentals College FC 1-2 Hwange Colliery, Zimbabwe Premier Soccer League, 25 May 2023

49 years 208 days, Billy Meredith: Brighton 1-5 Manchester City, FA Cup, 23 February 1924

49 years, 14 days, Stanley Matthews: Stoke City 2-2 Swansea City, FA Cup, 15 February 1964

Innocent Benza, aka IB9 and no we didn’t make that up, was on target when Herentals College FC lost 2-1 to Hwange Colliery in the Zimbabwe Premier Soccer League three years ago. He’s believed to be the oldest top-flight goalscorer. In fact he may have scored a more recent goal, as he was still going strong last season when he reached 200 games for Herentals College FC.

Benza has got another 20 years to go if he wants to become the oldest goalscorer on record, though. In March 2020, Ezzeldin Bahader scored a penalty on his debut for 6th of October SC in the Egyptian Third Division. He was – and you’ll like this – 74 years, 125 days old. For the sake of Portugal’s future World Cup chances, Cristiano Ronaldo should not be made aware of this record.

Top of the tree in women’s football appears to be Formiga, who scored for Brazil against Canada in November 2019 at the age of 41 years, 249 days. She retired soon after, having amassed 234 caps over a 26-year international career.

View image in fullscreen Formiga before the 2019 World Cup. Photograph: Naomi Baker/Fifa/Getty Images

With Andy Burnham succeeding Keir Starmer as Labour leader, the UK now has an Everton-supporting prime minister. (A few years ago, he appeared on our own Daniel Harris’s podcast to discuss the 1995 FA Cup final.)

We’ve made a list of PMs who have publicly spoken about being a fan of a particular team or have shown an allegiance in some other way, and, from our initial research, it looks like the balance of power is spread thinly, with no team belonging to more than one prime minister.

Boris Johnson once stated he “supports all London teams” but we are counting none of the capital’s clubs as belonging to him. Before the second world war it was very rare for a prime minister to talk about football, so our list doesn’t go beyond 1945. If you can add to it, or find a team supported by more than one of the country’s leaders, please get in touch.

View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham showing some retro support. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

Andy Burnham (2026-) Everton

Keir Starmer (2024-2026) Arsenal

Rishi Sunak (2022-2024) Southampton

Liz Truss (2022) Norwich City

David Cameron (2010-2016) Aston Villa (definitely not West Ham)

Gordon Brown (2007-2010) Raith Rovers

Tony Blair (1997-2007) Newcastle United

John Major (1990-1997) Chelsea

Edward Heath (1970-1974) Burnley

Harold Wilson (1964-1970 and 1974-1976) Huddersfield Town

Clement Attlee (1945-1951) Fleet Town (mainly because he played for them)

View image in fullscreen Labour leader Tony Blair takes part in a heading contest with Newcastle United boss Kevin Keegan in Brighton during a break at the 1995 party conference. Photograph: PA/PA Archive/Press Association Images

B teams and W teams

“Alphabetically, Tottenham Hotspur are the last club in this season’s Premier League,” notes Robert Johansson-Mars. “That feels weird as there are usually a couple of clubs below them (West Ham, West Brom, Watford, Wolves, Wigan, Wimbledon and whatnot). When was the last time the Premier League (or First Division) didn’t include any W team? However, a league without clubs beginning with the letter B would be truly shocking. Has that ever occurred?”

Prepare to be shocked, Robert. An English top-flight without a B-team is reasonably-common. It last happened in the Premier League just over a decade ago. Blackburn Rovers and Bolton Wanderers were relegated in 2011-12; Burnley rejoined the Premier League in the 2014-15 season. (If you list AFC Bournemouth thus, rather than Bournemouth, it also occurred in 2015-16 while Burnley were yo-yoing.) Those are the only examples in the Premier League era – but the last six years of the old Division One were similarly bereft after Birmingham City were relegated in 1985-86.

The answer to your first question depends on how pedantic you are feeling. This season will be the first in which the men’s English top flight has included no teams whose name begins with W, but there is one historical example where the only W-team subsequently changed their name. Between 1906-11, Woolwich Arsenal flew the flag for the Ws in the English top flight.

In women’s football it’s a more familiar sight – there were no W-teams in the top flight between Watford (2009-10) and West Ham (2018-19).

Knowledge archive

“Apart from Newcastle United how many other clubs using United in their name are actually two teams who merged together to form one?” wondered Keith Gilroy in 2011.

Unsurprisingly, the Magpies aren’t the only United formed by the merger of two clubs (in Newcastle’s case Newcastle West End and Newcastle East End), though there are surprisingly few in the Football League. Plenty of Uniteds seem to have simply plumped for the name – Lincoln Amateurs, for example, were forced into a name change once they began to pay players in the 1950s. With Lincoln City already taken, United just beat Rangers in the club’s vote for a new suffix.

Some that aren’t strictly united Uniteds are: Sheffield (formed from Sheffield United Cricket Club), Leeds (formed following the demise of Leeds City FC in 1919), Manchester (name change from Newton Heath LYR FC), West Ham (formerly Thames Ironworks) and there are plenty more. But here are a few clubs in the pyramid who truly are united Uniteds:

View image in fullscreen The Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company Limited was a shipyard and iron works straddling the mouth of Bow Creek at its confluence with the River Thames, at Leamouth Wharf (often referred to as Blackwall) on the west side and at Canning Town on the east side. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian

Scunthorpe United: The Iron’s website reports, slightly mysteriously that “in 1899 Brumby Hall joined forces with another team to call themselves Scunthorpe United”. Who this anonymous other team was is unclear, but in 1910 the new club merged with nearby Lindsey United just to make sure.

Hereford United: According to the club: “Before the formation of Hereford United there were four leading amateur clubs in Hereford and it was believed that a higher class of football could be sustained if they were to amalgamate. After a meeting in the city, both Hereford City and Hereford Thistle decided to remain independent while St Martins and RAOC (Rotherwas) decided to merge, and thus Hereford United was formed in 1924 with Dr E.W. Maples as chairman.”

Torquay United: A slightly labyrinthine one this. The original Torquay United merged with Ellacombe in 1910 to become, slightly counter-intuitively, Torquay Town. The new club took Ellacombe’s Plainmoor ground, sharing with Babbacombe FC, with whom they then merged in 1921, becoming Torquay United once more.

Maidenhead United: The wonderfully-named Maidenhead Norfolkians joined forces with Maidenhead FC in 1904. Initially Maidenhead Town, they became a United in 1920.

Sutton United: Formed in March 1898 by the amalgamation of two leading junior sides, Sutton Association and Sutton Guild Rovers.

Ebbsfleet United: A United formed of two Uniteds. Gravesend United and Northfleet United merged to form Gravesend & Northfleet FC in 1946, before becoming Ebbsfleet United in May 2007.

Hayes and Yeading United: One of the newest Uniteds, Hayes and Yeading were formed in May 2007 after the merger of Hayes and, yes, Yeading.

Chesham United: The merger of Chesham Town and their neighbours meant the football world was deprived of the brilliantly monikered Chesham Generals from 1917. United are currently flying high in the Zamaretto Premier.

Aylesbury United: The former Conference side “were founded in 1897 when three local sides: Night School FC, The Printing Works and Aylesbury Town decided to merge”.

Can you help?

“Malachi Fagan-Walcott’s final game of last season was for York City against Rochdale in the National League. His first competitive game of 2026-27 season was for Hearts against Sturm Graz in a Champions League qualifier. Has a player ever made a bigger leap in competitive levels between consecutive club games?” asks Tom Reed.

“On Sunday, Sean Murdoch was the referee for St Mirren v Dunfermline in the Scottish League Cup. Murdoch was previously a goalkeeper and played for Dunfermline. Are there any other examples of a former player refereeing a match for a club they had played for?” asks Ian Golightly.

“My beloved Kilmarnock have won only four of their 21 penalty shootouts, a 19% success rate,” writes Andy Kerr. “Does any professonal club have a worse record?”

“Seeing the picture of Omar Sivori in last week’s Knowledge, I noticed the referee in the background dressed in black, as was the norm. Were there any instances of colour clashes with the likes of Notts County, Newcastle, etc, causing problems during matches before referees went full spectrum?” wonders Paul Huby.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Eli Junior Kroupi to boost Barcelona attack?
Sports.content:
After waving Robert Lewandowski off into the sunset at the end of last season, Barcelona are in need of a new striker. The only one on their books scored the winner in the World Cup final. Julián Alvarez is at the centre of a Spanish tug of war this summer – he wants to leave Atlético Madrid and is wanted by Barcelona and Real Madrid, who had a £129m bid roundly rejected in June. With Atlético suits so far refusing to sit down with Joan Laporta for talks in a fashionable Catalan restaurant, the Barça president is beginning to look elsewhere.

Naturally, Laporta’s attention has turned to Bournemouth. Eli Junior Kroupi had an outstanding first season in English football and is said to be the basis of Barcelona’s Plan B up front. Bournemouth insist the 20-year-old is not for sale and, according to reports, value the striker at £110m anyway – about the going rate for a good young player in the Premier League. Other European heavyweights such as Paris Saint-Germain, Arsenal and, er, Tottenham are circling. Chelsea’s João Pedro is said to be an unrealistic Plan C for Barça. Maybe Plan D was Danny Welbeck.

Sticking with Spurs, Savinho has been keeping a keen eye on their big spending in this window and apparently wants to ditch the silverware at Manchester City for the golden cockerel of Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Meanwhile, Jack Grealish has been left out of City’s party for their pre-season tour of Asia, with the 30-year-old’s future well up in the air. “At the moment, he is here,” said the very non-committal new City manager, Enzo Maresca, last week.

In other transfer tussle news, Crystal Palace are reportedly weighing up a bid for the Lens midfielder Mamadou Sangaré – but they will have to be quick. Brentford are said to be in advanced talks over a £41m move for the 24-year-old Mali international, who could fill a Jordan Henderson-sized hold in their squad. Palace haven’t spent a penny this summer, with free agent Óscar Mingueza their only incoming so far. Former Arsenal defender Takehiro Tomiyasu is training with the Conference League winners with a view to another free transfer.

Fulham are still interested in making Gonzalo García their marquee summer signing but Álvaro Arbeloa’s desire to be reunited with the Real Madrid striker could be scuppered by the asking price, said to be upwards of £50m. Madrid’s Franco Mastantuono and Fran García are also said to be on their shortlist. It might be worth widening your search terms, Álvaro.

And as Barcelona continue to scramble around for a striker, their next pre-season opponents have added to their forward ranks. Luis Vásquez is through the door at Birmingham, who host Barça at St Andrew’s on Friday. Oh, the glamour.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso plays down Welbeck and Henderson moves after Chelsea win
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso refused to confirm Chelsea are interested in signing the veterans Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson after his first game in charge of the team, a 6-4 pre-season victory against Western Sydney Wanderers on Tuesday, but said he was looking to build a squad that had “proper balance”.

Chelsea are understood to be in talks over a surprise move to sign the 35-year-old Welbeck from Brighton, with the club also reportedly interested in signing the 36-year-old Henderson from Brentford. The links to two Premier League stalwarts reflects a revised transfer strategy under Alonso, with Chelsea seeking to recruit more experienced players into their squad as opposed to focused solely on signing young players, often tying them to lengthy contracts.

“I’m sure that from today to the last day of the transfer [window] there will be a lot of links, a lot of rumours, so to be commenting on all of them, it’s going to be a hard task,” Alonso said. “But for sure, we need proper balance in terms of qualities, in terms of positions, in terms of balance. We want to have a complete squad and we want to make a good team.”

The new Chelsea manager fielded a youthful side at the Accor Stadium at Sydney Olympic Park in Homebush, with Liam Delap and Tosin Adarabioyo the most experienced members of the starting lineup. Alonso waited until the 63rd minute to bring on a host of star names, including Cole Palmer and João Pedro. The Brazilian forward, who missed out on a place in Carlo Ancelotti’s World Cup squad, made a significant impact off the bench, scoring a hat-trick in just nine minutes as Chelsea took control of the game against their A-League opponents.

João Pedro scored 20 goals during an excellent debut season for Chelsea, having arrived from Brighton for £60m 12 months ago, and asked about the player’s mood before the upcoming campaign, Alonso said: “Very hungry. João is really, really determined to have a great season. He wants to, after a great last year, when he scored many goals. He wants to keep scoring more and more.”

A number of Chelsea’s youngsters showed plenty of promise, with the 17-year-old Dastan Satpayev opening the scoring after six minutes. The Kazakh forward is yet to sign officially for the club and is playing in pre-season as a triallist. His opening goal came from a defence-splitting pass from another teenager, Ryan Kavuma-McQueen, with Satpayev smashing the ball home at the near post.

Chelsea’s back four struggled in the first half against a lively Wanderers frontline and their reported new set-piece coach, Aston Villa’s Austin MacPhee, will have plenty to work on judging by the ease with which Brandon Borrello and Anthony Pantazopoulos won headers from a corner as the latter scored at the back post for the hosts.

View image in fullscreen João Pedro scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming on as a second-half substitute. Photograph: Mark Evans/EPA

The Wanderers took the lead through Aydan Hammond before a lovely finish from the Portuguese midfielder Dário Essugo made it 2-2 at the break. The goals kept coming in the second half when the left-back Landon Emenalo, who impressed going forward, saw his clearance deflected into the path of Dylan Scicluna, who put the Sydney side 3-2 ahead. Alonso then turned to his bench and his substitutions made an immediate impact. João Pedro held off a number of challenges on the edge of the box before pulling the ball back to Jamie Gittens, who fired home from close range.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But this topsy-turvy game, which felt like England’s third-place playoff against France at the World Cup and finished with the same scoreline, provided more entertainment as the Australian side went ahead for a third time after Estêvão Willian lost possession on the edge of his own area. Awan Lual was on hand to slide the ball through Robert Sánchez’s legs to put his side 4-3 ahead.

The Wanderers, who are also in pre-season, again failed to hold on to a lead as Chelsea overpowered a team that finished bottom of their domestic league last season. João Pedro looked sharp as he showed great composure to score twice in five minutes, before scrambling home an effort from a corner to wrap up his match-winning exploits.

João Pedro’s performance was in stark contrast to that of Delap, who has been repeatedly linked with a move away from west London. The 23-year-old endured another frustrating evening for Chelsea, going close on two occasions but failing to find the back of the net. Assessing Delap’s attitude since returning from the summer break, Alonso said: “I see him in a good mood, in a good desire to get proper fitness, proper football, feeling good and he’s doing great.”

Sports.title: Wrexham face Liverpool with Premier League still in their sights despite setback
Sports.content:
The Wrexham co-owner Ryan Reynolds called it a “punch-me moment” – his club playing Liverpool in a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium just five years after he and Rob McElhenney (now simply Rob Mac) completed their takeover of a club languishing in the National League. The knockout blow would be playing Liverpool at Anfield in the Premier League in 2027-28 and the manager, Phil Parkinson, accepts there is expectation on Wrexham to complete their remarkable rise through the divisions next season.

Parkinson’s team face Liverpool with confidence in the Bronx on Wednesday having defeated Manchester United and Leeds in pre-season so far and moved on from the anguish of missing out on the Championship playoffs on the final day of last season. The near-miss was undoubtedly a setback to an ambitious club’s grand vision but finishing seventh in the Championship at the first time of asking, Parkinson insists, was an accomplishment that should not be dismissed lightly.

The Wrexham manager said: “If we’re honest, to say five years down the line we’d have finished seventh in the Championship we would have said that was going to take some going. To get three promotions back-to-back-to-back is unheralded. Even though there’s always been ambition within the club and we’ve had resources, to take the club from the National League to seventh in the Championship is a lot of big steps and particularly the one last year. League One to the Championship is a huge step.

“Of course we would have loved to have got in the playoffs but I think the staff and the players should be really very proud of their achievements because that was a tough ask, especially with making so many changes.”

Wrexham are among the favourites for promotion next season but are the only Championship club not to make a signing – though a deal for Crystal Palace full-back Danny Imray is close – and will not be the only well-funded team with that aim, given the parachute payments available to relegated West Ham, Burnley and Wolves.

“I think the division is going to be stronger this season with the teams coming down,” Parkinson says. “We’ve got work to do within the squad to make us competitive again. We’re close to one signing but we need several more before the window closes. We have to be patient and we will be, but the squad’s not where we want it to be, to be competitive to meet the demands of a Championship season.
