Sports.title: Where to watch Liverpool v Wrexham plus UK kick-off time, squads and location
Sports.content:
Where to watch Liverpool v Wrexham plus UK kick-off time, squads and location

Liverpool continue their American tour against Wrexham tonight as they look to build on a winning start under Andoni Iraola.

The Reds defeated Premier League rivals Sunderland 4-2 in Nashville, Tennessee on Saturday despite missing several key players.



3 Jacquet is not being rushed into the matchday squad due to the risk of injury Credit: Getty

Wrexham also got off to a fying start Stateside, edging Leeds United 3-2 in their pre-season tie, after defeating Manchester United in Helsinki.

The Championship side will aim to beat a third top-flight opponent of the summer as they look to build momentum ahead of another promotion push.

Liverpool also face Monaco and Como this pre-season before their Premier League opening against Newcastle on August 23.



Where to watch Liverpool vs Wrexham

The fixture will be played on Thursday, July 30.

It is scheduled to kick off at 12:30am BST (7:30pm local time).

It will take place at the Yankee Stadium in New York - home Major League Baseball side, the New York Yankees.

It will be available to watch on All Red Video, Liverpool's dedicated streaming service.



All Red Video costs £42.99-a-season while you can also claim a 14-day free trial before paying £4.99-a-month.

All Liverpool's pre-season games can be viewed via All Red Video on their official website.



Liverpool are next in action when they face Leeds at Chicago's Soldier Field on Sunday while Wrexham take on Sunderland in Pennsylvania on the same day.

3 Iraola has a completely different project at Liverpool than he did at Bournemouth Credit: Getty

Liverpool vs Wrexham: Squads

Injury-prone Joe Gomez lasted only ten minutes before being forced off against Sunderland, as Iraola called it 'the worst news' of the day.

It was reminder to the Reds that they may need to call in reinforcements and cannot rely on Gomez to stay fit for an extended period of time.



Netherlands duo Cody Gakpo and Virgil van Dijk returned to training on Tuesday but are not in the USA yet.

Liverpool

Keepers: Giorgi Mamardashvili, Freddie Woodman, Vitezslav Jaros, Bailey Hall, Harvey Davies.

Defenders: Joe Gomez, Jeremy Jacquet, Milos Kerkez, Conor Bradley, Giovanni Leoni, Kostas Tsimikas, Jeremie Frimpong, Luke Chambers, Calvin Ramsay, Calum Scanlon, Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Midfielders: Wataru Endo, Dominik Szoboszlai, Curtis Jones, Harvey Elliott, Trey Nyoni, Josh Abe, Stefan Bajcetic, James McConnell, Kieran Morrison.



Forwards: Federico Chiesa, Hugo Ekitike, Lewis Koumas, Rio Ngumoha, Will Wright, Josh Sonni-Lambie.

Wrexham

Keepers: Arthur Okonkwo, Danny Ward, Callum Burton.

Defenders: Callum Doyle, Lewis Brunt, Max Cleworth, Dominic Hyam, Liberato Cacace, Dan Scarr, Zak Vyner, Aaron James.

Midfielders: Josh Windass, George Thomason, George Dobson, Ben Sheaf, Ollie Rathbone, Lewis O’Brien, Ryan Barnett, Matty James, Elliot Lee, Alex Moore, Harry Ashfield, Ryan Longman.

Forwards: Davis Keillor-Dunn, Kieffer Moore, Sam Smith, Nathan Broadhead, Bailey Cadamarteri.



3 Wrexham have beaten two Premier League teams prior to their game against Liverpool Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Liverpool vs Wrexham: What's been said

Following Liverpool's win over the Black Cats, Iraola said: "It's the first day, you could feel the heavy legs, the players have been training.

"So, we lacked some freshness. But it will give us a good starting point to improve things."

Meanwhile, Wrexham boss Phil Parkinson has been impressed by his sides performances.



He stated: "The lads will be pleased. Although it’s only pre-season, to beat a Premier League team is a feather in our cap and we’ll take it.

"It was a really good workout in very humid conditions. You have to be here to understand how tough it was but I thought the lads acquitted themselves really well.

"The work of all the lads on the pitch tonight was so good. The higher up you go, teams give you more problems with their movement and their rotations but the communication was just so good and it was a great exercise for us tonight.

"It was a good performance to take us into the Liverpool game."

Sports.title: Toby Alderweireld takes aim at Cristian Romero and admits Tottenham standards have dropped
Sports.content:
Former Tottenham defender Toby Alderweireld believes the club 'don't have the same standards' compared to when he was there.

He also took a swipe at club captain Cristian Romero, claiming the team can't always rely on him to deliver.



4 Alderweireld made a total of 236 appearances for Spurs Credit: Getty - Contributor

During Alderweireld's six years in north London, Spurs recorded three finishes in the top three and never ended a season lower than seventh.

The Belgian also helped the club reach the final of the Champions League and the League Cup, although both ended in heartbreak.

But since he exited in July 2021, Tottenham have finished inside the top four once, recorded successive 17th-place finishes and churned through five managers.



The only saving grace of the gloomy period was a Europa League triumph in 2025, which ended Spurs' 17-year wait for a trophy.

Alderweireld acknowledged that the silverware was 'good', but he couldn't ignore the alarming performances that had led to Tottenham's repeated flirts with relegation.



Spurs 'cannot have a season' like 2025/26 again

"On the other hand, you see that the team is struggling and they don't have the same standards anymore than we had," Alderweireld told Andy Goldstein and Andy Townsend on talkSPORT Breakfast.

“I think when I arrived, almost every season we got in the top four. We challenged for the title.



“Unfortunately, we didn't win it but I think there were difficult times as well because we left White Hart Lane, we went to Wembley, then we went to the new stadium.

“But still, we did well. Now you see that it hurts a little bit the last two years, but I see some difference now.

“The transfers that they did, it's all positive. I think it's Premier League-proven players because that's something you need. You cannot have a season like last season.”

4 Spurs finished just two points outside of the relegation zone last season Credit: Getty



When pressed on what he meant by his claim that the standards in north London had dipped, Alderweireld added: “I’m not every day in that group and it's easy to say this where I am. But my feeling is, in my time, everyone was so proud to play for the badge. We worked so hard. We did everything for the club and sometimes that's something I miss.

“You hear some things, you read some things about the captain (Romero) and he's not there. Then you get the red card and you don't feel like they are really involved.

“It's easy to see it from the outside but in my period it was totally different.”

Alderweireld: Romero can be 10/10, but you can't always count on him

Alderweireld was especially critical of Romero's disciplinary record, which has proved detrimental to Spurs in recent seasons.



Romero was sent off twice in the Premier League last term and missed a total of six games through suspension.

In fact, the 28-year-old has been sent off an alarming six times in all competitions since making his Spurs debut in 2021.

4 Romero seeing red has becoming a frustratingly familiar sight for Spurs fans Credit: Getty

No other Premier League player has matched that figure in the same time span, with his disciplinary record unsurprisingly being condemned by sections of the club's fan base.



Alderweireld noted such turbulence at the back for Spurs was rarely, if ever, an issue during his time at the club thanks to his formidable partnership with Jan Vertonghen.

“First of all, I think he's an unbelievable player. On his day, you see it with Spurs, Argentina, he's so good," Alderweireld said.

“The other thing is, for me, and I can only say how I see a centre-back, you have to have a standard from six out of 10, seven out of 10, eight out of 10. Sometimes he's 10 out of 10.

“Sometimes with a red card or with some sort of action, you think, hmm, that's not what a team needed now.



“For me, the centre-back pairing is so important in the team. If you compare Romero with Jan and myself, I think that's a big difference.

4 Vertonghen and Alderweireld were a dream partnership for a long time

“You can count on us and that's, for me, the most important thing. Like I said to Romero, an unbelievable player but sometimes he wasn't there.

Romero's ill-discipline with Spurs could become a thing of the past though, as the World Cup winner has held talks with Inter Milan over a summer switch.



Should that move eventuate, Spurs would have ready-made replacements thanks to the summer additions of Jan Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi.

Van Hecke was signed for £52million from Brighton while Senesi joined as a free agent having departed Bournemouth upon the expiry of his contract.

Sports.title: FA hit out at Infantino with England among teams who could boycott World Cup in shock shake up
Sports.content:
FA hit out at Infantino with England among teams who could boycott World Cup in shock shake up

The FA have responded to Gianni Infantino's plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Infantino intends to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would retain control of FIFA tournaments.

3 The FA have slammed Infantino's plans to sell stakes in the World Cup Credit: Getty

However, the remaining shares in events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup could then be sold off.

His plans have been met with widespread criticism, namely from UEFA of which England is a member, who could boycott the World Cup in response.

FA statement

The FA have now issued an official statement of their own hitting out at the FIFA president's proposal.

In a statement, they said: "We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached.

"Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved.

"When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further."

Infantino's plans have prompted discussions with the Donald Trump administration over potential investment.

Meanwhile, he intends to run the FFE as commissioner if re-elected as FIFA president.

The 56-year-old is currently set to run unopposed for a final term through to 2031.

However, his radical proposal has prompted further criticism of Infantino, who was already under fire following the World Cup and the manner of Folarin Balogun's suspended ban.

3 Infantino's plans have been met with widespread opposition Credit: Getty

The USA forward was cleared to play against Belgium in the last 16 after his red card ban was suspended for a year amid pressure from Trump.

Although Infantino has fired back at his critics, the FA have now joined UEFA and CONCACAF in opposing the plans.

UEFA and CONCACAF respond

European football's governing body issued a stern response after news of the proposals emerged.

Their statement read: "This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross.

"UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.

3 Infantino had already been under pressure for his relationship with the Trump administration Credit: Getty

"None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell."

Meanwhile, CONCACAF, the governing body for North, Central American and Caribbean football echoed UEFA and the FA's stance.

They explained: "CONCACAF was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release.

"We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

"We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.

"As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, FIFA, the Confederations and every Member Association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.

"This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the FIFA family will act in the same manner."

Sports.title: When does new Premier League season start? Opening weekend fixture dates and kick-off times in full
Sports.content:
When does new Premier League season start? Opening weekend fixture dates and kick-off times in full

The new Premier League season is now just a few weeks away.

With the World Cup summer now over, the top-flight is ready to return.

4 Mikel Arteta's champions face Coventry on the first day of the new season Credit: Getty



And Coventry will get the new campaign underway with their first game back in the Premier League for 25 years seeing them travel to champions Arsenal.

All 380 games for the 2026/27 season were confirmed in June and also sees newly-promoted Hull hosting Michael Carrick's Manchester United on the opening weekend.

Liverpool, under new manager Andoni Iraola, travel to Newcastle with a fit again Alexander Isak, who swapped the north east for the north west in a £125million transfer last summer.

Tottenham travel to Brentford and feel they have the right manager in charge in Roberto De Zerbi who guided them to safety on the final day of the 2025/26 season.



Xabi Alonso's first game as Chelsea manager takes him to Fulham on Monday night, while it could be a different looking Man City side that takes on Bournemouth with Elliot Anderson in the middle.

When does the season begin?

Arsenal, winners last season, begin the new season on Friday, August 21 as they take on Coventry at the Emirates at 8pm.



The top-flight opener will be exclusively live on talkSPORT.

Hull host Manchester United at 12:30pm on the first Saturday of the season - also on talkSPORT - while Brentford vs Tottenham is the 5:30pm match and there are a trio of 3pm games.

Newcastle vs Liverpool is the first 4:30pm Sunday match of the new campaign.



And Fulham vs Chelsea rounds off the opening weekend on Monday night, again live on talkSPORT.

Opening day fixtures Friday, August 21 Arsenal v Coventry City, 8pm - talkSPORT EXCLUSIVE Saturday, August 22 Hull vs Manchester United, 12:30pm - talkSPORT EXCLUSIVE

Everton vs Crystal Palace, 3pm

Ipswich vs Sunderland, 3pm

Nottingham Forest v Leeds United, 3pm

Brentford vs Tottenham, 5:30pm Sunday, August 23 Brighton vs Aston Villa, 2pm

Man City vs Bournemouth, 2pm

Newcastle vs Liverpool, 4:30pm Monday, August 24 Fulham vs Chelsea, 8pm - talkSPORT EXCLUSIVE

Who do the promoted clubs play?

Ipswich are back in the big time having last played against West Ham in 2025 and losing 3-1.

Their first home game is against Sunderland but fans are still waiting to see who will be in charge following Kieran McKenna's exit.

Hull, who were beaten by Tottenham 7-1 in their last Premier League game in 2017, won't have it easier against a revitalised United side led by Carrick who was given the manager's role having guided them to third place last season.



"What a great game for us," Hull assistant manager Dean Holden told talkSPORT. "We had an incredible season last year to get promoted.

"I was sat doing an interview at a similar time last year talking about the Championship fixtures, and people were having us as one of the relegation favourites.

"So, what the club did to get promoted is nothing short of incredible. And to then see the fixtures come out this morning, it just all seems very real."

Elsewhere, it has been a long time coming for Coventry whose last Premier League game was in May 2001.



A trip to Arsenal first will delight manager Frank Lampard who will relish the test of playing the champions.

4 Hull City celebrate their return to the top tier by hosting Man United on the first Saturday game of the season, which is live on talkSPORT Credit: Getty

4 Lampard's Coventry go to Arsenal on the opening day and he host former club Chelsea in December Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Opening weekend live on talkSPORT

talkSPORT will be across all of the opening weekend's action with three games to be broadcast live on the station.



Our dedicated team will be at the Emirates as Arsenal kick off their title defence against Coventry.

Likewise, fans can catch all of the action from the MKM Stadium when newly-promoted Hull host United at Saturday lunchtime.

The weekend's exclusively live action on talkSPORT concludes with the west London derby between Fulham and Chelsea on Monday evening at 8pm.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app.

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

4 Xabi Alonso makes the short trip to Fulham for his first Premier League match as Chelsea boss Credit: Getty



Boxing Day is back!

The Premier League has addressed the packed festive schedule over the Christmas and New Year period with no two match rounds taking place within 60 hours of each other.

Fans will be delighted to know that the traditional Boxing Day schedule will return to its usual slot on December 26.

Just one Premier League fixture took place on Boxing Day last season sparking major backlash from fans.

But there will be no such controversy this time around with multiple games expected to be televised on the day, pending broadcasting picks.

Sports.title: ‘Damaged’ Gianni Infantino tipped to back down after UEFA’s threat to boycott World Cup
Sports.content:
‘Damaged’ Gianni Infantino tipped to back down after UEFA’s threat to boycott World Cup

Gianni Infantino may back down on his controversial plan to sell World Cup stakes to private investors - but he won't be resigning.

The reprehensible FIFA president has been plotting a scheme to further line his pockets by auctioning parts of football's greatest tournament.

5 FIFA, with its head, Gianni Infantino, is working with bankers at JPMorgan to raise billions ⁠of dollars Credit: AFP

Under Infantino's plans, which have led to discussions with the Donald Trump administration, a new company will be in charge of top competitions across both the men's and women's game.

The 56-year-old would be lined up to run the enterprise as its commissioner when his final FIFA presidency ends in 2031, assuming he is re-elected unopposed, as is currently the bleak situation.

What is Infantino’s plan?

Infantino, who boldly slammed his critics for ‘spreading hate’, would see FIFA retain majority control of a new subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), that consolidates broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing, and licensing – including those for the World Cup and Club World Cup.

He then plans to see the rest sold, partly to each of FIFA’s 211 national associations in stakes worth around $20million (£15m), with another portion farmed out to private investment.

The Times' chief sports reporter Martyn Ziegler, who broke the news, believes the immediate backlash has damaged Infantino's position.

He told talkSPORT Breakfast duo Andy Goldstein and Andy Townsend: “Some people said that they think he's pushed it too far and he's going to have to back down.”

When asked if Infantino would resign or walk away, Ziegler said: “Well, not resign. Back down and let things calm down and make another sort of money-making effort enterprise in a few years' time.

“So I still think that his power base is so strong that he will.

“This won't affect him in terms of his future as FIFA president, but I think it would certainly leave his position damaged.

“I think he would have to probably pull back on his ambitions of having the Club World Cup held more often or even bigger or even expanding the World Cup to 64 teams, which the South Americans are proposing.”

5 Figures close to the Trump administration have been consulted about Infantino's plan Credit: Getty

What could it mean for football?

Infantino's latest money-making scheme would undoubtedly increase pressure to maximise profits for new private investors.

The most obvious ways in which to do so would be to expand the World Cup to 64 teams, further ramp up ticket prices, and revitalise Arsene Wenger's campaign to make the tournament biennial.

“I first got wind of it on Monday,” Ziegler continued on talkSPORT.

“It took probably 24 hours to get it across the line because obviously there was kind of top secrecy around it.

“FIFA didn't want people to know about it. I clearly knew it was gonna be hugely sensitive, but a bit of perseverance and managed to get it managed to get it there.”

5 The investment would be led by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, through his Thrive Eternal fund Credit: Getty

5 Jared Kushner is married to US President Trump’s daughter Ivanka (left) Credit: Getty

When asked about what the impact will be and if it will make the game more expensive, he said: “I think it's probably bigger than that because if you say, if you've got private investors owning around about a third of the World Cup effectively, you know what they want is return on their investment. That means pushing for more money.

“It could be anything, it could be tickets, but it could be more.

“A bigger World Cup means more money. So 64 teams holding the World Cup more often means more money.

“We've known before that Infantino's tried to get a biennial World Cup every two years.”

Would that pressure increase? “Inevitably.

“They want it to be in the big market, so does that mean going back to the USA much more regularly than it has been because that's where the biggest return is. That's what the pressure will be.”

5 UEFA and FIFA are at loggerheads over several huge items within the game Credit: Getty

A World Cup without UEFA?

The dastardly plot has sparked fresh fury from UEFA, who have already accused FIFA of 'crossing a red line' after talkSPORT revealed that Infantino received a call from US President Trump asking him to review Folarin Balogun's red card at the World Cup.

European football's governing body are now said to be considering taking drastic action to prevent the plans to sell World Cup stakes - with a potential boycott even being floated.

talkSPORT understands European nations will discuss this in an emergency meeting this week to figure out the next steps.

To that end, Ziegler added to Wednesday's Breakfast show: “UEFA are a powerful confederation within their own right.

“They are going to hold some sort of a virtual emergency meeting of their 55 member associations in the next few days.

“I imagine one of the things they will discuss is whether they can threaten to boycott the World Cup? Is that realistic? A World Cup without the European nations is obviously not going to happen.

“It's meant to be in Europe the next time in 2030. We've got the Women's World Cup before then next year, so they could do it, but I'd say it's the nuclear option.”

Sports.title: Liverpool unveil new away kit inspired by iconic 1980s which includes old-school heritage crest
Sports.content:
Liverpool unveil new away kit inspired by iconic 1980s which includes old-school heritage crest

Liverpool and adidas have officially unveiled their brand-new away kit for the upcoming 2026/27 campaign.

The new strip is white in colour with red details, matching their iconic kit worn from 1985 through to 1988.

4 Alexander Isak donned the new Liverpool away kit in its unveiling Credit: Adidas

4 The shirt's white and red colouring throws back to the mid-1980s Credit: Adidas

The shirts also include a pattern that has been inspired by match tickets and season tickets at Anfield.

Liverpool players will also be kitted out in new red shorts and white socks, alongside their white shirts.

As for the goalkeepers, they will be wearing a purple kit, with Alisson modelling the shirt in released images.

What do fans think?

When images of the new look leaked a few months ago, fans on a Liverpool sub Reddit were pleased with what they saw.

"That is a thing of beauty," one wrote, while another added: "Take my money, adidas."

One supporter said this was the first time they had seen a leaked kit and liked it straight away.

Older supporters were reminded of the mid-80s look, which it takes inspiration from, with one adding: "Adidas are crushing it with retro-inspired kits," and another saying it resembled one of their favourite Liverpool kits, posting a picture of Kenny Dalglish alongside it.

What has adidas said?

In the unveiling of the strip, they explained the details and meaning behind the kit further.

"Featuring the adidas Trefoil logo and a heritage Liver Bird crest, the jersey celebrates one of the most memorable periods in Liverpool's history while combining modern performance innovation with football culture and style.

"Drawing inspiration from the away shirt worn during 1985-88, the design revisits an era synonymous with some of the club's most celebrated teams and players."

4 A heritage Liver Bird crest has been included on the fresh strip Credit: Adidas

4 And the Reds' goalkeepers will have a brand-new purple kit to wear Credit: Adidas

Liverpool, with Dalglish in his first season as player-manager in the 1985/86 season, ended as champions and FA Cup winners, while they recorded an incredible 29-match unbeaten run in the 1987/88 season.

Adidas continued: "It was a period that helped define Liverpool's identity on and off the pitch, creating lasting memories for generations of supporters and establishing a visual legacy that remains influential today.

"Built on a clean white base, the jersey is complemented by strawberry red and grey detailing throughout. The colour palette takes inspiration from classic Liverpool away kits of the era, delivering a look that feels familiar while being modern in its execution."

It has been 76 years since the Liver bird first appeared on the white away kit, which was worn in the 1950 FA Cup final defeat to Arsenal.

"A key feature of the jersey is the return of the heritage Liver Bird crest, positioned on the chest alongside the adidas Trefoil logo," adidas added.

"Together, these two iconic symbols reinforce the jersey's connection to the club's history, celebrating a partnership and period that remain deeply embedded in football culture.

"The V-neck collar and sleeve cuffs feature coordinated red and grey detailing, creating a sharp contrast against the white base. Complementing these elements, adidas three stripes run along the shoulders, completing a clean and balanced aesthetic.

"Built into the fabric is a bespoke engineered pattern inspired by historic Anfield match tickets and season tickets.

"References to vintage ticket stubs and archival graphic elements are subtly integrated throughout the jersey, creating texture and depth while paying tribute to generations of supporters who have passed through the turnstiles of Anfield.

"Designed for elite performance, the jersey features lightweight, body-mapped engineered fabrics that enhance fit and freedom of movement. Incorporating adidas' latest CLIMACOOL+ technology, the jersey helps regulate temperature through advanced moisture management and strategically placed ventilation zones."

A new kit for a fresh start

Liverpool's new away kit will be the first under new manager Andoni Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot as head coach in the summer.

It will also be the first away kit worn by Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz who are among the done deals already completed in the transfer window.

The duo could also be joined at Anfield by Bradley Barcola, with the Reds set to make an opening bid for the PSG star.

talkSPORT understands they value Barcola at £80million.

Fans could get a glimpse of the top, which is out now, when the club play their pre-season fixtures in America. Among the glamour games Stateside are Wrexham, Leeds with games at Anfield against Como and Monaco.

Sports.title: Football must rally against Gianni Infantino's brazen bid to put World Cup up for sale - this is the most blatant ambush to disfigure sport imaginable, writes JONATHAN McEVOY
Sports.content:
Football must rally against Gianni Infantino's brazen bid to put World Cup up for sale - this is the most blatant ambush to disfigure sport imaginable, writes JONATHAN McEVOY

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

It can now never be contradicted that Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump share a bone-deep appreciation of all that it means to best serve the world’s oldest and most popular game. Namely, the pursuit of money.

This endeavour has proved itself an enduringly compelling sport since the apple fell in the Garden, so it is as old as sin itself, and a pastime that today endangers bastardising modern football more deeply than any of the bank-lining panjandrums who went before them could ever have envisaged.

My goodness, others have tried hard to pollute sport. Juan Antonio Samaranch, the old Spanish fascist who sold the International Olympic Committee’s flaunted reputation for sporting purity all those years ago, gave it a good heave.

His self-acclaimed Excellency was reputed not to have earned a salary for his services in the name of progressing a vision set by the modern Olympics’ founding father Pierre de Coubertin. But in fawned-to, limousine-conveying grandeur he sold out his inheritance to dubious courtiers who militated against an ethic centred on guaranteeing a fair playing field for the youth of the world.

The youth of the world! Ha, if you will. The Olympic hymn, white doves at opening ceremonies, the oath sworn by an athlete on behalf of his fellow competitors in the name of honest competition. It was a pledge best uttered by the well-meaning, co-opted liar with crossed fingers behind his or her back.

We are, alas, inured to such hokum, a reality that reached its public apogee of infamy when Ben Johnson ran like a god in Seoul and was exposed as not quite the clock-defying deity we had hoped him to be.

Football needs to rebel against Gianni Infantino's (left) bid to sell the World Cup

Lance Armstrong, East Germany’s state-sponsored doping, the Fuentes drugs scandal in Spain, and so the list goes on. Indeed, WG Grace, cricket’s founding father, was no stranger to sharp practices in the Victorian Age. Old as sin itself, as we were saying, long before Allen Stanford, the Texan fraudster, promised huge, ill-begotten riches to cricket or LIV golf’s accumulators entered the stage with their distorting avarice bankrolled by Middle Eastern riyals.

Sport being traduced from within is endemic. Yet, we must still rail against this latest and unprecedented news, a departure in its arching scope, of Infantino effectively putting the World Cup itself up for sale to the highest bidder.

This when his chief elected responsibility as the head of FIFA, football’s world governing body and its supposed guarantor, is to preserve the verities of the game from malign speculators.

It is the most blatant and brazen ambush to disfigure sport in elected office imaginable.

To get back to Trump, and his recent phone call to Monaco-domiciled Infantino that represented the nadir of a largely successful World Cup. It all becomes clear, now.

We are speaking about the word Trump dripped into Infantino’s ear in his successful intervention to overturn US striker Folarin Balogun’s automatic one-match suspension. Political neutrality, a sine qua non of FIFA, was waved aside.

Infantino ludicrously claimed: ‘Potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide. It’s curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising.’

Trump scoffed at criticism of his meddling. ‘I understand sports well,’ the president bloviated, while admitting from the Oval Office that he did not know what a red card or its implications for a non-negotiable ban implied.

It is the most blatant and brazen ambush to disfigure sport in elected office imaginable

Infantino doubled down this week, opining: ‘To those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours, I want to say that while you are sitting behind, we at FIFA are on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering the best show in the world. We experienced no violence, no incidents, 100 per cent safety and security, only joy and happiness.’

Thanks, Gianni. The dots can be joined now. Who is lined up to be a major investor in the scheme to sell shares in the World Cup to private investors? None other than Joshua Kushner, brother of Trump’s in-law Jared, a key agitator in taking the World Cup to America.

Trump and Infantino, who gave the former the bogus bauble of a peace prize, never awarded before and likely never to be awarded again, are in cahoots, hence the smoke they blow up each other’s posterior. US bank JPMorgan is also cited as a willing owner.

Under Infantino’s scheme, a company would be established to control the men’s and women’s World Cups and the Club World Cup. Which brings us to the point about money and what Infantino would be set to earn as a result of his brainchild.

All bosses of sporting bodies think a lot about this, their personal riches. They do not earn as much as the star performers, mostly men, accrue in the sport they (the governors) ‘serve’.

This disparity rankles. They want to get as rich as they can and seek to devise ways to do so.

So Infantino would, as it is understood, take on the role of ‘commissioner’ of his new World Cup order once his stint as FIFA president expires in 2031, offering him the potential to earn £37.5million a year, a some tenfold increase on his current wages. He will no doubt talk of wanting to grow the game. This is part of the playbook you would expect. He butters up the 211 members/sycophants who buttress his position – he will stand unopposed in office – by offering these supplicants shares in his folly, worth £15million to sell as they wish. That is nice earning possibilities for backwater associations if they then sublet their stakes.

And then we have the grotesque spectre of World Cups being staged more regularly than every four years, a dilution of world sport’s premier event, as all the moolah-grabbers look to exploit television rights deals, sponsorship, (exorbitant) ticket prices and hospitality sales on a more regular basis.

Joshua Kushner (pictured), brother of Trump’s in-law Jared, is lined up to be a major investor

The old framework of four-yearly World Cups would be swept away, just as wantonly as ‘hydration breaks’ were introduced spuriously over the last few weeks, with their advertising allure to TV networks clear.

Four quarters, rather than two halves, was a notion mooted, by the way, by Sepp Blatter ahead of the previous World Cup in America in 1994.

This latest abhorrence is of a different order. This, as Joseph Conrad wrote of another unchecked empire, is ‘a flabby, pretending, weak-eyed devil of a rapacious and pitiless folly’.

The emphasis is on greed, and football should rise up against it.

Sports.title: FA 'deeply concerned' after being left in the dark over FIFA's controversial proposal to sell the World Cup - as UEFA 'threaten to boycott the tournament'
Sports.content:
The FA have deep concerns over FIFA’s leaked plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.

News broke on Tuesday that FIFA boss Gianni Infantino was considering selling parts of the tournament to private investors and forming a new company in a deal that could be worth around £15billion, which the governing body later confirmed in a hastily-issued statement.

The report added that Infantino could become the commissioner of that company once his role at FIFA ends in 2031, a highly lucrative position that estimates suggest could pay him more than $50million-a-year.

The investment bank JP Morgan is FIFA's financial advisor on the project while Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital is expected to lead the proposed investor group. Kushner is the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared. The Trump administration is understood to have been consulted.

FIFA hope to raise more than £3 billion for the venture from a diversified, global investor group. The group is thought to include sovereign wealth funds.

Should their plans be successful, FIFA intend to give each of their 211 member associations a stake in the company - which they can choose to keep or sell - worth £15million each.

In a statement, an FA spokesperson confirmed they had been left in the dark over the controversial proposals which have sparked outrage amongst the football community.

The statement said: ‘We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached.

‘Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved.

‘When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further.’

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also voiced opposition to the proposition.

'Let me say this very directly,' Burnham posted on X. 'Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

'The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell.

'Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out. Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will.'

The plans would see FIFA set up by FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a new company responsible for the 'operational delivery of FIFA tournaments' - including both the men's and women's World Cup.

FIFA claim their plans would help advance the FIFA Forward development programme, which distributes capital to member associations. The governing body hopes to increase funding from £6m to £15m for the 2027-30 international cycle.

FIFA would need approval from the FIFA Council and majority support from the FIFA Congress (the 211 member associations) to launch the new enterprise.

UEFA have already opposed the plans, while Concacaf and now the FA have raised concerns about the lack of consultation.

There are major concerns over what the proposals could mean for the game, including whether FIFA could increase the frequency of tournaments to create more opportunities for financial backers to see a return on their investment.

The Club World Cup and men's World Cup are currently held every four years. FIFA have previously explored the possibility of staging both tournaments every two years.

FIFA maintain that they have a duty to control the development of this project, with external investors holding only a minority stake in FFE and having no operational role.

Sports.title: UEFA 'threaten to BOYCOTT the World Cup' over FIFA's proposal to sell stakes in the competition in a move that could make president Gianni Infantino millions
Sports.content:
European nations are to hold discussions over boycotting the World Cup after UEFA hit out at a leaked FIFA plan to sell stakes in the competition in a move that could make its president Gianni Infantino millions.

News broke in The Times on Tuesday afternoon that FIFA boss Infantino was considering selling parts of the tournament to private investors and forming a new company in a deal that could be worth around £15billion, which the governing body later confirmed in a hastily-issued statement.

The report added that Infantino could become the commissioner of that company once his role at FIFA ends in 2031, a highly lucrative position that estimates suggest could pay him more than $50million-a-year.

The bank JPMorgan is said to be handling the process and the Donald Trump administration is understood to have been consulted.

The proposal has already received widespread criticism from across football, with one source telling The Times it would be a 'nuclear bomb' for the sport and another arguing it would 'potentially be much worse than the European Super League'.

Now, according to Sky, UEFA members are set to hold an emergency meeting this week to discuss the possibility of skipping the competition and other details to oppose Infantino's ideas.

FIFA are reportedly planning to sell stakes in the World Cup in a hugely contentious move

UEFA launched a strongly worded statement slamming plans that 'crossed a line' (pictured - UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin)

That could mean the likes of World Cup holders Spain, as well as semi-finalists England and France, would no longer take part in the competition.

It is understood the English FA were completely unaware of the proposal before it was made public, and UEFA, which has been critical of FIFA and Infantino's actions in recent times, hit out at the plans almost immediately.

'This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross,' they said in a statement. 'UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association.

'So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

'The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell.'

The potential boycott could come as early as next year, with the Women's World Cup set to take place in Brazil in the summer.

It's understood UEFA do have some pulling power, with UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin making it clear five years ago that European nations would not participate in a World Cup held every two years instead of the current four.

Infantino said: 'Our next stage of growth needs a structure built for it, one where the commercial side of the game operates as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world.

Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, was reported to be one of the potential investors

'Every FIFA Member Association should have an opportunity to seek a fair share of the available funding to shape its own future, deciding for itself rather than relying on others. This is about the democratisation of football worldwide.'

Former FIFA president Sepp Blatter condemned the governing body's reported plan.

'The close relationship between the FIFA President and the US President has reached a financial dimension that is deeply damaging football,' Blatter wrote on X.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham also hit out at FIFA on social media, writing: 'No one has the right to sell our game.'

'Let me say this very directly. Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

'The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell.

'Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out. Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will.'

If the move was to go ahead, the global football calendar would likely be affected.

Join the discussion Should world football be controlled by private investors or remain in the hands of fans and nations?

For example, the Men's and Women's World Cup may be expanded or held more regularly than every four years, while the Club World Cup could face similar changes.

As part of the proposal, all 211 member associations would have stakes that would make up 20 per cent of the total company and be worth around $20million (£15million) each.

That is a larger figure than many of their annual revenues, and they would be given the option to sell them to raise funds.

FIFA would retain a majority stake in the new entity and private investors would be able to take on minority stakes.

FIFA is a not-for-profit organisation and enjoys tax-free status at its HQ in Switzerland.

For the most recent cycle of 2022-2026, their revenue is expected to be around $15billion (£11.3billion) – much of which came from this summer's World Cup – meaning this would provide a lucrative opportunity for individuals to be involved in.

The Times added that the blueprint for the potential selling of stakes has been discussed among senior FIFA figures and potential investors, which could include Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared – and they have signed non-disclosure agreements.

Some of those potential investors are understood to have even spoken internally about 'buying FIFA'.

Infantino's proposed new role could be extremely lucrative. Figures close to the plan are said to see it on a par with the NFL, whose commissioner Roger Goodell earns about $64million a year.

The reports come at a time when Infantino is already under fire for a variety of reasons following the World Cup.

This includes the US visa restrictions that affected supporters and officials from many countries, the extremely high prices of tickets and Infantino's links with Trump, which came to a head after Folarin Balogun's red card was suspended following a phone call by the US President to the Swiss administrator.

When contacted for comment, FIFA confirmed plans to launch a new body called FIFA Forward Enterprise, which they described as a 'controlled subsidiary consolidating FIFA's commercial and event operations'.

They added that 'FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions,' and claimed the move would increase the funding available to all 211 member associations.

Daily Mail Sport also contacted the White House for comment.

Sports.title: Brazilian footballer is slapped with a potential six-month ban after HORROR leg-breaking tackle - as a court rules his suspension can only end when his injured opponent is back playing
Sports.content:
Brazilian footballer is slapped with a potential six-month ban after HORROR leg-breaking tackle - as a court rules his suspension can only end when his injured opponent is back playing

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Internacional defender Victor Gabriel has been handed an unusual suspension after seriously injuring Cruzeiro forward Gabriel Pec, a Brazilian court said on Tuesday, with the ban lasting a maximum of six months or as long as it takes Pec to recover.

During a Serie A match between the sides on July 22, Victor Gabriel was sent off after committing a rash challenge that led to a fracture of Pec's left tibia.

Pec, who moved to Cruzeiro from Major League Soccer side LA Galaxy this month, was making his debut in the match eventually won 2-1 by the visiting Cruzeiro.

On Tuesday, Brazil's Superior Court of Sports Justice (STJD) determined that a standard penalty for Victor Gabriel was insufficient in light of the severity of the incident.

'The offender may remain suspended until the injured party is able to return to training, respecting a maximum period of 180 days,' it said, adding that the decision could be appealed.

In an appearance during proceedings, Victor Gabriel expressed remorse, adding: 'It was a completely unfortunate incident.

Internacional defender Victor Gabriel has been given a ban that could last up to six months for this horror challenge on Cruzeiro forward Gabriel Pec that broke his leg

The severity of the injury was plain to see as blood poured from his leg during the Serie A clash

Gabriel has apologised for the tackle but his ban could also last until Pec is back in action

Pec laid stricken on the turf following the challenge with the pain etched across his face

Pec was eventually taken off the field on a mobilised stretcher as he faces the road to recovery

'I apologised to him and offered my help. I asked him to forgive me for not having had any ill intent, and all I could do at that moment was pray for him.'

The court also questioned the authenticity of the evidence provided by Internacional, which contained audio from the match's VAR, with the club's defense then asking for it to be disregarded as its veracity could not be proved.

In a statement on their website, Internacional said the law firm representing them had used an audio recording circulating on social media in its defense.

'Both the law firm and Internacional emphasise that they never intended to act in bad faith in any way within the context of the proceedings in question,' the club added.

'There was, however, a recognized error in the collection and use of the content presented in the player's defense, which was immediately acknowledged through an express request to remove the audio from the case file.'

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp given strict instruction about managing Germany days after making quit threat
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp given strict instruction about managing Germany days after making quit threat

It has already been an eventful start to Jurgen Klopp's reign as Germany boss

View 3 Images New Germany boss Jurgen Klopp has been given an early warning (Image: JOHN MACDOUGALL, AFP via Getty Images)

Jurgen Klopp has received some potentially unwelcome advice from a leading German football official. The former Liverpool boss has landed his dream job in the wake of Julian Nagelsmann's resignation following Germany's last-32 defeat to Paraguay on penalties at the World Cup.

‌



In his very first press conference, Klopp threatened to quit the job if media criticism became too fierce. Now, he has been told how to set up his team by German football legend and DFB sporting director Rudi Voller, who wants the team to copy world champions Spain.

‌



Voller also praised England but slammed Argentina, whose cynical approach has attracted widespread criticism since an ill-tempered World Cup final. Speaking at the International Coaches' Congress in Mainz, Voller said: "We, Germany, need to defend better. Many people held up Argentina as an example, and I thought that was a bad example.

‌



"All of a sudden, the Argentinians became the gold standard. I found it a bit hypocritical. I don't want a team that plays like Argentina.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

"That has nothing to do with football. Yes, they were world champions and, this time, runners-up. But, honestly, I don't understand the praise from so many people."

‌



Jurgen Klopp threatens to quit Germany manager job in his first press conference READ MORE :

Trent Alexander-Arnold's pick for England manager has just taken different job READ MORE :

Voller added: "Spain deserved all the praise. Not only for the way they kept possession and attacked, but also for the way they defended. They really are a role model. I also really liked England."

Klopp has a big job on his hands, given it has been a decade since the country won a knockout-round match at a major tournament. As fans saw during his time at Liverpool, he will do things his way and won't stand for any outside interference.

View 3 Images Rudi Voller has said what he expects from Klopp's side (Image: Rene Nijhuis/MB Media/Getty Images)

‌



He has already warned that he will walk away if he faces the same level of scrutiny from the German media as Nagelsmann and former Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund boss Thomas Tuchel.

He said: "I'm not doing this job for myself. I'm doing it for you. I'm taking this job even though I've seen how you've treated Julian Nagelsmann and Thomas Tuchel.

View 3 Images Klopp has given the media an ultimatum (Image: Markus Ulmer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

‌



"If tomorrow Jurgen Klopp is s*** then I will be gone. But if the DFB says, 'Come on, let's discontinue the job,' then that is it.

"And if you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace I will be gone, I'll just turn away. I love this job, but I'm always ready to call it quits."

Sports.title: UEFA nations could BOYCOTT World Cup in light of FIFA's plot to sell tournament
Sports.content:
European nations will discuss the possibility of boycotting the next World Cup in response to FIFA's controversial idea to seek private investment. FIFA's announcement on Tuesday has sent shockwaves through the football world - and efforts to stop the plans are now being plotted.

World football's governing body says it wants to create a subsidiary worth $20billion (£15bn) and then sell off 20 per cent of FIFA Forward Enterprise to investors to raise $4.2bn (£3.16bn). If FIFA's members vote through the idea then Thrive Eternal, an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, would lead the investors.

During Gianni Infantino's time as president, FIFA has embarked upon a rapid commercialisation; FIFA is predicted to make $13billion (£9.6bn) in the four-year cycle up to 2026 - an increase of 72 per cent on the previous cycle. Infantino's expansionism has solidified his power, but it seems this step could be one too far.

The ideas have been met with an immediate backlash with Prime Minister Andy Burnham issuing a statement on X: "Let me say this very directly. Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Andy Burnham delivers passionate World Cup defence in face of FIFA plan to SELL competition READ MORE :

"The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out. Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will."

And according to multiple reports, UEFA is organising an emergency meeting with its 55 members this week where they will plan their response. The Football Association was blindsided by FIFA's announcement and will join UEFA's members in deciding the next step.

A boycott of the next men's World Cup in 2030, which is set to be held across Spain, Morocco and Portugal, is one of the options on the table. The women's World Cup is next year in Brazil and could also be used as a threat to FIFA.

‌



In a statement on Tuesday, UEFA reacted furiously: “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross. UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

View 4 Images Aleksander Ceferin will lead the pushback to FIFA's plans (Image: Getty Images)

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

The English Football Association has revealed the plans came out of the blue and were given no prior warning. They said: "We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached.

‌



"Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved. When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further. "

CONCACAF, the federation that covers North America, the Caribbean and Central America have issued a statement of their own, condemning the plans.

That reads: "Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release. We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

"We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.

‌



View 4 Images Joshua Kushner, founder of Thrive Capital and brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law would reportedly lead the investors

"As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, FIFA, the Confederations and every Member Association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.

"This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the FIFA family will act in the same manner."

Despite UEFA's strong words, Infantino remains secure in his position at the head of FIFA, with the Guardian reporting that he has the endorsement of 200 members for re-election. He worked hard networking during the World Cup and is on course for a fourth term as FIFA president, in large part due to the exponential increase in revenue, which has made him extremely popular with smaller members.

‌



However, he faces a significant threat from UEFA, which represents the strongest powerbase of nations. There is precedent for such a threat forcing FIFA to back down: in 2021 FIFA dropped a proposal to stage the World Cup every two years after UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin and his members said they wouldn't participate.

Tuesday's bombshell has been compared by some to the European Super League debacle of 2021 when 12 clubs unsuccessfully tried to break away from UEFA to form a new competition. The backlash against FIFA's idea has been swift and forceful.

View 4 Images Gianni Infantino is facing a backlash (Image: DeFodi Images, DeFodi Images via Getty Images)

La Liga president Javier Tebas posted on X: "It doesn't seem like a reform. It seems like an electoral campaign financed with the future of football. Development cannot be used to buy votes or silences.

‌



"The competitions and commercial rights of FIFA are not the personal patrimony of Infantino. Whoever mixes politics, discipline, money, and power without transparency cannot lead anything. Infantino is not the solution to FIFA's governance. He is the problem. We are venturing deeper into the Iceberg and what remains to surface."

Football Supporters Europe said: “The World Cup is not for sale. Enough of this charade. FIFA member associations - and everyone who cares about the future of the game - must stand up to the man who wants to sell world football. Gianni Infantino must go.”

Sports.title: Liverpool’s dream final month of transfer window as Iraola reunion secured and Barcola signs
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s dream final month of transfer window as Iraola reunion secured and Barcola signs

Liverpool face a crucial few weeks in the transfer window with Andoni Iraola in need of both attacking and defensive reinforcements

View 5 Images Andoni Iraola desperately needs reinforcements (Image: Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Liverpool need to find a replacement for Mohamed Salah and strengthen their defence before the new Premier League season begins. Following a tough campaign under Arne Slot, the Reds switched gears to Andoni Iraola and are aiming for a return to glory.

‌



Iraola's success at Bournemouth, culminating in the Cherries qualifying for European football for the first time, turned Liverpool heads. Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz have both signed deals at Anfield with Salah, Andy Robertson and Ibrahima Konate all leaving at the end of their contracts.

‌



The Spaniard will be well aware that he still needs positional upgrades before the new season starts, and the wing is a priority. At least two new signings are required if the Reds have any chance of reaching the heights they achieved in Slot's first season or Klopp's successful reign.

‌



Here, Mirror Football has detailed exactly what Liverpool should do to end their transfer window in the best way possible.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Federico Chiesa confirms Liverpool future stance and reveals new role under Andoni Iraola READ MORE :

Sign a winger

Munoz was brought in for £34.5million last month in a deal structured over six years, amounting to just £5.75m annually. This means there remains a significant war chest to land a marquee winger, which is understood to be the Reds' biggest priority this summer.

‌



View 5 Images Bradley Barcola is Liverpool's No. 1 target (Image: Sarah Stier - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

A number of wide players have been touted for a move to Anfield, but Bradley Barcola remains Liverpool's number one target. The Reds' bid to land the French international received a timely boost at the weekend when it emerged that Barcola had rejected a fresh contract offer from Paris Saint-Germain.

One stumbling block in securing a deal for the 23-year-old, however, is PSG's reported £140m asking price, which would set a club record. Liverpool are unwilling to match that figure and will reportedly seek a middle ground, with negotiations between the two sides said to continue this week.

‌



Should they manage to bring him in for a reduced fee, Iraola would have one of the most electrifying attackers in the world at his fingertips. Barcola possesses skill and pace in equal measure, equally capable of leading swift counter-attacks and unpicking stubborn defensive blocks.

View 5 Images Pedro Neto is another great option (Image: Catherine Ivill - AMA/Getty Images)

His versatility to operate on either flank is an added bonus, affording the Reds boss the flexibility to deploy him on the left or slot him into Salah's role on the right. Should Liverpool fail to agree a lower price with PSG, however, Chelsea's Pedro Neto could be a worthy fallback option.

‌



Chelsea are not actively pursuing Neto's sale but the Portuguese would command a lower fee than Barcola, while still representing a versatile and Premier League-proven addition across the forward line.

Boost the defence

After securing a wide forward, Liverpool must shift their focus to their struggling defence. Even prior to Konate's departure, the Reds were light at the back, considering Joe Gomez's persistent time on the sidelines and Giovanni Leoni's lengthy recovery from an ACL injury.

The situation appears even more problematic now following Gomez's withdrawal due to injury in the pre-season friendly against Sunderland at the weekend, while new signing Jacquet was omitted as a precaution.

‌



View 5 Images Joe Gomez's injury spells trouble for Liverpool (Image: Ian Horrocks/Sunderland AFC via Getty Images)

If doubts exist over whether Liverpool possess sufficient depth before the campaign has even started, it suggests something is fundamentally amiss. Iraola acknowledged as much last Monday, when he delivered his second press conference and the opening one of Liverpool's summer 2026 pre-season tour of the USA.

The manager referenced right-back Conor Bradley's own rehabilitation from a serious injury and emphasised that, while he views Bradley as the club's long-term right-back, the club are seeking a "solution" to their centre-back and right-back concerns. As a result, it would be smart to recruit a defender capable of performing both roles to a high standard, as Liverpool's extensive list of injured defenders continues their recovery.

‌



Pursuing James Hill appears to be the most logical move for Iraola, given the defender flourished under him at Bournemouth last season. Across 29 league outings, Hill proved to be one of the Cherries' most reliable figures at the back.

While predominantly a centre-back, he made three appearances at right-back - a versatility that suits Liverpool well, given Iraola has identified Bradley as the long-term first choice in that position. Hill registered 11.16 defensive contributions per 90 minutes, won 65.5% of his aerial duels, and came out on top in 63.8% of his overall duels.

No central defender in the league won more aerial duels per 90 minutes than Hill (4.88), and he also showcased an ability to drive the ball in the forward-thinking manner Iraola wants from his defence, crafting an impressive 0.56 chances per 90.

‌



View 5 Images Andoni Iraola could bring James Hill to Anfield (Image: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

At present, there is virtually no chatter surrounding a potential exit from the Vitality Stadium. But that is precisely something Liverpool ought to change by stepping up their interest.

He would represent a vital addition to the squad, bolstering depth and filling a homegrown slot in the Reds' domestic and European squads.

Article continues below

With Hill and Barcola brought on board, Liverpool could head into the new season with genuine confidence in a near-unassailable squad - one capable of bouncing back from recent setbacks and striking fear into their rivals.

Sports.title: Not Man Utd or Liverpool – this is who fans are backing most to win the Premier League
Sports.content:
Not Man Utd or Liverpool – this is who fans are backing most to win the Premier League

Manchester United and Liverpool enter the new Premier League campaign under the guidance of new permanent bosses but don't feature among the most heavily backed teams to win the title

View 2 Images Arsenal are targeting back-to-back Premier League titles come 2027 (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

Premier League fans are hard at work casting their predictions for who will come out on top of the 2026/27 title race. But Manchester United and Liverpool remain outside picks for the crown despite major changes this summer.

‌



Michael Carrick has been handed the permanent reins at Old Trafford, while Andoni Iraola has replaced Arne Slot at Anfield. Manchester City also reached the end of an era after Pep Guardiola concluded his 10-year tenure at the Etihad, with Enzo Maresca named his successor.

‌



However, punters are largely going with consistency above all else as Arsenal have emerged as the public's favourite to retain their crown. Mikel Arteta's men finally ended a 22-year search for another league title last season.

‌



According to wagers taken by bet365 up until now, the Gunners account for 34.4 per cent of all outright title-winner odds placed. That's perhaps to be expected given Arteta's side are the outright favourites to retain the trophy at odds of 6/4.

‌

Somewhat surprisingly, 6/1 United come in third with 13.8 per cent of wagers to claim the crown in Carrick's first full season as manager. The Red Devils have been busy in the market already having added Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans to their midfield after a third-place finish last term.

Sports.title: Matheus Cunha put on notice at Man Utd as exciting transfer sealed
Sports.content:
Matheus Cunha put on notice at Man Utd as exciting transfer sealed

Manchester United have a couple of new faces in attack, which could spell bad news for Matheus Cunha

View 3 Images Matheus Cunha has been put on notice (Image: Getty Images)

Matheus Cunha has already shown why Manchester United spent big to bring him to Old Trafford. But the Brazilian's biggest strength has also highlighted one of Michael Carrick's lingering problems.

‌



Cunha offers craft, technical quality and clever movement in the final third, yet he is not the kind of explosive winger capable of leaving defenders trailing over long distances. That lack of outright pace was something United struggled with throughout last season, particularly when trying to stretch compact defences or launch quick counterattacks.

‌



Carrick's side still needs that dimension, but the head coach may now have two answers at his disposal. One is a familiar face in Marcus Rashford, who appears set to return to Old Trafford after an unsuccessful bid to secure a permanent move to Barcelona. The other is exciting teenage signing Tynan Thompson, whose biggest asset is his blistering speed.

‌



Although United's new-look front three of Benjamin Sesko, Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo has shown plenty of promise, one obvious weakness still stands out - a lack of outright pace on the flanks. That issue is most noticeable down the left side, where Cunha has featured for the majority of pre-season.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Man Utd stance on hijacking Chelsea's Danny Welbeck transfer after secret talks READ MORE :

Man Utd star takes drastic action as Ruben Amorim plots transfer reunion READ MORE :

The former Wolves star enjoyed a productive first campaign at Old Trafford, scoring 10 goals and supplying four assists. There is little doubt he has justified his arrival. However, his strengths lie in his technical quality, creativity and intelligent movement rather than explosive pace, meaning United still lack genuine speed threat in wide areas.

‌



As a result, Carrick's side sometimes struggled when matches became stretched, lacking someone capable of making penetrating runs beyond the defence and exploiting open space. That, however, may be about to change.

Rashford is one player who could solve that problem. The forward looked set for a permanent switch to Barcelona, but after the Spanish champions spent £70million on Anthony Gordon instead, Rashford's hopes of remaining in Catalonia appear dashed.

Should he remain at Old Trafford beyond the summer, Rashford would hand Carrick qualities that very few of his forwards possess - electric speed, direct dribbling and an ability to push opposition back lines deeper. Rashford is hardly a new face at United, but because Carrick did not work with him last season, his return would effectively provide the head coach with a fresh tactical option.

‌



View 3 Images Marcus Rashford could be exactly what Michael Carrick needs to improve his attack (Image: 2020 Soccrates Images B.V.)

United also have another rapid attacker in the shape of new arrival Tynan Thompson. The 18-year-old winger completed his move from Tottenham earlier this month in a transfer worth an initial £4million, with another £4million included in performance-related add-ons.

Whether Thompson becomes part of Carrick's senior squad this season remains uncertain, but his lightning pace and eagerness to attack defenders make him an exciting talent. Like Rashford, he brings a contrasting profile and could supply the penetration United occasionally lacked throughout the previous campaign.

‌



His arrival bears comparison with Ayden Heaven's move in January 2025. The central defender joined from Arsenal's academy as an 18-year-old for £1.5million and has since gone on to make 24 first-team appearances.

View 3 Images Tynan Thompson completed a move to Manchester United earlier this month (Image: Manchester United/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Thompson, an England youth international, scored 13 goals and provided six assists across Tottenham's Under-18 and Under-21 sides last season. Seven of those goals came in just seven UEFA Youth League appearances.

‌



The teenager became United's first attacking addition of the summer. Before his arrival, the club's transfer business had been centred on reinforcing midfield, with Chelsea's Andrey Santos and Aston Villa's Youri Tielemans both joining earlier this month.

United had also been closing in on Atalanta midfielder Ederson after reaching an agreement for the Brazilian, only for the deal to collapse before completion. Attention has since turned towards alternative midfield targets, with AS Roma's Manu Kone and Brighton's Carlos Baleba both reported to be under consideration.

Although much of the club's focus has been on strengthening the centre of the pitch, United are looking to continue bolstering their front line ahead of the new season, leaving stars like Cunha under pressure to retain their place in the starting XI.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
