Aiken would like to see a firm cap on the length that anybody can be detained on immigration grounds, remembering that this is not a criminal sentence.

Global Affairs Canada said it is aware of "multiple cases" of Canadians in ICE detention, without providing specific numbers. An emailed statement from the department said consular officials attempt to contact detainees to help facilitate a return to Canada when appropriate.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

Came out a changed man: friend

Herman does not know how long it will take to get out of Adelanto, but assumes it will be via deportation.

"Maybe they'll see me as such a nuisance, they want to get rid of me. Maybe they'll just want to torture me for a while and keep me here for some indefinite period of time," Herman said.

Complicating matters is that he must now depend on Global Affairs Canada and ICE to issue paperwork required to deport him back to Canada, he said.

Consular officials told him he needs certain travel documents to get on a flight back to Canada, because he must prove he is a Canadian citizen before being allowed to board.

He said while he's in detention, he will help other detainees file habeas corpus requests — a legal mechanism that allows people who have been detained to challenge their imprisonment in court, and the procedure that freed him back in June.

Herman, who said he was served mouldy bread and "really awful mystery lunch meat" during his first detention in Adelanto, said the food in the new wing where he's now being held is slightly more palatable, but still "trash."

He's been eating out of nervousness, which was apparent during his video call with CBC, as he kept checking over his shoulder.

"[I] just can't help it, you know, when you're in a new place with 80 dudes," Herman said.

Sherry Owens, a friend of Herman's, says she's heartbroken to know he's back in indefinite ICE detention. (Zoom)

Sherry Owens, a friend of Herman's, drove him to his routine ICE check-in meeting last week. She had no idea she would leave without him.

"I was really kind of meditating on him coming out and saying, 'Let's get out of here. Let's go have a champagne breakfast somewhere,'" she said.

When an ICE agent came out and told her Herman was going back to Adelanto, she burst into tears.

"I was devastated. I was in disbelief," Owens said. "It's just so wrong."

Herman is a valued member in their community, she said. A local newspaper, the Ojai Valley News, said Herman was described by a friend as "very charismatic" and was known for the weekly dinner parties he and his late wife threw.

But Owens said Herman came out of detention a changed man from the trauma he endured, appearing distracted or distant at social gatherings and often opting to be alone.

"A lot of time was just spent in his little one room with his cats, just cuddling," Owens said." I think they bring him … more relief than any human can at this point."

Herman teared up when describing seeing his cats — Poquito, left, and Butters, right — for the first time in seven months after his release from ICE detention in June. (Robert Shepyer/Ojai Valley News)

Owens is helping to care for Herman's cats, Poquito and Butters, while he's in detention, and will make sure they're reunited with their "daddy" should he be deported to Canada.

As for Herman, he has a message for Global Affairs Canada.

"I just hope they just keep me in mind. Don't forget about me."

World.title: What is open-weight AI, the tech behind Kimi K3 that's turning heads in Silicon Valley?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

China's latest high-powered AI model is here — but if you thought it was just another chatbot, think again.

Beijing-based company Moonshot released the weights of its Kimi K3 model on Monday — meaning the parameters that guide the AI's answers are now public. Anyone can now download the weights and tweak them for their own purpose.

The freedom and lower price tag of open-weight models is turning the heads of business leaders in the west, where the merits have prompted letters from top tech leaders warning against restrictions on open models, despite the potential for security risks.

So what are open-weight models, and why are so many tech leaders talking about them? Here's what you need to know.

What does open weight mean?

AI models are trained on huge amounts of data. During the training process, the model's knowledge and understanding is encoded in "weights" — a set of numbers that dictate how the AI behaves and responds to prompts.

With open-weight models, those numbers are made public.

Founder of Moonshot AI Yang Zhilin delivers a speech in Beijing, China, on March 25. (Tingshu Wang/Reuters)

Think of it like a recipe, says Nicolas Papernot, a Canada CIFAR AI Chair and professor at the University of Toronto who studies AI security. Sharing the weights is like publishing a recipe for a cake, with the ingredients and their amounts listed so other people can bake it — and make substitutions.

On a practical level, making the weights available means that anyone with an internet connection and a powerful enough computer could download the model and use it.

"This makes already available open-weight models an affordable and accessible approach to using AI, since little experience is needed for common applications," Papernot said.

Many models that come out of China release their weights — including DeepSeek 's models, one of which drew lots of attention in 2025 when developers said they made it for less than $6 million US and claimed it could compete with North American tech while using less data.

WATCH | DeepSeek's rise in popularity in January 2025: DeepSeek AI app spikes in popularity, disrupts financial markets | Duration 2:49 An AI-powered chatbot from the Chinese company DeepSeek has become North America's most downloaded app. Its rapid ascent and low costs have disrupted financial markets and raised concerns among U.S. leaders in artificial intelligence.

The top five models on OpenRouter 's leaderboard, which gives access to hundreds of competing AI models, are all open-weight ones by Chinese companies.

Leading models from top U.S. companies like OpenAI and Anthropic tend to be closed, though some of them do have open-weight offerings — Meta's Llama model , for instance. But a program like ChatGPT is not downloadable and has to be used as is, with whatever guardrails and limits the company that owns it puts in place.

Control and cost are pros for businesses

Right now, business leaders still mostly rely on a mix of in-house AI technology and big-name AI companies, according to Lian Jye Su, chief AI analyst at Omdia, a technology research and advisory group.

Over one million companies were using OpenAI products to power parts of their business as of November 2025, while Anthropic said it was powering more than 300,000 business customers a month before.

But Su says more businesses are beginning to adopt open models.

That’s partly because the companies behind closed models could change them or revoke access at any time, he said. And as more businesses become reliant on AI to run parts of their operations, Su says the idea of building critical AI systems on a technology that could in theory disappear is concerning.

Data privacy reasons are also a factor, according to Bidhan Roy, founder and CEO of AI startup Bagel Labs, which makes open-weight models. Because users download and run them on their own technology, he says there is no need to share sensitive data with an outside company.

And the freedom of an open model could also help solve new problems.

Last week, OpenAI said an agent powered by one of its models escaped containment during a recent security test and launched a hack on AI startup, Hugging Face.

WATCH | Open-weight model helped contain cyber attack: OpenAI models went rogue and launched cyber attack on start-up | Duration 0:56 OpenAI models went rogue during a security test, triggering a hack that compromised the infrastructure of the AI startup Hugging Face last week. AI's expanding capabilities fuel worries about security, as even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.

Hugging Face first tried to use a model from Anthropic to stop the attack, but said guardrails prevented it from being able to properly identify and contain the threat.

In the end, it was the open-weight model GLM 5.2 from Chinese company Z.ai that was used to contain the threat "very quickly," according to Hugging Face's head of machine learning, Yacine Jernite.

Then, there's the cost savings. Business users pay subscription fees to use top U.S. models, but because open-weight models can be downloaded and run for free, Su says the only cost is the servers required to run the AI.

That's especially important at a time when businesses have been trying to reign in soaring AI budgets .

Su says these pros have started to turn the tide in favour of open-weight models.

That includes top tech CEOs in Silicon Valley. On Friday, Nvidia, Meta, Palantir, Microsoft and other massive names in the field released an open letter in support of open-weight models, encouraging governments to avoid "premature" restrictions that would drive innovation away from the U.S.

LISTEN | Canada's AI minister defends new strategy: Front Burner 31:15 Minister defends Canada’s new AI strategy

OpenAI, Google, Amazon and others added their names over the weekend, while Anthropic's absence drew criticism .

In a blog post on Monday night , CEO Dario Amodei said open-weight models that don't have "dangerous capabilities" are a public good. He argued in favour of safety testing for all powerful models — open and closed — rather than a ban on open-weight models, which he said wouldn't prevent misuse by bad actors.

If anyone can tweak it, is it safe?

Those dangerous capabilities are something security experts are thinking about as open models flood the market.

Closed models could be easily shut down if things go awry, Papernot said.

"You have a kill switch because you're controlling how people access the model. In an open-weight model, anyone can download it off the internet and so there's no way to enforce who is using the model," he said — or how.

WATCH | Canada launches AI watchdog: Canada launches AI watchdog to oversee the technology’s safe development and use | Duration 1:50 Amid rapid global advances and deployment of artificial intelligence technologies, the federal government has invested millions to combine the minds of three existing institutes into one that can keep an eye on potential dangers ahead.

Papernot and a team of researchers recently used an open-weight model powered with extra tools to show how the technology could be used to launch a sophisticated malware attack , capable of modifying its approach depending on the target and moving between devices.

But he says limiting access to open models isn't the solution. For one, bad actors likely have access to closed models that researchers don't even know about.

"Open-weight models are not the threat themselves," Papernot said. "Restricting access is going to lead to further concentration of power that is detrimental to society."

For all the talk of bad actors, Chris Pal, a professor at Polytechnique Montréal and a CIFAR AI Chair, says there are plenty of good ones, too.

And as more of these high-powered, open-weight models emerge, Pal says testing for vulnerabilities is a role that AI safety institutes would be well placed to take on.

"These are the kinds of things that those kinds of institutes could be involved with — auditing powerful open-source models for these security questions to see just what they're capable of and potentially giving guidance to the public about what they should be watching out for.”

World.title: Israel says it asked Canada for permission for Netanyahu to use Canadian airspace
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The government of Israel told CBC News it sought permission from the government of Canada for wanted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to enter Canadian airspace.

However, the Israeli government spokesperson did not respond to a second question about whether that permission had been granted.

An Israeli government Boeing 767, known as the Wing of Zion, overflew Newfoundland and Nova Scotia carrying Netanyahu to Washington, D.C., where his agenda included a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and attending the funeral of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham.

The Israeli leader has been sought by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza since Nov. 21, 2024, when the ICC issued an arrest warrant for murder, persecution and using starvation as a method of warfare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously said that he would arrest Netanyahu if he came to Canada. His predecessor Justin Trudeau had made the same pledge.

Spokesperson Audrey Champoux of the Prime Minister's Office declined to say whether Canada had granted permission, but said: "Canada does not currently link its overflight policy to law enforcement objectives except where an imminent security risk is present. This policy is regularly reviewed."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's flight can be seen entering Canadian airspace and traversing Newfoundland, the first of three provinces it overflew. (ADS-B Exchange)

"Relatedly," she said, "Canada continues to call on Israel to comply with international law and abide by the terms of the ceasefire, including allowing humanitarian aid to enter Gaza. Additionally, we further call on Israel to respect Lebanon’s territorial integrity and adhere fully to the ceasefire."

Additionally, spokesperson Charlotte MacLeod of Global Affairs Canada (GAC) told CBC News that "Canada is committed to upholding international law and the decisions of international judicial bodies. Canada's position remains that, as a State Party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, it must comply with its obligations under the Statute and under international law."

Carney government refuses to comment

But the same spokesperson declined to say whether the government of Canada had granted permission for Netanyahu to enter, suggesting that it was up to the leader of Israel to decide whether to use Canadian airspace. "Global Affairs Canada does not comment on which route a foreign state chooses to take."

"As a matter of law, it isn't up to Benjamin Netanyahu to choose where he gets to fly" if that means flying over Canada, said Mark Kersten, who teaches international law at the University of the Fraser Valley and wrote the book Justice in Conflict: The Effects of the International Criminal Court's Interventions on Ending Wars and Building Peace.

Canadian airspace is Canadian sovereign territory, which has no legal limit in terms of altitude, but which is usually held to extend to the Kármán line, 100 kimometres above sea level, where outer space begins.

Therefore an airplane overflying a country enters its national jurisdiction and is subject to its laws the moment it crosses its maritime boundary.

Kersten said that allowing Netanyahu to overfly Canada sends a dangerous message and sets a precedent that other foreigners may seek to take advantage of.

"When we're thinking about territorial integrity, you don't just think about the land," said Kersten. "You think about the seas nearby and the air above."

Kersten says it would be a mistake to take comfort in the fact that Netanyahu's plane did not land in Canada.

"It is our airspace. We have sovereign rights over that airspace. And whether it’s Netanyahu, or a Russian spy plane — and especially at a time when our sovereignty is being consistently called into question by the United States — it’s critical that we defend our sovereignty and that we articulate clearly to everyone that we will defend, and are in full control of, our territory, our coastal waters and the airspace above them."

Throwing caution to the wind

The government of Israel appears to have been more cautious when planning earlier prime ministerial flights from Tel Aviv to the United States, which manoeuvred to avoid Canadian airspace.

The Wing of Zion took a time-consuming, evasive route to the U.S. on Sept. 25, 2025, carrying Netanyahu over the waters of the Mediterranean and Atlantic rather than by the shorter, Great Circle route that passes over Greece, western Europe and Canada.

When Netanyahu flew to New York in September last year, his jet aircraft made several maneuvers to stay mostly over water and avoid certain countries' airspace, including that of Spain. (FlightRadar24)

But when he travelled again on Dec. 29, 2025, he overflew Newfoundland and Nova Scotia en route to Florida. On Feb. 10 of this year, he was back over Canada, crossing Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick before entering U.S. airspace in Maine.

Canadian protocol requires foreign government flights to seek permission well before entering Canadian airspace.

"Applications for foreign state, military or scientific aircraft to operate within Canadian territory should be submitted at least three working days (72 hours) before the proposed date of entry into Canadian airspace," reads the government's website. "This advance notification is critical."

“It seems implausible that [the government of Canada] didn't allow this to happen on some level,” said Kersten.

Two possibilities

The fact that Netanyahu crossed Canadian airspace does not mean that Canada granted permission, and Israeli officials have only stated that they requested permission, not that they received it.

It's possible that Canada has refused permission, and the government of Israel has chosen to violate sovereignty anyway. If so, the government of Canada has allowed violations to pass with no public response.

Kersten said that Canada's commitment to do what it can to deliver war crimes accused to The Hague is "unambiguous ... and if they aren’t going to be surrendered to the ICC, then at least their world is supposed to shrink."

Kersten says the overflight undermines both international law and Canadian sovereignty.

"We seem to be playing fast and loose with a core sovereignty question at a time when I don't think Canada can really afford to not be clear as to whether it is willing to act to defend its own sovereignty."

World.title: What climate science can tell us about the lost world that inspired The Odyssey
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

By the time The Odyssey was composed, the Bronze Age palace societies that helped inspire its fictional world had been gone for centuries.

Palaces had fallen, trade networks had fractured and populations had shifted across the eastern Mediterranean. Now, a new climate study suggests that centuries of repeated severe drought added to the pressures on that collapsing world.

Published in Science Advances, the study models drought conditions from roughly 1400 to 900 BC, overlapping the collapse of Mycenaean palace society in Greece and the Hittite state in what is now Turkey.

Cave formations, lake sediments, pollen and other natural records had already shown evidence of drought. The new model helps explain how several natural climate patterns may have aligned to intensify it, offering a historical backdrop to the scarcity and upheaval that echo throughout The Odyssey's fictional world.

The ruins of Mycenae, one of the great palace centres of Late Bronze Age Greece. Mycenaean palace society began to collapse around 1200 BC as prolonged drought and other shocks destabilized the eastern Mediterranean. (George Pachantouris/Getty Images)

A slow drying, then sharper shocks

Katherine Power, the study's lead author and a PhD student in physical geography at Stockholm University, says the model found a long-term shift toward drier conditions across parts of the eastern Mediterranean. Several shorter-term climate patterns then aligned in ways that intensified drought around the time of the Late Bronze Age collapse.

Those shorter droughts would not necessarily have been catastrophic on their own, Power said, but because they occurred on top of a long-term drying trend, their effects were amplified.

"Everything sort of happened at once, and that was very bad luck for them," Power said.

Power and co-author Qiong Zhang, a professor of physical geography at Stockholm University, reached that conclusion using a computer model that simulated 8,000 years of climate change, including shifts in Earth's orbit, greenhouse-gas concentrations and interactions among the atmosphere, oceans, vegetation and soil moisture.

Power says the combined effects could have meant shorter wet seasons, weaker harvests and strained water supplies, adding pressure to already stressed societies.

"We never want to say that climate was the sole driver," Power said. "We want to say that climate may have exacerbated problems that were already going on."

Claes Jansz. van der Willigen's 17th-century painting The Burning of Troy depicts Aeneas and other refugees fleeing as the legendary city burns. In Virgil's Aeneid, Aeneas escapes Troy and becomes an ancestor of the Roman people. (Finnish National Gallery)

When connected systems fail

Lynn Welton, an assistant professor of Near Eastern Archaeology at the University of Toronto, praised the study for showing how the region's climate changed over time and placing local evidence within a broader regional picture.

In the Late Bronze Age, the eastern Mediterranean was bound together by trade, diplomacy and political alliances, allowing disruption to spread when major centres weakened, Welton told CBC News from Tell Tayinat, an archaeological site in southern Turkey that preserves evidence from the transition between the Bronze and Iron Ages.

"What characterizes this period is the disintegration of a lot of the international systems that existed during the Late Bronze Age period, but how different regions responded in the subsequent period varies quite a bit," Welton said.

The Lion Gate at Hattusa, capital of the Hittite Empire in present-day Turkey. The Hittite state was one of the major powers disrupted at the end of the Late Bronze Age. (Bernard Gagnon)

Writings from the period also point to food shortages and dependence on grain shipments.

"We have some texts that seem to indicate that there were droughts or famines," Welton said. Other records describe poor harvests and reliance on grain shipments from elsewhere.

If harvests failed in several places at once, she says, trade could no longer provide the same protection.

Welton cautioned that the term "collapse" can obscure as much as it reveals. The Hittite state ended and the Mycenaean palace economy disappeared, for example, but she says that doesn't mean communities everywhere vanished. Some cities continued with little evidence of destruction, she said, while others show newcomers, changing material culture and political reorganization.

"Not all regions collapsed at the same time, at the same rate, in the same ways," Welton said.

J.M.W. Turner's 1829 painting Ulysses Deriding Polyphemus depicts Odysseus sailing away after escaping the one-eyed giant who imprisoned him and his crew when they entered his cave in search of food. (The National Gallery, London)

The imagined age behind the poem

Centuries after the Bronze Age palace societies disappeared, The Odyssey imagined a heroic world of palaces, warriors, vulnerable households and perilous journeys. Most experts agree that the poem cannot be read as evidence of a historical drought or Bronze Age migration. But its recurring concerns — scarcity, displacement and social disorder — echo pressures familiar in a region shaped by environmental and political upheaval.

Jonathan Burgess, a University of Toronto professor emeritus of classics and author of The Travels of Odysseus, says the poem doesn't preserve one clearly defined historical era.

"It's just a hodgepodge," Burgess said. "The material and cultural aspects of Homer come from different time periods."

A recurring theme in the poem is the role of food insecurity in shaping the epic's action.

"Hunger is very important," Burgess said. Because their wanderings are unplanned, the crew repeatedly arrives in unfamiliar places without reliable provisions.

"They don't know where they are. They're just landing at places here and there."

Friedrich Preller's 1865 painting Ulysses' Companions Steal the Cattle of Helios depicts hunger driving Odysseus's crew to kill the sun god's sacred cattle. (Kunsthalle zu Kiel)

Their search for food helps draw the crew into the cave of the Cyclops. Later, adverse winds trap them on the island of Helios until their supplies run out. Facing starvation, the crew kill the sun god's sacred cattle despite repeated warnings.

"They'd rather eat now and drown later than just die by starvation," Burgess said.

Scarcity also threatens order in Ithaca. Cattle represented wealth as well as food, he said, and the suitors consume Odysseus's livestock, wine and stores without replenishing them.

"It's a major interruption into a small and perhaps fragile food economy," he said.

WATCH | Why does The Odyssey remain relevant to this day?: CBC News speaks with Jaclyn Neel about why The Odyssey is still relevant to this day | Duration 7:28

Wanderers and difficult returns

The environmental and political upheaval of the period sharpens one of The Odyssey's central images: a displaced warrior struggling to return home in a world where food, shelter and belonging are never secure.

"Odysseus is lost much of the time or he's delayed by circumstances," Burgess said. "Homer goes out of his way to say that Odysseus eventually got home, but he did so alone."

Odysseus loses his fleet and repeatedly depends on others for food, shelter and passage. When he finally reaches Ithaca, he finds his household occupied, its resources consumed and his authority challenged.

That long struggle, Burgess says, is central to the story's emotional force.

"It's sort of a paradox," he said. "The story about travelling and not being able to reach home — being delayed from reaching home — makes Odysseus sympathetic."

In the poem, Odysseus reclaims Ithaca — but the real palace world that helped inspire it survives only in ruins, fragments and myth.

World.title: Canada urged to welcome Haitians fleeing U.S. deportations as Trump ends protected status
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Montreal refugee advocates say they are hearing from a growing number of Haitians in the United States who are considering coming to Canada after the Trump administration moved to end deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of people.

“They're real stressed. They don't go out. They stay in their apartment,” said Thierry Jean-Baptiste of the Bureau de la communauté haïtienne de Montréal (BCHM).

“They order groceries. They are in fear of ICE.”

This comes after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way last month for President Donald Trump's administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitian and Syrian immigrants of a humanitarian status — called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) — which protects them from deportation.

The U.S. first ​provided TPS to Haitians after a major earthquake in 2010.

Now, advocates are imploring Canada to withdraw from or modify the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA), which prevents some Haitians fleeing the U.S. — a designated "safe" country — from claiming asylum here.

WATCH | Haitians in the U.S. are looking to Canada for help:

Quebec advocates urge Canada to protect Haitian refugees fearing U.S. deportation | Duration 2:35 In June, the U.S. removed protections that prevented Haitians from being deported. Now, some advocates say Canada needs to rethink its Safe Third Country Agreement with the U.S. for Haitians seeking asylum.

Canada deporting people by proxy, advocates say

CBC spoke to a woman who came from the U.S. to Quebec this week, and has agreed not to name her because of the uncertainty around her immigration status.

She said she came because she feared being sent back to Haiti, which is facing political and economic instability and rampant crime.

“It’s very difficult because of the insecurity. You could get raped or assaulted. And then there’s no way to get around — nothing really works,” she said.

She has an advantage. Because she has relatives here, she can file an asylum claim and potentially stay. Canada still has a humanitarian moratorium on deportations to Haiti.

But for people who come here from the U .S. seeking asylum who don’t have family in Canada, it’s a different story.

“The problem is that under the Safe Third Country Agreement, many people would then be pushed back to the United States,” said Julia Sande, Amnesty International Canada lawyer.

Julia Sande, Amnesty International Canada lawyer, says Canada has a legal obligation to not send people back to Haiti either directly or indirectly. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Canada has this legal obligation to not send people to either directly or indirectly to face torture or persecution, she said.

By deporting Haitians back to the U.S., knowing they will be sent to their home country, “it's a violation of Canada's legal obligations. And so they know what's happening in the U.S. They know our systems are different and yet they're still pushing people back there,” she said.

Canada is essentially deporting asylum seekers to Haiti by proxy, according to Frantz André, an advocate for asylum seekers. He said that makes Canada complicit in a humanitarian crisis.

He said Canada should opt out of the STCA and welcome Haitians coming from the U.S. Otherwise, he said, Canada is effectively doing Trump's bidding — much as a "51st state" would — a reference to the president's repeated suggestions that Canada should join the U.S.

"Canada has the opportunity to show that we are a country, not a state, and we have the opportunity to show that humanity is still alive in our country,” he said.

WATCH | Temporary Protected Status to end for Haitians in U.S.: Push to let Haitians who’ve lost status in U.S. into Canada | Duration 1:57 More than 300,000 Haitians who have lived and worked in the U.S. for years are now at risk of being deported after the Trump administration terminated their temporary protected status. The move has ignited a push to let more of them into Canada.

Canada advises to avoid all travel to Haiti due to gang violence, kidnappings and civil unrest. The U.S. offers its citizens a similar warning, saying “do not travel to Haiti due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care."

STCA 'continually assessed': Immigration Department

In a statement, the federal Immigration Department said Canada has a proud humanitarian tradition and takes its international obligations regarding asylum seekers extremely seriously.

“Canada and the U.S. continue to apply the Safe Third Country Agreement to manage asylum claims at our shared border. The factors that were considered in designation as a safe third country are continually assessed,” the statement said.

According to Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) statistics, Haitians accounted for the highest number of asylum claimants processed at Canadian land border ports of entry in 2026 as of July 26.

The CBSA said it continues to monitor refugee claim volumes at the border but that current numbers have not triggered any contingency plans. The agency said it would not speculate on external factors that could influence asylum claims, including foreign government policies.

The agency also reiterated that asylum seekers arriving from the U.S. who do not qualify for an exception under the STCA are generally found ineligible to make a refugee claim in Canada and are returned to the U.S. as soon as possible.

CBSA said 827 asylum claimants had been removed to the U.S. under the agreement as of July 27 this year.

World.title: Japan PM says rescuers in 'race against time' for missing after powerful earthquake
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Soldiers and emergency workers combed through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors Wednesday after a powerful earthquake that killed at least 13 people and left many missing in southwestern Japan.

Bullet train services and some airport operations remained suspended and damage was still being assessed a day after the magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu.

"There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it's a race against time," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said. "We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can."

About 36,900 homes were still without electricity, 9,500 homes were without gas and communication networks were not working in some areas, chief government spokesman Minoru Kihara told reporters.

More than 9,000 people left their homes to stay in more than 500 shelters, and he said power sources were being added so the evacuation centres had air conditioning. Japan has had an ongoing heat wave, and temperatures in the area were forecast to exceed 32 C.

At least 13 people have been killed in the aftermath of a magnitude 7.1 earthquake. (The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images)

Japan's Self Defence Forces joined rescue workers in the search and rescue operations at the badly damaged Aeon Mall in the town of Kashima.

The building's second floor collapsed, trapping people, after an explosion suspected to have been caused by a gas leak. The number of people who still may be trapped was not available.

A chimney collapsed at the Nippon Paper Industries Co.'s Yatsushiro factory, trapping people under the debris, the Kumamoto emergency team said. As of Wednesday, seven people were feared still trapped. Two survivors and two bodies were removed, officials said.

Takaichi said the federal government was preparing to deliver food and other necessities to hard-hit areas. She also offered her condolences to the victims and sympathy to their relatives, while urging those affected by the quake to take care of themselves under the hot weather.

A mini truck is crushed by a fallen part of a pachinko parlor building, a day after an earthquake in Uki, Kumamoto prefecture, Wednesday, July 29, 2026.(Kai Naito/Kyodo News via AP) (Kai Naito/Kyodo News/The Associated Press)

The Kyushu Shinkansen bullet train remained suspended Wednesday. Aso Kumamoto Airport was resuming operations after closing one runway Tuesday, but officials said some flights may be cancelled.

Stone walls were damaged at Kumamoto Castle, a main tourist destination that was badly damaged in the 2016 quake and is still being repaired, Kyodo News reported.

"The shaking reminded me of the Kumamoto quake (10 years ago) and I was frightened," said Hiroki Shimoda, an official at Mifune town hall, who saw roof tiles of nearby homes crash to the ground.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that killed at least 50 people.
