There’s just one problem: the invitations only went out on Tuesday, and neither Kemi Badenoch nor Ed Davey will be in the room. The Conservative leader is sending the shadow health secretary in her place, while Davey will join by Zoom. Nigel Farage and the Green Party’s Zack Polanski weren’t invited.

Sam and Anne dig into what, if anything, today’s meeting could achieve.

Poland’s once-dominant Law and Justice party has split, with former PM Mateusz Morawiecki breaking with longtime leader Jarosław Kaczyński and preparing to build a rival force on the right. Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart examine whether the rupture offers current PM Donald Tusk a lifeline ahead of the 2027 election — and what it means in Brussels, where Morawiecki leads the European Conservatives and Reformists party.

They also look at plans to close Belgium’s Charleroi Airport for several months in 2028, leaving more than 10 million annual passengers, thousands of workers and Ryanair up in the air.

World.title: The French presidential candidate who wants to blow up the Franco-German engine
World.content:
Instead, Mélenchon wants France to strengthen ties with China as well as French-speaking countries in Africa, as well as South American countries. He sees the United States as an imperialist danger, while Germany — despite its turbulent relations with President Donald Trump — views the transatlantic relationship as paramount to its foreign policy. Mélenchon is opposed to Germany’s deeply held attachment to its free-market economic model and favors a planned economy instead.

Mélenchon is also critical of Germany’s rearmament and the continued presence of U.S. nuclear weapons on its soil, which he said: “raise serious security concerns for neighboring countries.” Berlin aims to become Europe’s predominant military power in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and American retrenchment from Europe.

Mélenchon’s 2015 book “Bismarck’s Herring,” subtitled “The German Poison,” was meant to be a response to the many politicians who at the time in France viewed Germany as a policy model thanks to its low unemployment and strong growth rates.

Mélenchon pointed to the poverty rate in Germany, which at that time was several points higher than in France, and low birth rates as examples of the model’s failures.

“My goal is to pierce through the veil of bliss surrounding so many commentators who are fascinated by Germany,” reads the book’s blurb. “A monster has been born right before our eyes — the child of deregulated finance and a country that has devoted itself to it, ravaged by the accelerated aging of its population.”

Parts of French media, even left-leaning outlet Libération, deemed the book excessively Germanophobic. In it, Mélenchon adopts a provocative tone and states that “political confrontation with German governments is one of the conditions for the liberation of peoples.”

World.title: As France burns, the far right sees an opening
World.content:
“All the proposals that we have been putting forward for years with Marine and Jordan [Bardella] … today we realize that those are the only ones that could have spared us these situations, from protecting us from wildfires to saving our children,” she said. “Current events, alas, prove us right.”

Whether that argument will gain traction remains uncertain. But National Rally may not need voters to see it as an authority on climate change; its opening lies instead in the declining credibility of the parties that have governed France — and a sense among some voters that the state is no longer capable of protecting them.

Recent research shared with POLITICO — based on four focus groups with former center and center-left voters who appeared unlikely to support those parties again — found repeated references to a country that was falling apart. Participants cited a series of recent crises, including the murder of an 11-year-old girl by a suspect previously known to police, as evidence that the government was failing to act.

Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella arrive to attend a ceremony in Nice, France on July 14, 2026. | Pool photo by Philippe Magoni via AFP/Getty Images

That frustration extends to climate preparedness. In a YouGov poll published this month, 74 percent of respondents said they were dissatisfied with Macron’s climate-adaptation policies.

“The National Rally mechanically benefits from its anti-system positioning whenever there is a news event that gives the impression, right or wrong, that successive governments have not taken effective action to address the difficulties faced by the French people,” said Mathieu Gallard, research director at Ipsos France, a polling firm.

The fires have burned more than 1,000 square kilometers across southwestern France since the start of the summer — an area roughly 10 times the size of Paris — and forced more than 200,000 people from their homes. Coming after an extreme heatwave left the countryside tinder-dry, they have already scorched nearly twice as much land as during the last devastating fire season in 2022.

World.title: What voters really think of Andy Burnham
World.content:
While there are still as many as three years to go before the next general election is called, Burnham’s arrival in No. 10 Downing Street — on the initial showing at least — seems to have changed the picture dramatically. Several pollsters in recent days have given Labour a small lead over Reform for the first time since the spring of 2025.

The POLITICO Poll delves deeper into voters’ first impressions of the new prime minister.

More than half the public — 54 percent — watched Burnham’s first speech on the steps of Downing Street after becoming prime minister, in which he set out his initial priorities for the job — and they gave him rave reviews.

Majorities agreed that he set out a clear vision for the country, that he’ll do the things he promised, and that he understands the problems that people like them face. He delivered the speech without notes or a lectern and voters seem to have approved of his communication style: Most said he is a good public speaker and his speech made them “feel more hopeful about the future” — a potentially significant mood shift, especially as Burnham promised to “bring back hope.”

That seems to have helped the new prime minister to make inroads among Reform voters — some of whom are former Labour voters the party hopes to win back.

Some 60 percent of Reform voters who watched Burnham’s first speech said they thought he was “a good public speaker.” One in three trusted that he would “do the things he promised” and said his speech made them feel more hopeful about the future. An even higher number — 44 percent — said Burnham “understands the problems facing people like me.” That’s more than the 38 percent of Reform voters who saw the speech and thought Burnham did not understand their problems.

World.title: Syria hunts down suspects in March coastal attacks, dismantles IS cells in Aleppo
World.content:
Syrian security forces killed two men accused of involvement in the coastal attacks of March 2025 and arrested several members of the so-called Islamic State group (IS) in separate operations across the country, authorities announced on Tuesday.

 

Brigadier General Abdulaziz al-Ahmad, head of Internal Security in Latakia province, said forces lured one of the suspects, identified as Sergeant First Class Bilal Adnan Dawood — also known as Abu Yaqub — into an ambush on the outskirts of the village of Falsqo in the Jableh countryside.

Dawood was travelling with Mohsen Ahmad Mansour, described by authorities as a commander in the Saraya al-Kummit militia. Both men were killed after opening fire and throwing grenades at the security force following repeated calls to surrender, al-Ahmad said.

Dawood was accused of orchestrating the planting of explosive devices targeting security forces and the Syrian army in the rural areas of Jableh and Tartus, and of leading one of the attacking units during the assault on the 107th Brigade in the village of Zama on 6 March 2025, an event Damascus describes as a "failed coup attempt".

A third man suspected of links to previous bombings was arrested during the same operation. Investigations are continuing, according to authorities.

Further attacks foiled

The March 2025 attacks on the Syrian coast killed more than 1,000 people, according to Syrian and international human rights monitors, and were carried out by fighters loyal to former al-Assad-era security structures in the Alawite heartland of Latakia and Tartus.

The Syrian transitional government described them as an armed insurrection, while critics accused security forces of reprisal killings against civilians in Alawite communities in the aftermath. The UN called for an independent investigation.

In a separate operation in Aleppo and its countryside, the Internal Security Forces and the General Intelligence Directorate arrested several IS members and dismantled cells in the cities of Aleppo and al-Bab.

Weapons depots, ammunition and explosive materials were seized. Authorities did not disclose the identities of those detained or the quantity of material confiscated.

The operations are part of a sustained security campaign across Syria. On 9 June 2025, the Ministry of Interior announced the arrest of 235 people on terrorism-related charges and said the Counter-Terrorism Directorate had foiled seven planned IS attacks over a three-month period in coordination with the General Intelligence Directorate.

In June 2025, the ministry also released figures showing it held detained officers and soldiers from the former regime's forces, ranging from generals to rank-and-file personnel, totalling several thousand individuals.

The IS or Daesh terrorist group, which once controlled large areas of Syria and Iraq and unilaterally declared a self-styled caliphate in 2014, has been significantly degraded but retains a network of sleeper cells in parts of Syria and Iraq.

The group has been responsible for a series of bombings and ambushes in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime in December 2024, targeting both the new security forces and civilians.

In November 2025, Syria joined the US-led international coalition against Daesh as its 90th member, signing a political cooperation declaration with the coalition, which has carried out military and security operations in Syria and Iraq since 2014.

World.title: Russia issues international arrest warrant for Telegram founder Durov
World.content:
Russia announced on Wednesday that it issued an international wanted notice for Telegram founder and CEO Pavel Durov over accusations of "complicity in terrorism".

 

"An international wanted notice has been issued... for the head of the Telegram administration, P Durov," Russia's main security agency FSB said in a statement.

Moscow is accusing Russian-born Durov of failing to remove channels, chats and bots used by Ukrainian intelligence agencies and "extremist organisations" that it says contributed to "attacks killing civilians".

The FSB said the platforms in question had aided "the preparation of terrorist attacks and cybercriminal activities in Russia, resulting in numerous human casualties, including women and children."

Russia's Investigative Committee said it was separately examining criminal cases involving the recruitment of teenagers into alleged terrorism and sabotage through a chatbot called "Dayvinchik/Leo" on Telegram.

The Kremlin frequently targets its political enemies on charges of supporting "terrorism" or "extremism".

Durov, who has lived outside Russia for years and holds French and UAE passports, described the case as politically motivated, saying on Telegram that the Russian authorities were seeking pretexts to restrict access to the platform inside Russia.

He has frequently clashed with the Russian authorities as Moscow has tightened its grip on the internet space.

Telegram is one of the most widely used communications platforms in Russia, with tens of millions of active users. Russian officials have made repeated attempts over the years to block or restrict the service, or to compel Durov to hand over user data.

Telegram was blocked in Russia from 2018 to 2020 before the ban was lifted without explanation. It has no end-to-end encryption by default but offers secret chats with that feature, and its architecture makes it difficult for governments to monitor.

Durov, 41, lives in France, where he has also faced legal issues over allegations over the spread of illegal content on Telegram.

Born in St Petersburg — Russian President Vladimir Putin's home city — Durov also founded VKontakte, a social media site widely known as "Russia's Facebook".

He was essentially forced out of the company as it came under pressure from the authorities in the mid-2010s, when he founded Telegram.

World.title: Czechia, Iceland and Spain among Europe’s top trending destinations for 2026, new data reveals
World.content:
The tourism industry continues to navigate a turbulent period with soaring jet fuel prices and the knock-on effect on travel costs. But amid all this, how is Europe faring?

 

Pretty well, or to be precise, “steady”, according to the Travel Insights 2026: Focus on Europe report published by Amadeus Travel Intelligence and UN Tourism.

Latest findings reveal that the continent remains resilient and continues to "hold up well overall", with passenger traffic having grown 2.3% as well as hotel occupancy up 2% from May 2025 to April 2026 compared to the year prior.

Europe remains the world’s largest tourism destination region, welcoming more than 130 million international tourists in the first quarter of 2026.

Reflecting a 4% increase, this builds on the “strong momentum of 2025”, the report said, with some European destinations having “benefitted from the redirection of tourism flow in March”.

Southern Mediterranean Europe and Northern Europe both saw a 4% increase in arrivals in Q1 2026, while Central Eastern Europe (+6%) consolidated its rebound. Arrivals in Western Europe recorded 2% growth in the first quarter of the year.

Where are travellers heading to in Europe?

Forecast air passenger volume and scheduled airline seats from April to September 2026 are expected to peak at just over 160 million, with the US, Spain and Germany being among the largest markets.

Aside from these top three, the report also found the strongest year-on-year growth from Japanese, Danish and Egyptian travellers to Europe at 19%, 11% and 8% respectively.

With regards to origin markets, Japanese travellers are the most likely to “pack their bags and travel to Europe”, the report said. A 62% growth in search from Japan translated into a 19% growth in bookings, surpassing Denmark, the next origin market in terms of bookings growth, by eight percentage points.

Just where is everyone travelling to?

Spain dominates as being both Europe's most searched-for and booked destination. However, Czechia ranked number one as the fastest‑growing booked destination among Europe’s top markets with year-on-year growth at 18%, ahead of Iceland on 11%.

The country also ranks highly among the top searched-for destinations within Central and Eastern Europe as well as hotel occupancy having risen from a 2026 new year slump to more than 60%.

Other destinations, including Iceland and Denmark, are also recording the strongest growth among the continent’s 30 most booked destinations.

According to the report, this signals a strong appetite among travellers for culturally rich city breaks and nature‑led travel in Northern and Central Europe, pointing to a shift away from what it calls “traditional tourism powerhouses”. The booking data also shows travellers are on the hunt for destinations that offer distinct experiences alongside seasonal balance.

Meanwhile, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan emerged as capturing travellers' attention online the most, with searches for both countries climbing 64%. Strong search growth also came from Switzerland (+36%), Sweden (+36%), Denmark (+34%), Ireland (+33%), Belgium (+32%) and Norway (+31%).

Southern and Mediterranean air routes and booking trends

Arrivals to Southern and Mediterranean Europe across July and August will reach a peak of almost 70 million in air passenger volume and scheduled airline seats.

Compared to anywhere else on the continent, the South and Mediterranean region is expanding air connectivity the most. Around 1,100 new flight routes have been launched in the past year, with 96 hailing from Germany, 58 from France and 51 from Italy and Spain. Among the emerging links are Slovakia to Spain, Ethiopia to Portugal, as well as China to Greece.

The report also found that travellers are booking their holidays well in advance. More than half of bookings, around 53%, to the South and Mediterranean region are made at least one month before departure, with the 61- to 180-day booking window accounting for around 26%, which is the largest share.

However, the region does still also see last-minute travel demand with around 29% of trips being made between one and 14 days before departure, with another 17% of travellers arriving 15 to 30 days from booking.

“Travellers are actively booking close to departure, creating space for flash promotions, weekend packages and dynamic pricing aimed at flexible last-minute demand," the report said.

Older travellers driving European demand

Who says wanderlust fades as you get older?

Europe-wide, adults aged 46 to 65 now account for approximately 30% of travel demand across the continent, which is the largest traveller demographic by age. This figure even increases slightly in destinations such as London, Paris and Madrid.

A previous report by Amadeus found that this demographic is especially interested in authentic local experiences, cultural discovery, wellbeing and a deeper connection to destinations.

“This mature, high-spending audience is well aligned with premium experiences and cultural offerings, while younger groups still hold meaningful share to support a multigenerational visitor mix,” the Travel Insights 2026 report said.

World.title: Wildfires: Europe on track for worst year on record as burned area reaches size of Luxembourg
World.content:
Spain is the EU country that's been worst hit by this year's wildfires, recording the highest share of burned land in Europe relative to its size in 2026.

 

That's more than 200,000 hectares, or around 0.4% of the country’s territory, according to the EU's Earth observation programme Copernicus.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez warned that difficult hours lay ahead, after more than 90,000 people were forced to evacuate areas around Madrid and Ávila.

Neighbouring Portugal is also facing a severe fire season, recording the EU's second-highest proportion of burned land, at 0.3%.

On Monday, every district in northern and central Portugal, along with the southern district of Faro in the Algarve, was placed under the highest fire risk alert.

Yet some non-EU countries, like Ukraine or Montenegro, reported even worse rates.

How much damage have the 2026 wildfires done?

France was another country hit hard, with around 260,000 people evacuated, and the southwestern department of Gironde suffering the worst damage.

Meanwhile, the EU as a whole could be bound for its worst wildfire season on record.

The bloc has already endured around 1,200 fires in 2026, which is more than double the annual average of 569, says the EU's Forest Fire Information System.

So far, more than 250,000 hectares have gone up in flames, according to figures from the European Commission. To put that into perspective, that’s roughly the size of Luxembourg.

Forest rangers take a break before returning to work on the fire near Condemios de Arriba, Guadalajara province, Spain, Wednesday, July 22, 2026 AP/Manu Fernandez

How are the fires affecting the environment?

Copernicus estimates that the 2026 wildfires have already spread more than 8 tonnes of CO₂ across the EU.

An average citizen emits around 5.55 tonnes over a whole year.

As "below-average rainfall" is also expected for this week, the situation is likely to get even worse, with "the strongest deficit stretching from France through the Alps and into the Balkans".

"Above-average rainfall spans Scandinavia and northern Europe, with the strongest surplus over Scandinavia," Copernicus said.

World.title: Sixth-generation wildfires multiply: why they are more dangerous and how to fight them
World.content:
The wildfires that broke out last week in France and Spain, which have already burned more than 115,000 hectares and displaced more than 320,000 people, have stood out for the sheer violence and scale of the flames. The French authorities admit that it could take months to extinguish them.

 

They are the latest examples of what the operational and scientific community has, since the second half of the 2010s, come to describe as "sixth-generation wildfires", especially after the fires in Pedrógão Grande in Portugal (2017) and in Greece (2018), each of which caused more than 100 deaths.

Burnt-out car on the road between Castanheira de Pêra and Figueiró dos Vinhos, near Pedrógão Grande, central Portugal, 18 June 2017 Armando Franca/Copyright 2017 The AP. All rights reserved.

This new pattern first became more evident in Europe, although it was also detected in 2017 in Chile, where it returned in an even more devastating form in 2024, a year in which 137 people lost their lives. These characteristics have also been observed in other latitudes, notably in Australia (2019-20), on the west coast of the United States (2020) and in Canada (2023).

The major shift in fire behaviour is driven by climate change, explains Domingos Xavier Viegas to Euronews, a professor at the Faculty of Science and Technology at the University of Coimbra (FCTUC) and an expert in rural fires. With higher temperatures, less rainfall and lower humidity levels, the soil and vegetation become drier, which greatly increases the "conditions for ignition" and the "area available to burn".

What sets a sixth-generation wildfire apart?

The destructive potential of these mega-fires stems from the energy they release, powerful enough to alter the weather conditions around them and to exhaust traditional firefighting methods, however robust they may be.

When more than ten megawatts (MW) per metre are released, the fire can no longer be extinguished through firefighters' direct action, Xavier Viegas clarifies. "If we translate this into flame length, a front that releases ten MW has flames roughly ten metres high," he adds.

"What happens is that, nowadays, we sometimes see fires which, in certain phases of their spread, reach intensities three, four, five, even six times higher. In other words, it is not possible to fight flames that can reach up to 60 metres in length," the specialist observes.

A thermal load of this magnitude means that this type of fire feeds itself, ceasing to be just a phenomenon controlled by the local atmosphere and starting to influence it as well.

Exceptionally dense smoke clouds are generated that carry intense heat, change wind direction, produce electrical discharges and hurl embers several kilometres away, triggering new ignitions.

Wildfire in Los Gallardos, near Almería, south-east Spain, 10 July 2026 Gregorio Marrero/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Out of season and in unusual regions

Sixth-generation wildfires are becoming increasingly frequent and, in the words of the University of Coimbra expert, "they are not an isolated event in summer". Take the case of Pedrógão Grande nine years ago, where the flames first broke out in June, still in spring, and later in October, already in autumn.

In addition, they occur over an "ever larger geographical area", notes Xavier Viegas. "In Portugal, these fires used to occur in the north and centre, and now, at times, they also appear on the coast and in the Alentejo, in regions where they were less common."

The same trend is seen in the rest of Europe, where the flames are no longer confined to the south: in recent weeks, central and northern countries such as Germany, Switzerland and Norway have been grappling with fires.

Wildfire in the village of Krokstadelva, in Drammen, Norway, Friday, 17 July 2026 Thomas Fure/Thomas Fure / NTB

This is a "global phenomenon" that demands an "integrated" approach, including in terms of prevention. "Even tourists need to be aware of this," stresses Xavier Viegas, referring to the recent wildfire in Almería, in south-east Spain, which led to the deaths of 14 people, 12 of them non-Spanish citizens. "They were not familiar with that reality," he underlines.

How can these fires be fought?

Ground resources and even the heaviest aircraft cease to be effective in halting the front of a sixth-generation wildfire. To protect people, property and infrastructure, the FCTUC specialist therefore recommends attacking the fire from the rear or from the flanks.

Areas of "discontinuity", or firebreaks, can be created, making use of any natural feature that may be present, for example a river or a zone without vegetation.

Another strategy is to open up a strip of land by "cutting the vegetation with tracked machinery" or to widen that strip "with the help of a backburn", something that "only the authorities can do". This operation is, however, risky if the wind is blowing strongly, as has so often been the case.

"Sometimes, an ember is projected beyond that barrier and, so to speak, all the effort goes down the drain," he emphasises.

In such circumstances, warns Xavier Viegas, pragmatism is needed to avoid tragedies. "Generally speaking, people expect firefighters to put out any fire, wherever it may be, and do not realise that there is a part of the fire that cannot be suppressed. We should not wish firefighters to risk their lives, not least because it is a hopeless struggle."

These fires are particularly devastating in forest environments because of fuels such as "vegetation and woodland". When they reach more urban areas, "they no longer have the same patterns of spread, and at that point houses and buildings can be safe places for people," he states.

Evacuating people to built-up residential areas is therefore a solution to consider.

"There are certain houses and buildings which, even if they were impacted by a fire of this intensity, could possibly withstand it and provide shelter," he concludes.

World.title: Skip the usual stays: These five hidden gem hotels deserve a spot on your holiday shortlist
World.content:
Looking for a getaway where the hotel is every bit as memorable as the destination itself?

 

Ranking guide La Liste has revealed the winners of its Discovery Gem Hotel Awards for 2026, recognising five little-known stays that are worth the booking.

Self-styled as "the world’s most selective guide for discerning gourmets and travellers”, La Liste compiles its rankings using 370 expert sources across 200 countries and 7,200 establishments to create its guide of the world’s top stays.

This year's Discovery Gem Hotel Awards feature just two European properties. Here are the five that made the cut.

Islas Secas Resort, Panama

This Panamanian private island resort sits in one of the most exclusive and secluded private island retreats in the Americas.

The hideaway of “casas” and “casitas", located in the country’s Gulf of David, Chiriquí Province, offers 14 bedrooms that can accommodate up to 20 guests. The residences, shaded by trees and cooled by the sea breeze, typically overlook sweeping views of the ocean.

Serving up seasonal, coastal flair, Islas Secas also caters to every diner.

“Dining at Islas Secas is flexible, and you get to choose where and when you dine,” the resort said, adding that guests can choose when and where they sample dishes – whether it's Panamanian barbecue or ocean-to-table dining.

Les Sources de Vougeot, Burgundy, France

Set in the heart of Burgundy, Les Sources de Vougeot occupies a 14th-century residence once inhabited by the Cîteaux Abbots.

Offering guests an insight into the “true essence” of the French region, the hotel has 49 keys, including Le Moulin, which can host two adults and features a private Nordic bath, terrace and private garden.

Unsurprisingly, the gastronomy concepts serve fine dining that showcases the region's dishes, through multi-course menus, starting at €90.

Beyond the dining table, Les Sources de Vougeot also offers insights into the heritage and craftsmanship behind local favourites, such as Dijon mustard, burgundy cheese, Dijon gingerbread and blackcurrant through workshops and guided tour visits to artisan producers.

Arctic Bath, Harads, Swedish Lapland

The only other European entry to make this year’s cut is a floating hotel and spa on the Lule River in Swedish Lapland.

Inspired by the region’s timber-floating heritage, the circular Arctic Bath hotel becomes a sight to be seen when it freezes into the river during the winters. The retreat includes 12 rooms and cabins, all designed with Scandinavian interiors and offering panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.

Its spa and wellness centre offers guests cold baths, sauna, hot pool and treatments, including clay, ayurveda, massage, scalp and mind, starting at 1,595 Swedish krona (€144.10).

During the winters, guests can also brave the cold on a husky tour, go dogsledding and enjoy other seasonal excursions.

The Six Bells Countryside Inn, New York, USA

Bringing a slice of the British countryside to the Big Apple with its design around the fictional English village of “Barrow's Green”, this boutique inn is a whimsical take on cottage-core, a digital subculture centred on a romanticised rural lifestyle.

With names such as Innkeeper's suite, Mildred's Plum and Double Duke, the hotel’s 11 rooms are part of the stay’s concept of being a “storybook you can sleep in”.

In contrast to the English theme, the restaurant and tavern is rooted in early American and traditional country cookery.

Gangtey Lodge, Bhutan

Overlooking the pristine Phobjikha Valley nature reserve in Bhutan, this luxury retreat places guests in the Himalaya’s most picturesque settings.

The property features 12 farmhouse suites, each kitted with hand-cut stone floors. The suites also have “bhukharis”, which are traditional wood-burning stoves, as well as free-standing English roll-top bathtubs set next to a panoramic, valley-facing window.

The Lodge's “5 Keys to Wellbeing” experience involves immersing guests in nature, wellness, spiritual experiences, learning about Bhutanese gastronomy and local culture and customs for physical and mental rejuvenation.

World.title: India news: Police issue FIRs over 'abusive' posts against Modi
World.content:
07/29/2026 July 29, 2026 Supreme Court orders release of minors arrested during CJP protest

India's Supreme Court has issued orders for the release of minors arrested during the CJP protests.

It said authorities must ensure surveillance footage is preserved after petitioners alleged police brutality against demonstrators.

Chief Justice Surya Kant also told authorities to preserve the digital and personal data of people who joined the protests, while also barring any coercive action against ​them, according to the Indian media.

The court also told authorities to ensure protesters' data was not made public.

Reportedly, the Supreme Court's intervention came after petitions were filed by student protesters and activists. The protesters seek ​action against police for allegedly using excessive force and pellet guns during the CJP rallies.

Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Whoever has committed excess ... atrocities on innocent people, the law will take care of them. For that, there needs to be a completely independent and fair investigation," Kant said, according to legal website Live Law, one of several outlets reporting the ruling.

"A probe is meaningless if ​no responsibility is fixed," he said, before ordering the interim steps.

World.title: US bans Chinese and foreign-made humanoid robots
World.content:
The Trump administration has banned the import of humanoid and quadruped robots manufactured outside the United States, citing national security concerns. The ban could strain diplomatic tensions with China.

The United States has announced a ban on the import of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots in a move which will likely exclude Chinese manufacturers from the US market and could strain tensions between Washington and Beijing.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Tuesday that "advanced robotic devices" produced abroad posed national and cyber security risks to the United States.

The decision was based on findings from a White House task force which concluded that foreign-built robots could create "a cybersecurity risk that threatens the security of critical infrastructure" and "the safety and security" of US residents.

The FCC defines the relevant mobile robots as devices weighing more than two kilograms that use sensors, network connectivity and software to achieve autonomous navigation, including the avoidance of obstacles.

Humanoid robots steal the show at German trade fair To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China dominates the market in humanoid robots

The market for humanoid and quadruped (also known as four-legged "robot dogs") is seen as a major international growth area, with US and Chinese companies competing to develop the technology.

And China has a clear lead, with analysts at Barclays estimating that Chinese-made humanoid robots account for around 85% of the global market share. Morgan Stanley experts predict that China's humanoid robot market could be worth $15 billion (€13.2 billion) by 2030.

"Chinese manufacturers have been scaling production and reducing costs faster than most overseas competitors," Morningstar analyst Kangyuxiao Li told the Associated Press.

In the US, firms such as Figure AI are already deploying humanoid robots on production lines, while tech giant Tesla plans to begin production of its "Optimus" robot this year.

Currently, however, US robot exports remain in their hundreds while Unitree and AGIBOT, two of China's biggest advanced robotics companies, each shipped more than 5,000 humanoid robots in 2025 alone, according to the technology research and advisory group Omdia.

FCC chairman Brendan Carr said the ban was also aimed at "secur[ing] America's critical supply chains."

But Li said the measures would not "materially slow China's overall humanoid development, given the size of its domestic manufacturing base and opportunities in other export markets."

Humanoid robots outrun humans at Beijing half-marathon To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump-Xi summit: the diplomatic ramifications

Beyond the industrial market effects, the FCC ban could also have diplomatic consequences ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping in September.

The US has already banned imports of Chinese-made drones and is considering restrictions on Chinese open-source artificial intelligence (AI) models, citing cybersecurity concerns including espionage, surveillance and data collection.

The Pentagon recently placed Unitree and several other major Chinese technology companies on its list of firms which it claims have links to the Chinese military, a claim that Beijing said it "firmly opposes."

"It's a steady drumbeat of potential flashpoints heading into [the] Trump-Xi summit," said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at New America, a think tank focused on Chinese technology policies.

Most humanoid robots are currently used for industrial applications in confined spaces, such as automobile factories or storage warehouses. Stationary industrial robots are to be exempt from the FCC ban but the definition could also cover advanced robot vacuum cleaners.

The FCC also added foreign-made power inverters to the list – devices that, among other functions, convert direct current from solar panels into standard alternating current, which can be used by the electrical grid.

The agency cited similar cybersecurity concerns, saying network-connected inverters could be remotely disabled or used to collect data.

Like the ban on humanoid robots, the restrictions on inverters are also expected to hit Chinese manufacturers hardest, given that they currently dominate the global solar inverter market.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

World.title: Europe wildfires: France expands mass evacuations as Spain battles record blaze
World.content:
Over 20 aircraft have been deployed to fight new fires west of Bordeaux, and Spanish firefighters fear two fires could merge west of Madrid. Scientists say climate change is fueling more extreme fires across Europe.

As Spain battled its largest wildfire on record and France carried out one of Europe's biggest evacuations since World War II, scientists warned that extreme wildfires are becoming more frequent worldwide.

On Tuesday, French authorities evacuated another 4,000 people from Atlantic coast resorts adding to the 220,000 other people fleeing a blazing wildfire in southwest France.

While new fires were reported in France's Gironde, authorities in Landes said the advance of the wildfires had stopped Image: Jeanne Accorsini/SIPA/picture alliance

Fresh fires broke out near the Atlantic resort of Grand Crohot west of Bordeaux, prompting authorities to deploy 23 planes and helicopters to contain the flames.

"The situation remains complicated. We're not out of the woods," said Sophie Brocas, the top government official in the coastal region of Gironde, where Grand Crohot and Bordeaux are located.

The Gironde wildfire has burned an area four times the size of Paris, and resisted the firefighting efforts of a dozen countries.

Evacuees allowed to return in Spain

In Spain, there was a respite for the evacuees as thousands of residents were allowed to return home after firefighters managed to contain major blazes.

However, authorities remained on alert for a fourth summer heatwave with temperatures expected to exceed 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) on Wednesday.

Spain's meteorological agency AEMET announced a new heatwave starting on Wednesday Image: Cordon Press/picture alliance

The biggest concern for firefighters in Spain was two large fires that had at times come close to merging into a single blaze in wooded hills to the west of Madrid.

In Avila, to the northwest of Madrid, a pyrocumulonimbus cloud was seen over the blaze. Scientists describe these clouds as fire-generated thunderstorms forming over intense heat sources like wildfires or volcanic eruptions.

"We are feeling a lot of anger and helplessness. It's something inhuman," 48-year-old gardener David Gonzalez said about the destruction caused by the fires in Avila.

Experts fear that incoming heat waves might cause the blazing fires to worsen.

Climate change exacerbating wildfires

Scientists say climate change is fueling hotter, drier summers that are intensifying wildfires across Europe. The warmer temperatures are also extending fire seasons and making these blazes harder to control, straining the resources of European nations.

Currently, the European Union only coordinates the deployment of extra resources pooled from its member states when a ​country requests emergency help. As fires on the continent grow more extreme, however, the bloc called for greater investment in forest management and wildfire prevention.

Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brussels is purchasing its own permanent firefighting fleet.

"Climate change ​is accelerating. So, our response must evolve just as quickly," Hadja Lahbib, the EU's Crisis Management Commissioner, told Reuters.

World.title: How Iran, Ukraine wars and El Nino could fuel world hunger
World.content:
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East haven't yet crippled global food supplies. Add a powerful weather pattern like El Nino, however, and the risks multiply.

A potentially record-strength El Nino is now intensifying across the Pacific, bringing either drought or flooding to the world's key farming regions.

Earlier this month, the US National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted a 63% chance that the unusual weather pattern could be "very strong" this year.

JP Morgan, meanwhile, warned last week that El Nino, combined with $100 (€88) oil prices, could spike food inflation by up to 1.5%.

The arrival of El Nino follows two major conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, during which global food supplies have held up remarkably well.

So, could this third crisis bring the perfect storm that tips the balance?

Are African nations underestimating the risks of El Nino? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Triple blow to global food security

Russia's war in Ukraine still hangs over one of the world's major grain-exporting regions, where repeated attacks on ports and farmland continue to threaten one of the planet's key breadbaskets.

The Iran war has driven up energy and fertilizer prices, raising the cost of growing food worldwide and causing temporary supply disruptions for key soil nutrients.

El Nino, which shifts rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, is expected to be so strong that the World Bank warned recently it could cut rice output by 20% to 50% in affected regions.

Maximo Torero, chief economist of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned of a "compound effect" that could create "a very complex situation" by the end of the year.

"We are very concerned about El Nino and the delay of the monsoon ... in India," Torero told DW.

El Nino is expected to slow down and weaken India’s monsoon season, a vital time for rice planting. June already saw around 40% less rainfall than normal, according to local media.

India produces nearly a third of the world’s rice, the vast majority of which is consumed domestically.

Aside from South Asia, the FAO thinks the El Nino risks are highest in Africa's Sahel region, southern Africa, Southeast Asia and in the Dry Corridor of Central America.

The UN food agency warned this month that some of these regions face a more than 50% chance of drought in the next few months.

World producing more food than ever

Despite the geopolitical strife, food prices remain nearly 20% below their 2022 peak, according to the FAO Food Price Index.

The world brought in the biggest grain harvest in history last year. This is because farmers planted more land, the weather has been favorable and the crops produced more per acre.

While this year is expected to be slightly smaller, the harvest will still be the second-largest ever.

“We are seeing improvements in agricultural productivity," Simone Bunse, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), told DW, citing India and Latin America as notable examples.

"These have helped sustain food production and reduce undernourishment. And this is balancing some of the localized impacts of conflict.”

UN experts expect a 50% chance of drought across much of southern Africa Image: Jekesai Njikizana/AFP/Getty Images

Millions still go hungry

War is a major barrier to getting hunger under control globally. The UN says 266 million people are still facing acute hunger, more than half of them due to conflict.

The worst of it is concentrated in just a handful of conflict-hit countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan and Yemen, where supplies cannot reach the people who need them.

"We have enough calories produced in the world to feed everybody," Torero said. "Those calories are not distributed in the same way across the world, and that's the challenge."

War often destroys local food sources, displaces millions of people, damages infrastructure and severely cuts humanitarian access. In some hotspots such as Sudan and Gaza, experts say hunger is increasingly being used as a weapon.

"Parties deliberately destroy farmland, livestock, water systems, food storage facilities, and transport routes. They jeopardize access to markets and obstruct humanitarian assistance," SIPRI's Bunse told DW.

Farmers pinched by elevated fertilizer prices

Another risk to global food supplies is fertilizer, around a third of which normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz. The strait remains heavily disrupted after a failed ceasefire between the US and Iran, along with attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.

Some farmers have been paying substantially more for fertilizer, delaying purchases or switching to crops that require less fertiliser. If they ultimately apply less, yields could suffer in the next harvest.

Food security experts believe the Middle East conflict alone could leave millions more people hungry by 2030 — and that projection does not yet account for the effects of El Nino.

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean expected to rise by 3.6 degrees Celsius (38.4 degrees Fahrenheit) — almost double the 2015/6 El Nino — climate think tank Berkeley Earth now predicts this year's weather pattern will be strongest on record.

If oil prices leap past $120 a barrel again, if grain exports from Ukraine are successfully blocked, or if El Nino bites harder into next year’s crops as farmers plant less, then the world could face a spike in hunger, experts predict.

If all of those happen at once, the impact would be far worse, with JP Morgan predicting that food inflation will surpass 5% in 2027 and that emerging markets would take the biggest hit.

Additional reporting by Daniel Winter.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: The Slovak village questioning its UNESCO status
World.content:
The picturesque village of Vlkolinec in Slovakia has been on UNESCO's World Heritage List since 1993. Vlkolinec was recently in the headlines for wanting to be taken off the list. DW visited the village to find out why.

From the headlines in the world's media, the story seemed simple: A tiny Slovak village wanted UNESCO to remove it from the World Heritage List because of the pressures of overtourism.

But that's not quite what is happening in Vlkolinec, central Slovakia.

Interviews with residents, local officials and visitors suggest that the debate was less about UNESCO itself than about how to protect a living community from the pressures of tourism.

Accelerated transformation

"Those who come with humility, to admire the village and understand how people lived here, are always welcome," said 68-year-old Anton Sabucha. "They don't bother me. It's the rude ones."

Sitting beneath an awning outside his wooden house, Sabucha leafed through a history of the village, pointing to photographs of neighbors and relatives. His wife brought out a tray of fried dough pastries.

Vlkolinec in bygone days: Anton Sabucha says that the village's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated its transformation Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW

He remembered when around 200 people lived in Vlkolinec. Today, only 17 remain year-round.

UNESCO did not create Vlkolinec's tourism problem. The village was designated a Folk Architecture Heritage Reserve in 1977, during the Communist era.

But Sabucha argued that its inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated the transformation, bringing visitors who too often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses.

Diminishing privacy

"You come out into your yard, wanting to sit quietly and have a coffee with your friends. Then the first tourist comes and asks, 'How are you? What's it like living here?' Then another. Then another," he told DW.

Sabucha has erected a barrier at the entrance to his property bearing the notices "No Trespassing" and "No Photos." He said that despite this, some visitors still wander into private gardens, trampling flowers and treating the village as an attraction rather than a community.

Vlkolinec resident Anton Sabucha says that some tourists often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses they come to admire Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW

"Someone sees the 'No Photos' sign and still has to take a picture. They simply don't respect people's privacy."

Disappearance of traditional village life

But the biggest loss, he said, has been the gradual disappearance of traditional village life.

The surrounding meadows are no longer cut, the old agricultural terraces have become overgrown and many of the people whose lives have shaped the landscape are gone.

Tourism income, he argued, has done little to reverse that decline.

Residents receive around €400 ($455) a year from ticket revenues — "barely enough to buy a pallet of briquettes for the winter" — while many of those who now earn a living from tourism no longer live in the village, he said.

"For an ordinary tourist, these are just wooden houses. For us, they're people. We know exactly who lived in each house."

A living village

Justine, a tourist visiting from France, said the village's appeal lay precisely in the fact that people still lived there.

"Usually places like this are museums. Here, people still live here. That's unique," she told DW.

When told that some residents wanted Vlkolinec removed from the UNESCO list because of tourism, she said she understood their frustration.

Why Vlkolinec, Slovakia, wants to lose its UNESCO status To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Having people walking around your village every day could become unpleasant," she said. "But at the same time, tourism also supports the region. It's difficult to know what's best."

UNESCO status helps preservation

Not everyone agrees that UNESCO is the problem.

Miro Parobek, who oversees tourism for the town of Ruzomberok, which administers Vlkolinec as a municipal district, acknowledged that tourism had brought challenges. But he argued that the answer was better management, not removing the village from the World Heritage List.

"Our first priority is to preserve the traditional architecture," Parobek told DW. "But our goal is also for this to remain a living village. We want to support the people who live here."

He said the town had already responded to residents' concerns by replacing large festivals with smaller cultural events, while residents now met regularly with local officials through a dedicated working group.

Miro Pirobek, head of Culture and Tourism in the nearby town of Ruzomberok, says that the priority is to preserve the traditional architecture of the village and support the people who live there Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW

The municipality also helped homeowners apply for grants to restore historical buildings and even provided twice-weekly transport into nearby Ruzomberok for older residents.

Parobek said every entrance ticket carried the same message: "Vlkolinec is not an open-air museum. Please respect the privacy of the people who live here."

Balancing tourism, heritage and residents' wishes

He acknowledged that the balance between protecting residents and welcoming visitors was not always easy.

Much of Parobek's optimism rested on plans that had yet to materialize.

Ruzomberok was seeking Norwegian funding for a package of measures aimed at reducing pressure on the village, including a park-and-ride below the hillside settlement, improved footpaths and drainage, the restoration of traditional barns and terraces, and the conversion of the former village school into a community and cultural center.

The project would also create more opportunities for local residents to work as guides and custodians, he said.

Is removal from the list possible?

Anton Sabucha is in a minority. But even if he somehow gets his wish, having Vlkolinec struck off the World Heritage List is an almost impossible task.

It looks unlikely that Vlkolinec will become the first site to be removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List at the request of its residents Image: Rob Cameron/DW

UNESCO has removed sites only three times since the program was established in 1978: Germany's Dresden Elbe Valley after the construction of a four-lane bridge, Liverpool's historical waterfront following large-scale redevelopment and Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary after most of the protected reserve was stripped of its status.

In each case, UNESCO acted because the sites had irreversibly lost the qualities for which they had originally been inscribed.

There is no precedent for a community asking to be removed voluntarily.

And there is no sign that Vlkolinec is about to become the first to succeed in its request.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with aiding terrorism
World.content:
Moscow has escalated its pressure on Telegram, accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.

Russia's Federal Security Service on Wednesday said it had charged Pavel Durov, the billionaire founder of the Telegram messaging app, with aiding terrorist activities.

The agency also issued an international warrant for his arrest.

The FSB said the charge formed part of "an ongoing criminal investigation" against Durov.

Why is Russia charging Durov?

The security service accused Telegram's management of failing to remove channels, chats and bots allegedly used to organize attacks and acts of sabotage inside Russia.

According to the FSB, Ukrainian intelligence services had used the platform to prepare and coordinate sabotage, terrorist attacks, mass killings and cyberfraud.

These actions, as well as crimes committed by what the FSB described as terrorist and extremist organizations, had allegedly caused numerous deaths, including those of women and children, as well as billions in material damage.

Soon after the news of the warrant broke, Telegram's account on X posted a picture of Durov giving a middle finger to the camera.

What does Russia say about Telegram?

Russia began restricting Telegram's operations in the country last August.

In February, communications regulator Roskomnadzor said Telegram was still failing to comply with Russian law and that restrictions would remain in place until the company met its requirements.

Putin's strategy behind Russia's largest missile attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russian courts have fined Telegram more than 100 million rubles (around $1.26 million, €1.1 million) since the beginning of this year, law enforcement sources told the Interfax news agency.

The penalties were imposed mainly for failing to remove content banned in Russia.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Monday said that officials had discussed restoring Telegram's full operations, but claimed the company's representatives had shown little initiative.

Who is Pavel Durov?

The Russian-born billionaire Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013. The platform currently boasts over a billion users.

Durov previously founded VKontakte, Russia's leading social network.

The tech mogul left Russia in 2014 after resisting demands to hand over user data, and is currently based in Dubai.

He describes himself as a libertarian and has repeatedly clashed with governments seeking greater access to the platform.

Durov has promoted Telegram as a defender of privacy and free speech, while critics say weak moderation has allowed propaganda, disinformation and criminal activity to flourish.

World.title: Germany: How weather extremes impact local agriculture
World.content:
Heat, drought, heavy rain and late frosts are taking a toll on German farmers. They increasingly respond with adapted varieties, new crops, modern breeding techniques and modified farming methods.

For many German farmers, the heat wave in late June couldn't have come at a worse time. While barley was already ready for harvest across much of Germany, the drought struck other crops during a particularly vulnerable stage of development.

"This year is another difficult one for farms," Horst Gömann of Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia Chamber of Agriculture told DW.

Corn has been particularly hard hit, as the extreme heat coincided with the flowering period, he said. "We're already seeing some corn plants failing to form cobs. That, of course, essentially amounts to a total crop failure," Gömann said.

In corn, the energy is concentrated in the cobs. If they're missing, yields plummet dramatically.

The heat wave in June, with peak temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius, hit other European growing regions even harder. According to a recent analysis by Coceral, the European association of grain traders, this reduced the value of the grain harvest in Europe by more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion), with France and Hungary suffering the greatest losses.

Due to the heat wave, Coceral lowered its expectations for grain production in the European Union and the United Kingdom by just under 9 million metric tons, a decline of 3%. The London-based research institute Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) even expects a 5% decline. Corn accounts for the largest share of the downward revision in Europe's grain forecast, representing about half of the adjustment.

A heat wave in late June impacted this year's harvest in Germany negatively Image: Boris Roessler/dpa/picture alliance

German farmers need to diversify

The weather also took its toll on wheat and barley. In some cases, barley was harvested several weeks earlier than usual.

According to Gömann, this year's barley harvest is likely to be slightly below average. For wheat, he expects losses of about 10%.

Risk diversification is therefore an important adaptation strategy. Instead of growing just one kind of grain, many farms are relying on different kinds with varying maturity rates.

"You never know when such extreme heat will strike," Gömann said. He explained that farmers who grow multiple varieties spread the risk across different stages of development.

Barley has a natural advantage in this regard. It matures earlier than wheat and often completes grain formation before the major early-summer drought sets in.

Experts say that irrigating is only worthwile with crops but not with all fruits Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

Fruit farming struggles with late frost and sunburn

While drought threatens crops in the fields, late frost is a major concern in fruit farming. Due to climate change and mild winter temperatures, flower buds, from which the fruit will eventually develop, form earlier. However, frosty nights can occur well into spring.

Many fruit growers, therefore, protect their blossoms with frost-protection sprinklers. Water is sprayed over the blossoms, forming a layer of ice. "This traps enough heat inside so that temperatures don't drop as low as they would without frost-protection sprinklers," explains Gömann. These systems can also be used for irrigation during long dry spells in summer.

There are also technical solutions for combating heat. Today, hail protection nets serve more than just protection against severe weather, as they also shade the fruit and prevent sunburn.

In addition, experiments are already underway in fruit and wine growing with semi-transparent photovoltaic films. They generate electricity and protect the plants from excessive sunlight while allowing enough light to pass through.

However, while irrigation is an important tool, Gömann believes it is not always economically viable. He said vegetables, potatoes and fruit generate high returns and justify the investment. He added that for grains or corn, irrigation is not worthwhile. "The costs are simply too high," he said.

The water comes primarily from groundwater. Despite frequent periods of drought, Germany is not a water-scarce country. "We basically still have enough water in Germany," the Gömann emphasized. The problem, he said, is rather the uneven distribution. Heavy rainfall occurs in winter, while dry spells are becoming more frequent in summer.

Scientists are experimenting with crop varieties that are more resilient to heat and drought Image: picture-alliance/dpa/F. Rumpenhorst

New breeds suitable for a warmer climate

Plant breeding plays a central role. Varieties whose genetic origins lie in warmer regions of Europe are already being cultivated in North Rhine-Westphalia.

"With wheat, for example, we're already making extensive use of genetics from France," said Gömann. The climatic conditions there have, in some respects, already shifted to Germany.

Grains with shorter stalks, known as semi-dwarfs, have been around for many years. Short stalks can bear significantly heavier ears, are less likely to snap during heavy rain, hail, or wind and require less water.

In addition, research is being conducted on wheat varieties with deeper roots. Current research at the German Julius Kühn Institute, the Federal Research Centre for Cultivated Plants, aims to develop wheat whose roots respond dynamically to drought by growing deeper only when water becomes scarce in the topsoil.

Farmers protect peach buds with a thin layer of ice from frosty temperatures in spring nights Image: Sebastian Willnow/dpa/picture alliance

Soybeans and millet are only niche products

The agricultural sector is also experimenting with new crops. Soybeans are now being grown in parts of Germany, albeit on a very small scale. Experiments are even being conducted with millet, a crop known from arid regions around the world, also only on a very small scale. Even winegrowing is slowly expanding further north, which is a visible sign of the shifting vegetation zones.

For Gömann, the condition of the soil is at least as important as new crop varieties. He said it is crucial to avoid soil compaction so that roots can penetrate deep into the ground.

Farmers, modern agriculture adapting to climate change

Farmers have always had to adapt to changing conditions, said Gömann. What's new, however, is the pace. While climate change used to take place over generations, now it is noticeable within just a few decades.

"The whole thing is happening quite quickly now," he said.

At the same time, modern agriculture has significantly better options than previous generations. New varieties are developed within a few years, and international breeding companies are continuously working on plants that are more tolerant of drought and heat.

For the agricultural expert, one thing is certain: the increase in extreme weather conditions in the past years is no coincidence. He sees the severe droughts of 2018 and 2019, as well as the recent heat waves, as part of a trend.

"This can certainly be attributed to the emerging climate change," Gömann told DW.

Agriculture must therefore continue to adapt, just as it has done for centuries, he noted, adding that it must do so much faster than before.

World.title: US: Trump's intelligence chief pick Jay Clayton confirmed by Senate
World.content:
Clayton's appointment comes as Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the midterms.

The US Senate on Tuesday confirmed Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence at a time when President Donald Trump has started reiterating his false claims about the 2020 election, which he lost.

The 51-47 vote in the Senate was along party lines with Republicans supporting the appointment and Democrats voting against.

After the vote, Trump heaped praise on Clayton posting on Truth Social: "Jay is outstanding in every way, and will do a spectacular job as Director!"

Clayton stresses he isn't 'an election denier'

Clayton will now lead the 18 intelligence agencies, including the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), National Security Agency (NSA), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which have been reeling from leadership turmoil and staff cuts.

He is a former Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) chairman and US attorney for the Southern District of New York.

Democrats opposed Clayton's nomination after he repeatedly declined during his confirmation hearing to explicitly state that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election, saying only that the result had been "certified."

"I'm not an election denier," Clayton said, without directly answering the question.

Trump renews voter fraud claims

Clayton replaces Tulsi Gabbard, who resigned in June, and Trump temporarily installed Bill Pulte as acting intelligence chief.

Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no national security experience, oversaw a tumultuous tenure marked by a roughly 30% staff reduction and the release of 2020 intelligence documents detailing China's capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system.

Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the US midterm elections.

California Democratic Senator Adam Schiff told CNN that Clayton's refusal to unequivocally state that Biden won the 2020 election "suggests that if the president [Trump] wants the intelligence agencies to cook up something to justify voter interference in the midterm elections, that Jay Clayton doesn't have the backbone to stand up to him."
