World.title: Heat wave to spread across Romania from July 30, peak expected in early August
World.content:
A heat wave is expected to spread across Romania from July 30, bringing increasingly hot weather and heat stress across much of the country, with the most intense conditions forecast between August 3 and 6, according to the National Meteorological Administration (ANM). The weather agency also issued a yellow heat warning for seven western and southwestern counties valid from Thursday morning through Friday morning.

The yellow warning is in effect from 10:00 a.m. on July 30 until 10:00 a.m. on July 31 for the counties of Dolj, Mehedinți, Caraș-Severin, Timiș, Arad, Bihor, and Satu Mare. Maximum temperatures will range from 33 to 37 degrees Celsius, with the highest values forecast in the Western Plain.

For the coming days, the meteorologists said the hottest weather will initially affect the country's western regions before gradually expanding eastward.

“From July 30, we will be talking about a heat wave that will gradually expand and intensify across our country, starting from the western regions, with its maximum intensity most likely between August 3 and 6," ANM said.

Temperatures in the regions of Banat and Crișana are expected to reach 35-36 degrees Celsius on Thursday, July 30, rising to 37-38 degrees on Friday, with isolated highs of up to 39 degrees Celsius.

Then, during the weekend of August 1-2, temperatures around 35 degrees Celsius are also expected locally in Maramureș, Transylvania, and Oltenia, and in isolated areas of Muntenia and Moldova. Heat discomfort is also forecast to increase gradually, first in western Romania and then across other parts of the country.

According to ANM, weather models indicate that maximum temperatures in western Romania could remain around 38-39 degrees Celsius until approximately August 6 before beginning to ease. In southern Romania, however, the hottest conditions are expected to develop later, from around August 3, and could persist until around August 9.

The meteorological agency noted that, despite its nickname as Romania's hottest month, July has so far been relatively moderate this year.

“Up to this point, July has not seen significant temperature extremes, with very few periods of heatwave conditions," ANM said, adding that the country's average temperature up to July 27 stood at 20.2 degrees Celsius, 0.1 degrees below the 1991-2020 average and lower than in each of the previous three years.

ANM attributed the upcoming heat wave to a persistent high-pressure system over much of Europe combined with the advance of very warm North African air across southern and southeastern parts of the continent, creating conditions for prolonged hot and dry weather.

irina.marica@romania-insdier.com

World.title: Romania travel: Five day trips from Bucharest
World.content:
Within a few hours of the capital or less, visitors can discover traditional crafts, a landscape of mud volcanoes, a historic palace, and one of Romania's best-known mountain resorts. Here is a selection of five destinations to try as one-day trips from Bucharest.

Piscu School Museum and Workshop

Set in a former village pottery, the Piscu School Museum and Workshop is a cultural and educational hub. Founded by art historian Adriana Scripcariu and sculptor Virgil Scripcariu, the initiative grew into a venue bringing together cultural heritage, contemporary art and ceramics. Launched in 2007, the project began by researching local heritage and sharing those discoveries with the community, with a focus on children. Nearly a decade later, the project of a new cultural space to exhibit artefacts, receive visitors, and host cultural and educational events, emerged. Built with the help of volunteers, the venue combines the area's pottery tradition with contemporary architecture. In 2022, it received a Europa Nostra Heritage Award in the Education, Training and Skills category. Their offering this summer has included pottery workshops, ceramic painting and linocut printmaking workshops, an exhibition of linocut prints from the designs of the Via Transilvanica milestones in Șona by painter Ștefan Câlția, and the garden of sculptures by Virgil Scripcariu. The venue, open on selected dates, is located in the village of Piscu, in Ciolpani commune, in Ilfov county.

Photo by Laurian Ghinitoiu, courtesy of Muzeu Atelier de la Piscu

Comana

Comana, a village in Giurgiu county about 40 km south of Bucharest, offers nature, history, and outdoor activities. At its heart lies the Comana Nature Park, a wetland known for its rich biodiversity, birdwatching opportunities, and scenic waterways. The more active types can enjoy here the various activities offered by the Comana Adventure Park. Those interested in traditional crafts can explore the Paper Mill and the Crafts Village Complex, developed by the Paper Mill Association (Moara de hârtie). The project grew from a small workshop-museum, dedicated to old book-related crafts, which was inaugurated in 2011. Building on the enthusiasm of visitors getting acquainted with the activities there, the team of the association decided to open a small village dedicated to Romanian traditional crafts. The complex consists of ten creative workshops based on old crafts that used to be practiced in the Romanian traditional village: weaving at the hand loom, reed mace processing, blacksmithing, pottery and ceramics, woodwork, traditional kitchen, traditional mill and bakery, as well as book-related crafts: handmade paper, letterpress printing, and bookbinding. Throughout the year, the association organizes workshops for children and adults, on topics related to creativity and crafts.

The Mud Volcanoes Photo: Porojnicu | Dreamstime.com

Buzău Land

The region of Buzău region is where spectacular landscapes, authentic gastronomy, and rural heritage come together. From the Buzău Land UNESCO Geopark, home to the Mud Volcanoes, the Living Fire, and ancient rock settlements, to wineries and traditional villages, the area rewards travelers looking to venture beyond the country's better-known attractions. Last year, the geopark opened additional destinations, namely the Oil Seeps in Beciu, Odăile Mushrooms, and the Living Fire in Lopătari, as part of its strategy to diversify the visitor experience and reduce pressure on already popular attractions. It also added an interactive visitor center in the village of Bozioru. Named Povestea Trovanților/The Trovants’ Story, the center tells the secrets of the stone formations known as trovants and the prehistoric Delta. For a farm-to-table experience, visitors can stop at Grigorescu Mansion, a restored country estate which also hosts a variety of food-related events and workshops.

The gardens of Mogoșoaia Palace Photo: Radub85/ Dreamstime

Mogoșoaia

Mogoșoaia offers an easy escape from the bustle of Bucharest, offering history, architecture, and green spaces. A highlight is Mogoșoaia Palace, an early 18th-century (1702) residence built by Prince Constantin Brâncoveanu. It is an example of the distinctive Brâncovenesc architectural style, also called the Romanian Renaissance. The estate includes the d'Elchingen Villa, rebuilt between 1927 and 1936. Beyond the main courtyard, visitors can find St. George's Church, founded by Brâncoveanu and built in 1688, as well as the Italian-style gardens laid out by Martha Bibescu in 1921–1922. The estate invites leisurely walks, while the palace museum showcases Romanian art and decorative objects. Meanwhile, Mogoșoaia Park hosts various events in the summer. An upcoming one is Big Little Festival, which positions itself as an event for the entire family. Taking place between August 21 and August 23, it will line up several local artists, among them Vama, Andra, and Smiley, and host a variety of areas and events for children.

Sinaia

Sinaia, one of Romania's best-known mountain resorts, often pops up in travel recommendations and for good reason. A one-day escape here combines royal history and spectacular scenery, in the heart of the Carpathian Mountains. A stroll through Sinaia will reveal its elegant villas, grand hotels, and eclectic architecture, where Neo-Renaissance, Neo-Romanian, Art Nouveau, and Alpine chalet influences coexist. The town's crown jewel is Peleș Castle, the 19th-century summer residence of Romania's royal family. Built between 1873 and 1914 as the summer residence of Romania's first king, Carol I, the castle blends Neo-Renaissance architecture with various other influences. Nearby, visitors can see the smaller Pelișor Castle and the 17th-century Sinaia Monastery. The George Enescu Memorial House, the composer's former residence known as Villa Luminiș, offers further insight into the life of the celebrated Romanian musician. Visitors can also try the nearby hiking trails or simply enjoy the town's central Dimitrie Ghica Park.

World.title: Counting the Dead: Kosovo Compiles List of 13,190 War Victims
World.content:
Twenty-seven years after hostilities ended, Kosovo will publish on Wednesday the first official list of victims of the 1998-99 war – dead and missing.

Based on physical files stretching hundreds of metres and more than 22 terabytes in digital form, the list compiled by the state Institute of Crimes Committed During the War in Kosovo, ICCW, runs to 13,190 names, but remains ‘preliminary’.

“For each victim, at least eight different sources of information were used before being included in this preliminary list, and I believe each case underwent thorough verification,” said Atdhe Hetemi, director of the institute.

“This is a preliminary institutional list and remains open to additions and revisions based on new documents and evidence.”

World.title: Why Serbia’s Most Successful Football Club and Party Appear Unchallengeable
World.content:
Ludogorets Razgrad surrendered their title to Levski Sofia last season in the Bulgarian league, ending their streak of 14 consecutive league titles. The ripple effect of that reached Belgrade – the nine-time consecutive champions of the Serbian SuperLiga, Red Star Belgrade, now possess the longest winning streak in European football, dating back to the 2013-14 season.

The domestic winning streak enjoyed by Red Star (or Crvena Zvezda, as they’re known at home) is surpassed only by that of the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, whose election victories began in 2012. The SNS has “scored” six successful election wins since then. Meanwhile, Red Star will be looking to continue their victories in the new Serbian SuperLiga season, which just got underway this month.

Football and politics are often the two biggest topics in many European nations and Serbia is no different. What is starkly different to other European nations, however, is how connected and similar Serbia’s football and politics are.

Usually, when looking at sporting success, such as Red Star’s title victories, fans would refer to this as a dynasty – the type of dynasty that deserves praise for every aspect of the club, from the top to the bottom.

World.title: After the Flock: A Greek Island Mourns its Sheep, Ponders its Future
World.content:
Less than 80 kilometres from Mytilene, the capital and main port of Lesvos, the road to Chrousos – a small coastal village in the municipality of Mesotopos – crosses the western side of Lesvos through low hills and sloping, silvery olive groves before reaching the coast.

Come midday, the heat settles over the fields and the reeds barely move, while dust still hangs above the roadside long after the dirt track disappears beneath asphalt.

Stavritsa, Stavros’s wife, was setting tables when I arrived at her family restaurant.

From the terrace, the Aegean stretched out beyond a line of pine trees, although hardly anyone seems to notice the view anymore. Just weeks earlier, the couple had watched as their flock of around 500 sheep and goats was destroyed as part of the effort to contain the outbreak.

As lunch was being prepared, Stavros strolled slowly through the yard, stopping every few steps to point to a stone wall or a flowerbed. “I built this,” he said, as if reminding himself.

The restaurant has evolved over the time, shaped by what he calls his ‘sevdas’, a quiet, lifelong devotion, and ‘meraki’, meaning ‘to leave something of your soul in what you do’.

After long days spent on building sites, Stavros would return in the evenings to lay another row of stones or tend the plants before dark. A pomegranate tree stood near the entrance, its branches reaching towards the fields beyond while geraniums and rosemary spilled over the garden’s low walls.

Lunch arrived, starting with courgette flowers filled with rice and herbs, followed by wild greens and marathos dressed in lemon, as well as ladotyri cheese and bread that had barely had time to cool.

Preserved in olive oil for months, the cheese brings together the two products that have shaped Lesvos for centuries, a marriage of sheep milk and olives. Few families could get by on one source of income alone; instead, they moved between their herds and their orchards and did seasonal work as required.

In 2025 alone, Lesvos produced around 52,000 tonnes of sheep and goat milk. The island accounts for 5-6 per cent of Greece’s PDO feta production. When thousands of animals were slaughtered, those income streams disappeared overnight, with consequences for dairies, cheesemakers, feed suppliers and transporters.

Almost everything on the table in front of me had come from the surrounding fields: so it was only a matter of time before someone noticed that much of what we were eating could easily have been absent. The conversation drifted organically from lunch to livestock.

More than a flock

World.title: Montenegro Approves Paid Leave for Menstrual Pain Sufferers
World.content:
Rights groups have expressed satisfaction after Montenegro’s parliament amended the Health Insurance Law for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea – painful menstrual cramps – to grant two days of “menstrual leave” per month.

The measure, adopted by MPs on Monday, applies to women suffering such symptoms as a result of serious underlying conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

The initiative was submitted in March ahead of International Women’s Day by independent MP Jevrosima Pejovic. The bill previously received support from the parliamentary Health, Labour and Social Welfare Committee and the Legislative Committee.

The Women’s Rights Centre, an NGO, welcomed the adoption of paid menstrual leave, describing it as an important step toward recognising women’s health needs in the workplace. It also praised the persistence of MP Pejovic, who advocated for the measure.

“This is a valuable example of how the presence of women in politics helps give political significance to women’s experiences, which have long been pushed into the private sphere and treated as ‘secondary’ issues,” the NGO said on Tuesday.

The Centre recalled that it had proposed including this right into law two years ago, but the relevant ministry rejected the initiative at the time. “What matters now is that it does not remain merely a right on paper but becomes a concrete opportunity that provides women with safer, healthier and more dignified working conditions,” it said.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

The law defines the condition as symptoms caused by previously diagnosed gynecological disorders and lists symptoms including pain in intercourse, painful urination, infertility and unusually heavy menstrual bleeding. Diagnosis must be confirmed by a medical specialist.

Women seeking the new benefit will be required to renew their medical certificate by December 31 each year and submit it to their employer by January 30 of the following year.

The amendments also regulate compensation during leave. Under Montenegro’s Health Insurance Law, compensation for temporary incapacity for work is generally set at no less than 70 per cent of the salary base, while employers may provide a higher amount through collective agreements.

The law provides 100 per cent compensation for certain categories of illness and medical conditions, including occupational diseases and injuries, pregnancy-related complications, malignant diseases, haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, epilepsy, muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy, paraplegia and quadriplegia, systemic autoimmune diseases, chronic renal failure requiring dialysis, HIV, psychoses and some other serious conditions.

The amendments do not say how the law will be implemented, including how employers and state institutions will verify eligibility and prevent possible abuses of the new entitlement.

BIRN was unable to reach MP Pejovic for comment on implementation of the law and safeguards against potential misuse.

The amendments are expected to enter into force after their publication in Montenegro’s Official Gazette.

World.title: Mayor Acquitted of Obstructing Justice in Kosovo War Crimes Trial
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



The defendants celebrate the acquittal at Pristina Basic Court, July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Pristina Basic Court cleared local wartime commander Sami Lushtaku and seven others on Tuesday of obstruction of justice, witness intimidation and participation in a criminal group.

Sami Lushtaku, a commander in the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, for the region of Drenica, was accused of having from 2013 until 2015 forced two defendants to change their testimonies in the so-called Drenica case, in which Lushtaku and other KLA commanders from the Drenica region were accused of committing war crimes.

Lushtaku was not present when the judge announced the verdict, which was applauded by the public in the courtroom.

“The court could not find any convincing evidence which would prove the guilt of the defendants,” Judge Leon Perlaska said, reading the verdict. “The court assessed the testimony of the witness codenamed ‘Witness C’ where he denied that he was forced to change his statement,” Perlaska added.

Lushtaku, now mayor of the Kosovo town of Skenderaj/Srbica, was sentenced in 2015 to 12 years in prison by the Basic Court in Mitrovica for a murder committed in 1998, although the victim’s name was unknown and no body was found.

He was cleared on appeal in 2016 but his conviction for “command responsibility for allegedly violating the [bodily] integrity and health of an undefined number of civilian Albanians held at the Likovc detention centre” was upheld.

His sentence was reduced from 12 to seven years in prison by the Appeals Court. He was cleared by the Supreme Court in July 2017.

World.title: Kosovo Retrial Confirms Serbian Police Ex-Inspector’s Ten-Year Sentence
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Sacir Lutvija in court om July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.



Sacir Lutvija, a 65-year-old ethnic Gorani former member of the Serbian police force, was sentenced to ten years in prison in a retrial at the Pristina Basic Court, for war crimes committed during the 1998-99 war in Kosovo.

Serbian police and military forces staged a campaign of arrests of ethnic Albanian civilians and 11 of them were taken to Prizren police station in southern Kosovo, where Lutvija was among the inspectors who questioned them, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors said those arrested were beaten during the interrogation and subjected to electric shocks on their hands and genitals. One civilian died and ten others sustained serious injuries.

Lutvija, who has both Kosovo and Serbian citizenship, was arrested in October 2023 and has been in detention since then. The time in custody will be counted towards his sentence.

The Kosovo Special Prosecution charged Lutvija with unlawfully arresting and beating civilians, inhumane treatment and murder in his capacity as an inspector and police officer in Prizren. Lutvija pleaded not guilty in September last year.

Judge Kujtim Krasniqi on Tuesday ordered Lutvija to pay a court fee of 400 euros as well as 100 euros to the crime victims’ fund.

The verdict can be appealed.

Lutvija was initially sentenced to 10 years in prison by the Pristina Basic Court in November 2025.

But the Court of Appeals sent the case to a retrial in June this year having concluded that the Pristina Basic Court had not “concretely clarified the actions attributed to the accused in relation to each of the injured parties”.

The Court of Appeal also said the Basic Court failed to explained the accused’s participation in committing the crimes and “did not clarify the evidence upon which the conclusions presented in the verdict were based”.

The Gorani are a small Slavic ethnic group who mostly follow Islam and inhabit a highland triangle between Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia.

World.title: Left High and Dry: Drought Exposes Central Europe’s Water Crisis
World.content:
Water management and retention

Described as the proverbial “roof of Europe”, Czechia sees all its rivers, streams and waterways flow out of the country – a systemic and geological drainage which makes the country particularly dependent on precipitation from above.

“This is a significant disadvantage, because most of the water we manage has to be retained: in the landscape, soil, hydrogeological structures or water reservoirs,” says Adam Vizina, head of the hydrology department at the Water Management Research Institute.

Water management and retention are, therefore, key for this landlocked country, yet the authorities appear short on solutions.

“Water will always flow away, but we can reduce our vulnerability,” argues Vizina, listing measures such as slowing runoff, interconnecting water supply systems, managing water reservoirs better, or protecting the quality and quantity of groundwater.

The state reportedly spent 75 billion crowns (about 3 billion euros) in the past three years on drought adaptation, yet experts – including a report by the Supreme Audit Office published last March – have criticised the slow pace and limited scope of the measures.

The Slovak Academy of Sciences recently released its “Vision for Slovakia 2040”, an extensive 90-page framework document commissioned by the government of Robert Fico laying out the key policy challenges for the next 15 years.

Among those, the forward-looking blueprint “identifies more frequent droughts as a key consequence of climate change and argues that strengthening water management, increasing landscape water retention and improving the resilience of agriculture and ecosystems should be central priorities for Slovakia’s long-term development.”

Whether the authorities will act on the recommendations is another matter, with experts long highlighting key shortcomings in Slovakia’s water management practices, from fragmented governance between different institutions and ministries, a lack of concrete follow-through, and scattered water data hindering real-time monitoring.

Czechia and Slovakia’s subpar water-management has deep roots dating back to decades of intensive farming that followed its collectivisation in the 1950s and 1960s under Communism – with all that entailed in terms of land consolidation, water erosion and reduced soil fertility, among other environmental impacts.

On the upside, the Czech Republic continues to receive roughly the same amount of rain on average every year as it used to, according to some estimates. But the way, time and place it does are changing, as must the measures meant to retain and manage it more effectively, experts say: less rainfall in the spring but more in the fall, more intense precipitation during storms, but less frequent episodes of long-term and widespread rain.

According to Milan Vitek from the local branch of Greenpeace, Czechia might soon be faced with the choice of keeping its scarce water either in the rivers or in its fields, but won’t be able to do both. “Adaptation is something that we are decades behind when we could’ve been much further ahead,” he previously told BIRN.

Water management or retention are also recently being cited as a silver bullet to solve Hungary’s problems. Although Hungary has a renewable water reservoir of 11,833 cubic metres per person, one of the largest in Central Europe (only Slovenia and Serbia have more in the region), 95 per cent of that originates from outside and simply flows through the country.

The building of dams or hydroelectric power plants has been a politically sensitive issue since the controversial plan to build the Bos-Nagymaros dam on the Danube helped trigger popular revolt against the Communist government in 1990. Since then, proposals for new dams and hydropower projects have remained politically off-limits in Hungary.

But times are changing. Laszlo Gajdos, the new Hungarian government’s environment minister, said at the height of the extreme heat at the beginning of July that “water is one of our most valuable resources for the future”.

Gajdos said the government must do everything it can to improve water retention, even with dam construction where necessary. “We should not let water flow through Hungary; it needs to be retained somehow. Personally, I don’t like this method, but it seems inevitable building some dams,” he told RTL.hu.

The government of Peter Magyar is working on a new climate and environmental law, expected by late autumn, which is set to address water management issues.

Gajdos, who became Hungary’s first environment minister in 16 years, stressed that water retention is a regional issue requiring cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Andras Szollosi-Nagy, who used to advise international organisations including the UN on water diplomacy and is the founder member of the World Water Council, could not agree more.

“Water retention is always somehow part of national sovereignty,” Szollosi-Nagy says. “The country upstream believes all the water is theirs, but if they retain it, neighbouring countries are affected. We need integrated water management in the region.”

He says there is no silver bullet to solve all the problems: dams, reservoirs, new technologies, satellite-based monitoring and controlled flooding could all play a role.

“Hungary’s water management system has been systematically dismantled in recent decades,” he says. “Now we need to rebuild it from scratch.”

World.title: Letter from Washington: US Seeks to Score Material Goals in the Balkans
World.content:
Greetings from America, which this month celebrated 250 years of independence from the British crown under a president who has called himself a king – and is also seen that way by the many thousands of people who have joined the “No Kings” protests in the US.

Donald Trump would not even allow the kings of football, the Spanish national team who won the World Cup, to enjoy their rightful moment on the throne this month. Instead, he lingered on stage after presenting them with the trophy at the stadium in New Jersey. An awkward situation was averted by Trump’s pal, FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who pulled the US leader aside, suggesting that it was time for him to step away.

Meanwhile, beside the footballing euphoria, the US-Iran memorandum of understanding has turned out to be more of a major misunderstanding. The war has escalated, bringing new American casualties and higher fuel prices, while reopening an uncomfortable question: what is the actual endgame? If the goal is to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, to prevent further escalation in the Middle East, why is the United States simultaneously signing an agreement that would allow Saudi Arabia to develop the very same capability?

While all this has been happening, the Trump administration’s policy towards the Balkans has started to become increasingly clear. It is moving more aggressively into areas it considers important, such as energy, defence and infrastructure, while trying to push Russia, China and the European Union out of those spheres. Washington does not appear to be choosing its friends based on how developed their democracies are. Nor is it particularly troubled when someone in the Balkans talks about “ethnic cleansing”.

World.title: Croatian Inspectors Step Up Crackdown on Illegal Holiday Rentals
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatian inspectors have begun stepping up their crackdown on illegal holiday rentals up and down the coastline in particular, with plenty of fines already issued.

As Poslovni reports, Croatia’s State Inspectorate has intensified its inspections of holiday accommodation advertised on platforms such as Booking.com and Airbnb, targeting property owners who rent to tourists without meeting the country’s latest, strict legal requirements. The inspections form part of a broader effort to combat the shadow economy in the tourism sector and ensure fair competition among registered accommodation providers.

thousands of euros seized, thousands fined…

According to the State Inspectorate, inspectors have already uncovered numerous cases of illegal short-term rentals during this year’s tourist season. As a result, authorities have confiscated 343,000 euros in income believed to have been earned through unlawful renting, while fines imposed have exceeded 81,000 euros.

The inspections focus on identifying individuals advertising tourist accommodation without the required registration or operating in breach of Croatian tourism regulations. Authorities are checking online listings as well as conducting on-site inspections to verify whether accommodation providers comply with the law.

inspections will continue throughout summer

When inspectors discover illegal activity, they can issue fines, prohibit further renting and confiscate the financial gains obtained through unlawful operations. Officials say these measures are intended to discourage unregistered rentals and protect hosts who operate legally and meet all regulatory obligations. The State Inspectorate said inspections will continue throughout the peak summer tourist season, with online booking platforms remaining one of the primary tools used to identify suspected illegal accommodation.

Officials stress that the goal is not only to punish offenders but also to ensure equal market conditions, protect consumers and improve the overall quality and transparency of Croatia’s tourism sector. As demand for private accommodation continues to grow, authorities say stronger enforcement is necessary to prevent unfair competition and safeguard public revenue.

World.title: Airbnb Loses Its Advantage Over Booking.com for Croatian Hosts
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Airbnb no longer has any advantages or particular benefits over Booking.com for Croatian hosts after the company announced significant changes recently.

As Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni, Croatian private accommodation hosts are facing a significant changes after Airbnb announced a new commission model that many say removes one of its biggest advantages over Booking.com. Under that company’s new system, Airbnb will no longer charge guests a separate service fee. Instead, hosts will pay a 15.5% commission, replacing the previous model in which hosts paid around 3% while guests covered most of the platform’s fee.

According to Vedran Tomić, president of the Save Small Family Renters Association (SMOi), the change has been met with negative reactions from Croatian hosts. He said Airbnb’s biggest advantage had been its lower direct cost for hosts, but that will now disappear. He also pointed out that Croatian hosts must pay VAT on the commission, meaning they will now pay VAT on the full 15.5% fee instead of just the previous 3% commission.

one last summer of airbnb advantage for croatian hosts…

The new commission structure will apply as of the 13th of October. Airbnb says the change responds to feedback from hosts who found the previous pricing model confusing because guests saw an additional service fee added to the advertised accommodation price. Under the new model, guests will simply see the final price, while the commission is deducted from the host’s payout.

The changes come as Croatia’s short-term rental market is already evolving. Data from analytics platform AirDNA shows that the number of active listings has fallen in the country’s largest cities. In Split, active listings dropped from around 10,300 in June 2025 to 8,906 in June 2026, a decline of 13.5%. Zagreb recorded an even steeper fall of 25%, with analysts linking the decline to more property owners switching to long-term rentals. The market is increasingly favouring larger and more professional operators, while less profitable listings are leaving the sector.

Tomić believes the commission change is unlikely to reduce demand from travellers, but it could weaken Airbnb’s position in Croatia because it no longer offers hosts a financial advantage over Booking.com. He estimates that Booking.com controls around 70% of the Croatian market, while Airbnb accounts for roughly 20%, with the remaining 10% shared by other booking platforms.

accommodation competitiveness isn’t even the biggest issue for croatian tourism

Damir Krešić, director of Croatia’s Institute for Tourism, said higher commissions are not good news for the sector, but argued that accommodation is not the biggest competitiveness issue facing Croatian tourism. In his view, greater concerns are the rising costs of food, drinks and transport services, where Croatia has become less competitive.

Krešić also encouraged private hosts not to rely on a single booking platform. He said global platforms have given small Croatian hosts access to guests worldwide, but becoming too dependent on one intermediary weakens their bargaining position. Instead, he recommends that hosts advertise across two or three platforms to diversify their bookings and reduce risk.

World.title: Luka Modrić Visits Unfinished Villa Construction Site in Istria
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatian footballing legend Luka Modrić has paid a visit to an unfinished villa construction site in Istria before heading off on a yacht. Could he be thinking of buying it?

As Poslovni reports, a jet black limousine with tinted rear windows stopped at a construction site in Istria a few days ago, shortly before midday. Luka Modrić, 40, captain of the Croatian national football team, got out at the parking area in front of an unfinished villa that still requires final stonework for a Mediterranean appearance.

He was accompanied by experts who went around the site with him explaining different things and pointing out important construction details. The group then entered the private property and remained inside for about half an hour. According to one of the site’s neighbours who contacted the media about the group, Luka Modrić appeared interested in the property as a possible investment, though that is not confirmed.

The same day he was later seen boarding a yacht that he rents each summer for roughly a week or ten days of family holiday along the Adriatic coastline. Media reports state that, after earlier investments in central Dalmatia and the far south of Croatia, members of the Modrić family have shown interest in property in Istria. Vanja Modrić is said to have expressed interest on several occasions in locations around Rovinj, but no purchases have so far been officially completed.

the football legend has acquired multiple properties in both croatia and spain

Over the course of his career Modrić has acquired several residential properties in Croatia and Spain.

In the elite Zadar suburb of Kožino, near where he grew up, the family owns a villa with an outdoor pool, children’s playground, garden, sea view, wine cellar, ten-car garage, gym, an eighteen-seat cinema, children’s playroom and massage room. It is used as a family base during the summer break in the football season. In October 2024 a storm damaged the access road; the damage was later repaired. The property had earlier attracted attention over reports of beach concreting in front of the estate; Modrić stated that the area in question is public land, not a private beach.

In Zagreb, the family owns a 286-square-metre villa on Pantovčak, purchased back in 2017 from former footballer Zvonimir Boban. Land-registry records show Modrić transferred ownership to his wife Vanja shortly afterwards. Before that purchase the family had lived in apartments in Ravnice and Babonićeva Street. Modrić also owns a 220-square-metre penthouse with a 29-square-metre loggia in a newly built building on Tkalčićeva Street in the city centre; media estimates placed its value at around 1.4 million euros.

Over in the Spanish capital of Madrid, where Luka Modrić spent many years playing for Real Madrid, the family owns a villa in the La Moraleja district, acquired in 2019 on a 10,000-square-metre plot. Spanish media describe it as having nine bedrooms and nine bathrooms, with the main living areas, kitchen and sitting room on the ground floor and guest rooms upstairs, plus an outdoor pool, garden and recreation space. According to media reports, part of the portfolio is formally registered in Vanja Modrić’s name.

World.title: Croatia Opens Its First Biological Swimming Pool in Čazma
World.content:
July the 29th, 2026 – Croatia has opened its very first biological swimming pool in the continental town of Čazma, representing a significant step forward in terms of sustainable tourism.

Croatia has officially opened its first biological swimming pool, marking a milestone in sustainable tourism and environmentally friendly recreation. Index reports that the new facility is located in the town of Čazma, around 60 kilometres east of Zagreb, the new facility is part of the much wider Čazma Natura project, which has the primary goal of transforming the town into a leading green tourism destination.

Unlike conventional swimming pools, the biological pool uses natural filtration instead of chlorine or other chemicals. Water is purified through biological processes involving aquatic plants and microorganisms, creating a safe swimming environment while preserving the natural ecosystem. It is the first public facility of its kind in Croatia.

The swimming area spans approximately 1,665 square metres and is divided into separate sections for swimmers and non-swimmers. Alongside the pool, visitors will find sunbathing areas, changing rooms, showers, a catering facility, children’s amenities and recreational spaces designed for families and visitors of all ages.

The pool forms part of the Bio Park Čazma complex, which also includes educational facilities, walking trails and nature-focused attractions. The project promotes sustainable tourism while highlighting the area’s biodiversity and encouraging visitors to explore the surrounding landscape.

Officials say the biological pool represents a new direction for Croatian tourism, combining recreation with environmental protection. Similar facilities have become increasingly popular across areas of Europe because they reduce chemical use, consume less energy and blend more naturally into their surroundings. With the opening of the country’s first biological swimming pool, Čazma is hoping to attract visitors looking for a different kind of summer experience, one centred on nature, sustainability and chemical-free swimming.

World.title: Croatian Firefighters Continue Battling Bordeaux Wildfire
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Croatian firefighters are continuing to battle the intense Bordeaux wildfire ravaging southwestern France, and which keeps being rekindled by problematic winds.

Croatian Air Force firefighting pilots are continuing their mission in southwestern France, where they are helping battle the massive wildfire near Bordeaux. Index reports that this intense operation has now entered its fifth day, with crews facing increasingly difficult conditions as strengthening winds threaten to reignite areas that had previously been brought under control.

The members of the 855th Firefighting Squadron are operating in the Saumos area, just west of Bordeaux. According to Major Ivan Dukić, conditions improved after overnight rain, but rising temperatures and stronger afternoon winds have caused the fire to become active once again.

“The situation is much better than it initially was thanks to some rainfall. However, temperatures are increasing, and as the day progresses the wind is strengthening. The fire has been waking up again, so we’ll see what the days bring,” Dukić said from France.

Since arriving in France, the Croatian crews have carried out 118 flights, logged 20 hours of flying time, and dropped 576 tonnes of water on the catastrophic French wildfires. They are working alongside French and other international crews as part of the rescEU civil protection mechanism.

Despite the demanding mission abroad, Croatia’s aerial firefighting forces remain heavily engaged at home during the peak wildfire season. Between the 15th of June and the 27th of July, the 855th Firefighting Squadron took part in extinguishing 39 wildfires along Croatia’s coastline and on the islands.

Commander Colonel Željko Bukvić said Croatia’s ability to respond both domestically and internationally is the result of careful planning, good organisation and the experience of its firefighting crews. He stressed that the squadron remains ready to assist both Croatia and its European partners whenever needed. The enormous wildfire near Bordeaux remains one of France’s most serious emergencies, with strong, problematic winds, high temperatures and dry vegetation continuing to fuel the blaze repeatedly despite efforts. Croatian pilots remain on the front line as authorities work to prevent the fire from spreading further.

World.title: July 1377: Dubrovnik Introduces Organised Isolation of Arrivals to Combat Plague
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Turning the clock back to July 1377, we saw how the ever-diplomatic Dubrovnik organised the isolation of new arrivals in order to combat the plague.

In July of the aforementioned year, the former Great Council of the Republic of Dubrovnik adopted a decision requiring people arriving in the city (and then autonomous state of Ragusa) from plague-affected areas to undergo a period of isolation before entering the city or its surroundings.

trentina – strict isolation for a period of one month

Dubrovnik was one of the most important medieval trading centres on the Adriatic. Its wealth depended on shipping, merchants and goods arriving from across the Mediterranean and the European hinterland. Those same connections also carried infectious diseases. After the Black Death swept through Europe in the mid-14th century and caused catastrophic issues, the authorities faced a clear problem. A complete ban on foreign arrivals and goods would have protected the population but would also have severely damaged an economy based on trade. Instead they introduced a compromise.

Arrivals from infected regions were not allowed to enter Dubrovnik immediately. Index writes that they had to spend a fixed period separated from the local population so that any symptoms of disease could appear. The initial isolation period lasted 30 days and was known as the “trentina”.

dubrovnik tried to stop the disease at the city gates

Isolation was carried out at Cavtat and on nearby islets such as Mrkan; later Bobara and Supetar were also used. The underlying principle was that a person who showed no signs of illness after a sufficiently long interval posed a substantially lower risk of introducing infection. Medieval physicians had absolutely no knowledge of the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which was identified much later at the very end of the 19th century. They did, however, observe from experience that the disease spread through contact and the movement of people, and that symptoms could appear only after a delay. Dubrovnik therefore tried to stop the disease at the gates rather than respond only after an outbreak inside the city.

Rules were strict. People from affected areas had to complete the prescribed isolation, and contact between Dubrovnik residents and those in isolation was limited, creating a sanitary buffer.

dubrovnik’s decision eventually became a global practice in epidemiology

The period was later extended from 30 to 40 days. The modern word “quarantine” derives from the Italian quaranta (forty). The precise reason for choosing 40 days is not certain; explanations range from medical observation to the symbolic importance of the number in Christian tradition.

In subsequent centuries Dubrovnik developed a more elaborate system, including lazarettos where travellers, merchants and goods could complete the required period of observation before entry. The arrangement allowed trade to continue under controlled conditions rather than forcing a choice between an open city exposed to disease and a completely closed one without commerce.

The 1377 decision is regarded as one of the earliest organised applications of a practice that later became a standard method of epidemic control worldwide.

World.title: Split is Launching One of Croatia’s Largest Environmental Projects
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Split is set to launch one of Croatia’s largest environmental projects as part of a massive 100 million euro investment.

Poslovni reports that construction works on this enormous project will last 28 months from the contractor being introduced to the site until the start of the plant’s trial operation. The total duration of the contract itself is 43 months, including the trial operation period and obtaining the operating permit.

One of the most important infrastructure projects in Croatia’s water management sector is now beginning in Split. On Tuesday, the 28th July 2026, the start of construction works on the Stupe Wastewater Treatment Plant (UPOV Stupe) will be officially marked. The project is a key part of the “Improvement of Water and Utility Infrastructure of the Split–Solin Agglomeration” initiative.

With the expansion of the Stupe wastewater treatment plant, Split will receive a modern wastewater treatment system that, once completed, will become the second-largest wastewater treatment facility in all of Croatia and the central point of a unified sewage system serving the Split–Solin agglomeration.

The value of the contract for the design and expansion of the facility amounts to 99,056,751.25 euros including VAT. The works will be carried out by a consortium consisting of WTE Wassertechnik GmbH (lead partner) and HERING d.d.

The future facility will have a capacity of 275,000 population equivalents, with secondary biological wastewater treatment. The construction of the Stupe wastewater treatment plant will provide modern treatment of municipal wastewater for Split and the surrounding area, helping to further protect the environment, preserve the quality of the Brač Channel, and improve the quality of life for residents.

As part of the second phase of the project, eligible costs amount to 243,149,745.48 euros. Of this, €165,365,077.30 euros will be financed through non-refundable European Union funds from the Cohesion Fund, while the remaining amount will be secured through Croatian national sources.

World.title: Approval Granted for Construction of Key Croatian Four-Lane Road Section
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Approval has been granted for the construction of a key Croatian four-lane road section, and it is being hailed as one of the country’s most significant motorway projects.

Croatian drivers are a step closer to improved transport links after the government approved the construction of one of the country’s most important road projects. The decision clears the way for the development of a new four-lane section that is expected to improve traffic flow, increase road safety and strengthen connections between key parts of the national road network.

The approval relates to the 21.9-kilometre Podravska Expressway section between Pitomača and Virovitica, after the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition completed the environmental impact assessment and declared the project environmentally acceptable.

The project has received official approval following the completion of the necessary planning procedures, allowing preparations for construction to move forward. Poslovni reports that the new road section will be built with four traffic lanes, significantly increasing capacity compared with the existing road and helping to reduce congestion, particularly during periods of heavy traffic. According to the project plans, the upgraded route will form part of a wider transport corridor designed to improve connections between regions, shorten travel times and support economic development. The investment is also expected to enhance access for businesses, tourism and freight transport.

The planned road will include modern infrastructure designed to meet current safety standards, with features aimed at improving traffic efficiency and reducing the risk of accidents. Officials say the project represents one of the country’s most significant transport investments in recent years.

The approval marks an important milestone, but several stages remain before construction begins, including the completion of procurement procedures and the selection of contractors. Once the boots are actually on the ground, the project is expected to be carried out in multiple phases.

The new four-lane road is otherwise a large part of Croatia’s broader strategy to modernise its transport infrastructure and improve connectivity across the country. Once completed, it is expected to make journeys faster, safer and more reliable for both local residents and visitors, while supporting long-term economic growth.

World.title: Estonia's women's épée team climb to number 4 in the world
World.content:
The Estonian women's épée team have risen three spots to fourth place in the international fencing rankings after their strong performance at the world championships which saw them take team silver.

This means also that the team is in strong contention for qualification to the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

The foursome of Julia Beljajeva, Irina Embrich, Katrina Lehis and Veronika Zuikova performed disappointingly in the individual events in Hong Kong, but came together as a team to go all the way to the finals, losing to Olympic champions Italy by just a point, 31-30.

Before the world championships, Estonia was ranked seventh. The performance reached 291 points overall which moved them up three spaces in the world rankings, especially as on the way to the final they overcame Olympic runners-up France in the quarter finals, and reigning European silver medalists Hungary in the semis.

Only South Korea in first place (376 points), Italy (316) and the U.S. (296) are ahead of Estonian in the table now.

The promotion is also significant as the top four teams in the rankings automatically qualify for the next Olympic Games in Los Angeles in two years' time. They will be joined by the top teams from each of the four worldwide zones.

The qualification period for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics begins on April 1 next year.

Three of the four who competed in Hong Kong – Lehis, Beljajeva and Embrich, were in the team which took team gold at the Tokyo Olympics held in 2021, while Lehis took individual bronze at the same games. In Paris two years ago, another fencer, Nelli Differt, was just outside the medals in the individual category.

The épée class uses a heavier thrusting weapon where the entire body is a valid target, whereas the lighter foil is a thrusting weapon restricted to the torso for points-scoring purposes.

World.title: Advertising agencies: AI overuse erodes a company's credibility
World.content:
AI is getting to be a powerful tool in advertising, excessive or inappropriate use could harm companies, marketers and advertisers have warned.

AI overuse could lead to more misinformation appearing in the public sphere, as well as misleading customers and ultimately damage companies' credibility.

Media reports have recently pointed out the phenomenon of event posters and s which have seemingly been created using AI

Anniken Haldna, CEO of the Estonian Association of Marketing Communication Agencies, said nearly 80 percent of international firms already use AI in advertising, primarily to save time and money. However, Haldna added that AI is still mainly used as a tool. Human beings are still behind the overall creative drive of an ad, she said. "Human creativity, the human strategic perspective and dimension of marketing – that is critically important."

Alvar Lonks, creative director at Tallinn ad agency Tabasco, confirmed AI has made the work at his company faster and more efficient.

"From an agency's point of view, I can say that it makes things like creating mock-ups much easier. In the past, we had to do a lot of drawing, which took many working hours, but thanks to AI, producing mock-ups is much simpler," Lonks explained.

He agreed that AI still lacks creativity aspects, and it would not be viable to create high-quality, distinctive advertising from start to finish using AI alone. AI in ad production is nonetheless here to stay, Lonks added.

AI apps on a smartphone. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Above all, the use of AI should not be deceptive, he noted. "People generally like s that speak to them, that use their language or show them familiar images. Authenticity is what matters here," Lonks said.

Haldna added the biggest challenge going forward is helping companies stand out, given ads with significant AI input tend to look a bit uniform. She also highlighted the spread of misinformation, and the challenge of earning customers' trust while still using AI.

"Critical thinking about the use of AI in marketing is vital, including from the perspective of our association. We would certainly encourage people to think critically and also to consider the issue of trust. The initial global studies suggest that people actually do not trust AI-generated s," Haldna went on.

Haldna and Lonks concluded that even as AI is a useful tool for producing s, advertising will remain human-centred for the foreseeable future.

"Creative people are at the heart of an agency, not artificial intelligence. That human perspective is essential if we want to create valuable marketing communications that genuinely resonate with people," Haldna said.

"It is not a case of writing a single prompt, getting a result and immediately printing it on a huge billboard," Lonks noted.

World.title: New nature-focused spa hotel opens on Lake Peipus in Ida-Viru County
World.content:
A new spa has opened on the shores of Lake Peipus in eastern Estonia for the first time in more than 40 years, offering guests a break from the daily grind and the possibility to relax in nature.

Kurro Nature Spa Hotel is the first major holiday complex to be built on the northern shore of Lake Peipus in more than 40 years. The buildings, constructed in the forest, seem to have been lowered into place by helicopter.

Visitors are sold the opportunity of leaving daily life behind and relaxing in unspoilt nature.

Kurro Nature Spa's managing director, Killu Maidla, believes this is what people need as society becomes increasingly fast-paced and digitized.

"There simply isn't a place where you can go to the countryside, into the forest, into nature, listen to the wind rustling through the treetops and watch the wild, foaming August waves on Lake Peipus, while at the same time enjoying good service, a pleasant environment and a cosy room," said Kurro founder Andres Linnas.

He believes that the more time passes, the more society will need this type of holiday.

The spa will open the northern shore of Lake Peipus to year-round tourism and bring nearly 100 new jobs to Alutaguse Municipality.

Alutaguse Mayor Tauno Võhmar acknowledged that the first few years would certainly attract everyone who is curious and wants to visit the spa at least once. He added that long-term sustainability would be the biggest challenge.

There are already seven spas in Ida-Viru County. The arrival of the distinctive Kurro will increase competition, but will also bring more tourists.

Karina Küppas, managing director of Narva-Jõesuu Medical SPA, explained that Ida-Viru County will receive positive PR. That, in turn, will draw attention to the region. She added that demand may not currently be as great as the level of supply that is emerging.

The spa cost €37 million to build, one-third of which was funded by the Just Transition Fund.

World.title: Minister: Estonia sends extra border guards to Latvia as Belarus drives migrant surge
World.content:
Estonia will send additional police and border guard forces to Latvia to strengthen the European Union's external border. The decision came after several dozen illegal migrants who entered the country through Belarus and Latvia were detained in Estonia in recent days.

Pressure on the Latvian‑Belarusian section of the border is growing, and attempts to cross illegally have increased significantly in recent weeks.

Interior Minister Igor Taro, who visited the Latvian‑Belarusian border last week, said the situation there is very serious.

"It is rush hour at the border, you could say. The Belarusian regime is deliberately sending these migrants into the forest, gathering them in special camps, preparing them, giving them all kinds of tools to overcome obstacles on Latvia's external state border. The situation is quite complicated," he said.

"This is part of Russia's overall aggression tactics, and Belarus is their ally. Even if they are not acting actively in a military sense, they still support logistics and various relays used to direct drones toward Ukraine. And one form of this supportive activity is sending illegal migrants toward European countries that help Ukraine, to create additional problems and force them to spend resources," the minister continued.

He said illegal migrants create problems for the entire society. When migration centers are overcrowded, resources are needed to house these people and to find interpreters and other specialists. All this creates a serious burden that Latvia feels most acutely right now, but there have also been cases of people detained on Estonian territory.

In recent days, more than 30 migrants who entered Europe after illegally crossing the Belarusian border were detained in Tallinn.

Taro said Estonia is much better prepared today for possible migration challenges than it was several years ago. In recent years the state has steadily strengthened the external border: a border fence has been built, and work continues on installing modern surveillance systems and other equipment to control the area.

He also stressed that the fence itself is not an absolute barrier. Its main purpose is to give border guards time to respond to attempts to cross illegally.

At Belarus-Lithuania border, underground digging attempted

Lithuanian border guards discovered an underground tunnel near the Belarus border recently that may have been built to move illegal migrants into the country. The tunnel already extended several meters into Lithuanian territory, but an exit had not yet been completed.

Estonian Police and Border Guard Board deputy director for border management Veiko Kommusaar said in an interview that there is no information suggesting anyone has tried to dig such a tunnel on Estonia's eastern border, but it cannot be ruled out in the future. History shows attempts to bring contraband alcohol or other goods underwater using cables or even divers.

Stenbocki maja sisehoovis esitleti droonide teekaarti 2026–2030 Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Kommusaar added that Estonia's land border is well covered by various surveillance and camera systems. "Surveillance systems are definitely something that shows activity levels. These tunnels are not dug by hand."

Of Estonia's 130 kilometers of land border with Russia, 110 kilometers are essentially fenced, and more than half of the surveillance systems have been installed. The infrastructure will be completed in 2027, ensuring full surveillance coverage along the entire border.

In Belarus, tunnels are being dug because the pressure to enter the European Union illegally is so great that all possible methods are being tried. "This is actually enabled by the Belarusian regime itself. You cannot just dig something in a border area. Belarusian border guards facilitate this activity and provide information on possible crossing points at specific times," he added.

Kommusaar said migration pressure on Latvia and Lithuania comes from Belarus, while no similar migration attack is currently being carried out from Russian territory. At the moment there are no signs the Russian Federation is organizing anything similar, but that could change overnight.

Why is there no pressure from Russia now? "One could speculate that if Belarus is doing the dirty work for them, part of the answer lies there."

Kommusaar said this migration attack in our region has been ongoing for five years. Every day more than 100 people are blocked from entering the European Union at the Latvian border. Unfortunately not all attempts are stopped, and some still manage to cross.

This article has been updated on July 29 with comments by Estonian Police and Border Guard Board deputy director for border management Veiko Kommusaar.

World.title: State considers replacing bankruptcy trustees with civil servants
World.content:
Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta is proposing to replace bankruptcy trustees with civil servants or to cover trustee fees from the state budget in certain proceedings. The state's Insolvency Service said the idea is worthwhile, and one way to fund it could be an insolvency tax.

The Ministry of Justice said Estonia's insolvency system is not sustainable in its current form. As a result, problems must be addressed to prevent the entire system from collapsing.

A bankruptcy trustee is an impartial official appointed by a court whose main task is to manage and carry out bankruptcy proceedings. The trustee acts as an intermediary who must protect the legal interests of both the debtor and creditors and ensure transparency.

One way to make the insolvency system more sustainable, the ministry said, would be to cover trustee fees from the state budget in cases where there is no property or only minimal assets.

Right now trustees cannot declare bankruptcy if it is clear there is no property. "No one pays the trustee from the state budget or from creditors' pockets when there are no assets. If a deposit is paid, bankruptcy is declared, but if it is not paid, then it is not declared because there simply is no property," said Andres Hermet from Estonian Chamber of Enforcement Agents and Trustees in Bankruptcy

Bankruptcy proceedings (illustrative). Source: Sergei Stepanov/ERR

The ministry said trustees should not have to perform mandatory work for an unknown period without any guarantee of reasonable compensation. If the state paid reasonable compensation, the ministry said the quality of bankruptcy proceedings could improve.

The ministry did not specify how much the possible solution would cost the state. It noted that the budget impact could be significant.

Hermet said such additional state funding is a good idea, because no one would refuse money if the state wants to invest in the field.

But he did not agree with the ministry's assessment that the insolvency system is collapsing. He said new recruits are needed because entering the profession is difficult for people who have never been trustees, and trustee fees are completely unpredictable.

The Ministry of Justice said that if civil servants handled bankruptcy proceedings, it would mean additional costs for the state budget. Under this solution, civil servants would need salaries, and there would be IT development, space and support service costs, training costs and transition costs. The ministry said the state's workload would increase significantly.

Signe Viimsalu Autor/allikas: Kirke Ert/ERR

Insolvency Service head Signe Viimsalu said creating such a state competence center would be the most reasonable option.

Viimsalu wrote to Prime Minister Kristen Michal last week, saying that widespread insolvency could cause economic, social and institutional uncertainty and pose a threat to Estonia's internal security.

Viimsalu said the system that has been in place for the past 30 years urgently needs reform so creditors can recover their money more effectively. She said it would be an additional cost for the state budget, but in the long run it would be the most reasonable and cost‑effective solution for society as a whole.

She also could not say how much it would cost the state to nationalize the current trustee system. "I think the ministries need to calculate that themselves," Viimsalu said.

The Insolvency Service head said there are several ways to fund a new type of system.

"Certain proceedings could be handled entirely by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry's arbitration court. One option is to create an insolvency tax in Estonia to fund the system. Another option is a middle ground where, for example, wrongdoers pay part of the system's costs. Another option is that the bankruptcy estate itself funds part of the system, such as the IT system," Viimsalu said.

Viimsalu said the idea of an insolvency tax still needs more thought.

Hermet from the trustees' chamber said any proposal to create state bankruptcy trustees is not adequate.

"I do not see any economic logic in this. The issue where I have no criticism of the service is that we are fighting against bankruptcy masters and late bankruptcy filings. But a state trustee would not help solve this problem in any way."

He added that he does not see how a civil servant could work more effectively or cheaply than a bankruptcy trustee.

World.title: Estonian firefighters to help put out wildfires in Italy
World.content:
Estonia's Rescue Services Agency will send a team of 20 firefighters to Italy to support local efforts to put out wildfires as southern Europe battles blazes and extreme heat.

France, Spain, northern Portugal, and northern Italy have been hit hardest by wildfires so far this year as temperatures have soared above 40 degrees Celcius.

The Estonian team will be based in Monte Pisano in northern Sardinia and will depart on July 31, the agency said in a statement.

Sardinia, located off Italy's west coast, is mountainous, with its highest peak at 1,834 meters. Approximately half of the island is covered by forest.

"The past week has been very demanding for firefighters. The largest and most complex forest fires are raging in southern Sardinia, which is quite typical for this stage of the fire season," said team leader Kaarel Langemets.

"Last week was the most critical of the year so far, as very high temperatures accelerated the spread of fires," he added.

Temperatures approaching 40 degrees Celsius are also forecast for the coming weeks.

The rescue team is scheduled to return in the early hours of August 16.

All-terrain vehicles will be provided for the Estonian rescuers on site, and up to three members are needed to assist the helicopter crew at the scene.

My heart goes out to everyone affected by the devastating wildfires across Southern Europe.



Estonia stands with the affected communities. In the coming days, an Estonian Rescue Services Agency (@paasteamet ) wildfire firefighting team will deploy to Sardinia, Italy,… pic.twitter.com/2gxGJjYleI — Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) July 27, 2026

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said that the Estonian Rescue Services Agency wildfire firefighting team will join local response efforts to fight the fires.

"We are deeply grateful to every firefighter and emergency responder risking so much to protect lives, homes and nature," he said in a statement on social media.

"These devastating wildfires remind us that strengthening our resilience, caring for our environment and preparing for a changing climate is ultimately about protecting people, their homes and the places they cherish," he added.

Summer forest fires have become a major problem in southern Europe in recent years. The fires are becoming gigantic and devastating. Last year, Estonia sent several teams of firefighters to Spain to help battle wildfires.

World.title: 'Tartu Buzz' 2-week festival starts Saturday
World.content:
This Saturday, August 1, sees the start of the "Tartu Sumin" fortnight-long Old Town summer festival in Estonia's second city.

"Tartu Sumin" ("Tartu buzz") kicks off with an Old Town open day on the Saturday, which will see the streets and courtyards get jam packed with flea markets, live music and a diverse cultural program.

The epicenter of the festivities is the central artery of Rüütli tänav, specifically the stretch between Munga and Lai, which organizers say will bring renewed life to a normally quieter part of the Old Town. The main stage will be located on the lawn beside St. John's Church (Jaani kirik), while the program invites visitors to explore the entire Old Town.

From 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. on the Saturday, visitors can browse a fashion flea market on Rüütli, a book market on Kompanii tänav, a creative fair in the Antoniuse õu coutyard, as well as a sports-themed flea market in the courtyard of the Estonian Sports and Olympic Museum (Spordi- ja Olümpiamuuseum, Rüütli 15). A flea market featuring children's items will go ahead in the courtyard at Magasini 3.

Abakhan (Rüütli 11), the adjacent Kivi Bar (Rüütli 13), the Saiko shop in the courtyard of Paper Tiger (Kompanii 2), are other flea markets open to the public.

Of other events, From 11 a.m. to 12 noon, the Tartu City Library (Kompanii 3-5) will host a guided tour for those interested. Advance registration is required, and from 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., the library will also hold an open dance class introducing participants to different styles of dance-based movement.

Tartu Art Museum curators Aavo Kokk and Andres Eilart will present the exhibition "Köögikunst. Pintsliga tõmmatud toidulugu ("Kitchen Art: A Food Story Painted with a Brush") from 1 p.m. to 2 p.m. Participants will need to purchase an exhibition ticket.

Regular Saturday guided tours of Tartu's Old Town will be going ahead through the festival, with Estonian-language tours from 12 p.m. to 1 p.m. and English-language tours from 2 p.m. to 3 p.m. Tickets are available through Fienta.

The Open Old Town Day (Avatud vanalinna päev) concludes at 7 p.m. on August 1 with a concert by Maris Pihlap at the "Tartu Sumin" festival main stage, followed by the Night Buzz event on Rüütli Street, featuring Kepler and DJ Daysleeper from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m.

Rest of the two weeks

The "Sumina" themed evenings will explore different aspects of Tartu's Old Town, with discussions at 7 p.m. and concerts at 8 p.m. on the main stage beside St. John's Church.

On August 3, Tartu stories, myths and legends are to be discussed by Ants Siim, Ants Johanson and Eda Kalmre, moderated by Risto Lehiste, with music from Vaiko Eplik and Priit Võigemast.

On August 5, Old Town food culture will be explored by Inna Jürjo, Anu Kannike, Max Mõttus and Henri Loodmaa, moderated by Susanna Aleksandra Veldi, followed by an Eleryn Tiit trio concert.

On August 10, the focus will be on the Old Town as a living environment and its impact on wellbeing, with speakers including Elo Kiivet, Marie Valgre and Hans Orro, moderated by Heleri All, followed by Sten-Olle and Haldi.

August 12 will feature Youth Day, with workshops, emerging artists, a social media discussion with Hensugusta and a closing performance by Clicherik & Mäx.

On August 14, writer and critic Berk Vaher will moderate a discussion on Tartu's nightlife and subcultures, followed by a performance from Kitty Florentine.

World.title: Parties not hurrying to back diplomat's presidential bid
World.content:
Politicians across party lines have reacted to diplomat Hannes Hanso's statement that he would run for president if asked, though none have pledged their support for him yet.

Hanso, 54, incoming Estonian ambassador to the U.S. and a former politician, said on Tuesday he was ready to run for the presidency in September if he was asked to, adding he would make a good head of state.

The two parties which have not declared in favor of any candidate yet, Isamaa and the Center Party, similarly would not rule Hanso in or out.

Hannes Hanso. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Lauri Laats, chairman of Center's Riigikogu group, told "Aktuaalne kaamera" the news is welcome in that the party has always striven for a range of candidates to choose from While the party has not discussed a possible Hanso presidential bid yet, it considers him a highly worthy candidate, Laats added.

It is still too early to say whether Center would back Hanso if nomination signatures from other parties' MPs started to be gathered. "We are still waiting for more candidates, and we will certainly make our decision sometime in August," Laats said.

Lauri Laats. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Isamaa's leader, Urmas Reinsalu, said the party has not discussed Hanso's possible candidacy, but also spoke favorably of Hanso.

"It is encouraging when people feel ready to take on such a mission and say so clearly. Isamaa has not discussed his candidacy, but he is certainly a credible person with diplomatic experience. At this stage, we are not taking any exclusionary positions," Reinsalu said.

Hanso, a former MP and a former defense minister, used to belong to the Social Democrats (SDE). However, his former party-mates have not ditched their preferred candidate, Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise, in favor of Hanso, following his announcement.

Isamaa Chairman Urmas Reinsalu. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"As for Hannes Hanso, he is certainly a worthy candidate and his name has come up in various discussions before. Our current preliminary assessment is that his support base in parliament is not as broad as Ülle Madise's," said Tanel Kiik, SDE's vice chair.

With 37 seats and 68 or more votes needed at the 101-seat Riigikogu to elect a president, support from the Reform Party is essential for any candidate to have a realistic chance.

Reform's secretary general, Kristo Enn Vaga, told "Aktuaalne kaamera" that the party continues to back a Madise candidacy, and effectively ruled out Hanso.

Kristo Enn Vaga. Source: Katriin Krünberg/ERR

"Hannes Hanso is a very capable ambassador, and I wish him every success in Washington, in his next posting," Vaga said.

"The Reform Party supports Ülle Madise's candidacy, as do two other parliamentary parties – the Social Democrats and Eesti 200. We would now like to hear the position of the Center Party, EKRE and, why not, Isamaa. If one of these were to support Ülle Madise's candidacy, it would be mathematically sure that she would get elected at the Riigikogu," Vaga said.

While Madise has said she has not given her consent to anyone to run, Reform says it would only consider other proposed candidates if Madise declines.

Ülle Madise has been Chancellor of Justice for over a decade and is backed by Reform, Eesti 200 and SDE for a presidential candidacy, though she has not given her consent as yet. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

In 2021, Alar Karis was elected unopposed, whereas in 2016 Kersti Kaljulaid was only elected after a lengthy process which reached its final stage, with the Riigikogu's Council of Elders. Parties this time around have expressed a desire to avoid both scenarios.

The official nomination window for candidates is August 21-24, with the first round of Riigikogu voting to follow on September 2.

Other figures who have announced a willingness to run are businessman Indrek Laul, EU official Maive Rute and retired military officer Riho Ühtegi, while several other names have been floated – in most cases these figures have indicated they would not like to run. Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) co-founder and MP Mart Helme is the only candidate to have been formally put forward by a party so far.
