World.title: One of WA's worst serial paedophiles set to be released from jail
World.content:
One of Western Australia's worst serial paedophiles appears set to be released from prison under strict supervision, as prosecutors argue he is a high-risk serious offender.

Dennis John McKenna abused dozens of boys in the 1970s and 80s while in charge of St Andrew's Hostel, a student boarding accommodation facility in the town of Katanning, about 290 kilometres south-east of Perth.

McKenna's brazen and repetitive offending was revealed over the course of four separate court cases between 1991 and 2015.

Dennis McKenna has been declared a High Risk Serious Offender but will be released from jail.

He was denied parole in 2024, and prosecutors have since sought to have the serial paedophile declared a High Risk Serious Offender (HRSO), which could have kept the octogenarian behind bars for the rest of his life.

In court today, the prosecution argued McKenna should be declared an HRSO, but could be released from prison under strict conditions.

That could happen as soon as November, as McKenna completes his 15-and-a-half-year sentence.

Reoffending risk 'low' despite 'distorted views'

McKenna, 81, watched on via video link from Acacia Prison dressed in a green jumper with short, thinning grey hair. He spoke only to confirm his name.

Prosecutor Brett Tooker told the court McKenna posed "an unacceptable risk that he will commit a serious offence … against a male child."

The former St Andrew's Hostel in Katanning where McKenna abused his victims was demolished last year. (ABC Great Southern: Rosemary Murphy)

The court heard from one forensic psychiatrist who considered his risk of reoffending was "low", primarily due to his advanced age and lack of offending in the 17 years between his 1991 and 2011 jail sentences.

Forensic psychiatrist Peter Wynn Owen, who interviewed McKenna twice for around five hours over the past year, said the serial paedophile continued to "categorically" deny any offending after 1981.

"[He] attributes blame to victims, suggests victims in fact instigated aspects of the offending," he said.

"If an individual is denying offending, it suggests they are not going to be able to engage with treatment."

Mr Wynn Owen said McKenna continued to hold distorted views that in his mind minimised or justified his offending.

"This distortion … enabled him to continue to offend over a long period of time," he said.

McKenna 'knows how vilified he is'

McKenna's lawyer Joel Grinceri said he saw "no reason" why McKenna needed to see victim submissions tended to the court and didn't anticipate he would seek to view them.

Unmasking a notorious paedophile Maggie Dawkins's efforts to shine a light on the horrific abuses committed by Dennis McKenna against a generation of boys in Katanning are set down in a new book.

"He is well aware of his notoriety in the community and he is essentially a man with no friends," Mr Grinceri said.

"His family has abandoned him and he has been in custody for many years now.

"There is, obviously, on his behalf significant trepidation at the prospect of being released in the community, knowing how vilified he is and how notorious he is in the community.

"He is scared himself in that regard."

Loading...

Mr Wynn Owen told the court he had significant concerns about McKenna's proposed address following release, given he would be sharing a home with a fellow offender.

"Mr McKenna is a very isolated man and will remain isolated other than [with] this individual," he said.

"To live with another offender who is also a denier would potentially increase his risk [and] is likely to reduce his compliance with supervision and monitoring."

Victims got 'life sentences'

Among those eager to be present for the decision on McKenna's future was Kaye Anderson.

Three of Ms Anderson's five children attended St Andrew's, with Ray and Quenton both reporting they were sexually abused during their stay between 1985 and 1987.

Ray, Quenton, Bevan, Nathan and Damian Anderson. (Supplied: Kaye Anderson)

Ray later took his own life, while Quenton died from drug and alcohol abuse.

Ms Anderson said McKenna will never be able to remedy the harm caused to her family.

"My kids got death sentences, so did others. Those kids he abused, they got life sentences.

"They never got parole; they had to live with that.

Kaye Anderson, the mother of one of Dennis McKenna’s victims, attends the Perth Supreme Court. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer )

"McKenna should be the same. No release from jail whatsoever."

Whistleblower Maggie Dawkins said she too was disappointed McKenna will likely walk free.

"We're going to have probably 40 different clauses. He's got to wear one of those electronic bracelets and all that sort of stuff," she said.

"But he's still out, isn't he?

"That's using police resources that they've got to monitor all the time, when that could be better spent elsewhere."

McKenna's lawyer and the prosecutor agreed about the need to declare him a High Risk Serious Offender and that he should be subject to a supervision order.

The specifics of those conditions were being negotiated. A final decision on McKenna's future will be made at a later court hearing.

World.title: Queenslander could face execution over alleged killing of Australian in Syria
World.content:
A 20-year-old Gold Coast mobile phone technician faces a possible death penalty in Syria for the alleged shooting murder of another Australian man.

Patrick Stevenson has been detained for nearly seven months in Idlib province, in the war-scarred country's north-west, on a charge of premeditated murder: an offence punishable by death.

An ABC investigation has established that Mr Stevenson, a Muslim convert with learning disorders, ADHD and suspected autism spectrum disorder, travelled to Syria late last year after becoming radicalised on the Gold Coast.

Mr Stevenson was arrested shortly after 40-year-old Australian citizen Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess was shot dead in the town of Darkush on December 31.

Syrian authorities allege Mr Stevenson confessed to firing at least eight shots from an AK-47 at Mr Burgess inside the victim's home.

Patrick Stevenson converted to Islam in 2023. (Supplied)

Authorities initially investigated whether Mr Stevenson had links to the Islamic State group (IS) but later concluded that the killing was not linked to the terrorist group, according to information provided to his family by Australian officials and his legal team.

The ABC has established that Mr Burgess was living in Syria with his Australian wife and children last year after leaving their home in northern New South Wales and spending several months travelling through Afghanistan.

It is unknown what brought the family to Syria. The ABC does not suggest they had links to extremist groups.

People who knew the two men said Mr Burgess took Mr Stevenson under his wing late last year and that they became close in the lead-up to the killing.

According to Syrian authorities, Mr Burgess's wife and their daughters were in another room when he was shot but were not physically injured.

Even if convicted, Mr Stevenson could be spared execution if Mr Burgess's widow, Amatullah Laurie Duniam, grants him forgiveness under Syria's legal system.

Ms Duniam could instead accept a payment of blood money, known as diya, from Mr Stevenson's family.

Mr Burgess's family, including Ms Duniam, declined to speak to the ABC.

Do you know more? Contact Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop on Signal: @seanrdunlop.01 and on Protonmail: seanrdunlop@protonmail.com

on Signal: and on Protonmail: Please use this form to get in contact with the ABC Investigations team, or if you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

Mr Stevenson's legal team has told the ABC it holds grave concerns about his prospects of a fair trial and his welfare in Sarmada prison, where it says his mental health has deteriorated significantly.

No Australian official has visited Mr Stevenson in prison or attended his court hearings to verify his identity and assess his welfare.

Australian authorities have also been unable to independently monitor the investigation into Mr Burgess's death.

Mr Stevenson's father, Clay Stevenson, travelled to Syria last week and visited his son in prison for the first time.

He also attended his son's court hearing on Sunday to submit Australian medical records, including a psychiatric report documenting Patrick's ADHD and learning disorders, as well as suspected autism spectrum disorder.

The ABC understands DFAT has told Mr Stevenson's family that the Syrian government has shown little engagement over the case.

Unlike allies including the United States and France, Canberra has struggled to establish diplomatic ties with Syria's new government. Australian sanctions remain in place against the militant group from which Syria's new leadership emerged.

The case also raises questions about whether Syria could again become a destination for radicalised Australians as it emerges from a 14-year civil war that drew thousands of foreign fighters to terrorist groups including IS.

The mayor of a nearby village in Idlib province, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the quaint riverside town of Darkush, near the Turkish border, had become a stronghold for Australian former fighters and Islamists.

Killing initially treated as an accident

After Mr Stevenson's arrest on December 31, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) told his family that Syrian authorities initially treated the shooting as accidental.

But a week later, DFAT advised the family by email that Syria's "Intelligence Bureau is investigating Mr Stevenson's possible affiliation with ISIS".

According to information provided to the family, that terrorism investigation ended in February when authorities referred the case to the civilian criminal courts.

The civilian prosecution will be a significant test of Syria's fractured legal system and is likely to attract international scrutiny.

Patrick Stevenson was living in Idlib province, the former rebel stronghold in Syria's north-west. (Supplied)

Australia has no embassy or consulate in Syria, severely limiting its ability to provide consular assistance.

Correspondence seen by the ABC shows DFAT repeatedly told Mr Stevenson's family that it could not obtain information from Syrian authorities and had no access to the country's detention facilities.

DFAT told the ABC it was providing consular assistance to Mr Burgess's and Mr Stevenson's families but was unable to comment further because of privacy obligations.

"We send our deepest condolences to [Mr Burgess's] family at this difficult time," the department said in a statement.

From the Gold Coast to Idlib

Mr Stevenson converted to Islam in his final year of high school in 2023, according to his family.

By last year, he was showing signs of radicalisation, including sharing speeches online by Anwar al-Awlaki, the US-born Al Qaeda cleric and propagandist killed in a drone strike in Yemen in 2011.

Mr Stevenson left the Gold Coast on a flight to Bali on October 10 and later travelled to Syria.

He soon moved to Idlib province, Syria's former rebel stronghold, in the country's north-west.

The province is home to former foreign fighters, including Australians, some of whom have been stripped of their passports.

Patrick Stevenson previously worked as a mobile phone technician on the Gold Coast. (Supplied)

Idlib was governed for years by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) before the group led the offensive that toppled dictator Bashar al-Assad. HTS formally dissolved in January 2025.

The former Al Qaeda affiliate, previously known as Jabhat al-Nusra, remains a designated terrorist organisation in Australia.

Syrian legal sources told the ABC it could take up to a year for the court to reach a verdict.

Mr Stevenson's fate may ultimately depend as much on diplomacy and clemency as on the evidence against him.

Under Syrian law, a death sentence imposed by an ordinary criminal court must be reviewed by the Court of Cassation, considered by a special clemency committee and approved by the president before it can be carried out.

World.title: 'Jealous, possessive man' appeals against sentence for murdering zoo colleague
World.content:
A chef sentenced to 30 years in jail for murdering his co-worker at Canberra's National Zoo and Aquarium is appealing against his sentence, arguing the court failed to properly account for his mental impairment when determining his punishment.

Warning: This story discusses a violent crime.

Jude Wijesinghe was handed a 30-year sentence and a 20-year non-parole period by the ACT Supreme Court in December last year, after he admitted to murdering his co-worker Tshewang Choden at the zoo in 2023.

The 32-year-old trapped Ms Choden in a storeroom and fatally stabbed her 14 times in what Chief Justice Lucy McCallum described as "murderous violence against a vulnerable woman at the hands of a jealous, possessive man".

It was one of the ACT's most significant sentences, with Chief Justice McCallum stopping short of imposing life in jail, after taking into account Wijesinghe's guilty plea and mental health at the time of the offending.

She found his mental illness provided "some explanation" for the murder and reduced his moral culpability, but did not warrant a reduction in the overall sentence given the "very serious objective features" of the offence.

Sentencing judge erred, defence argues

The ACT Court of Appeal heard submissions on Wednesday from Wijesinghe's defence barrister Kylie Weston-Scheuber, who argued the sentencing judge made four errors when determining the length of his sentence.

Ms Weston-Scheuber said Chief Justice McCallum accepted psychiatric evidence that Wijesinghe was suffering from a major depressive disorder and pathological infatuation with Ms Choden, but "expressly failed to give any reduction" to the head sentence.

She argued that, having found his mental illness reduced his moral culpability, the court ought to have reduced the overall sentence.

"Her Honour failed to distinguish between a person who is motivated by a desire to possess someone or take revenge without the effects of that mental impairment, where in this situation that emotional state and motivation was produced by that mental impairment," Ms Weston-Scheuber said.

She also argued the sentencing judge erred in finding Wijesinghe's mental impairment did not reduce the objective seriousness of the offending, despite accepting it was causally linked to the murder.

Chief Justice McCallum stopped short of imposing life in jail when sentencing Jude Wijesinghe in the ACT Supreme Court. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Counsel for the Director of Public Prosecutions, Elizabeth Ruddle SC, who is seeking to have the original sentence maintained, argued an offender's moral culpability and the objective seriousness of the offending were separate considerations in sentencing.

She argued Chief Justice McCallum was entitled to find Wijesinghe's mental illness reduced his moral culpability without also reducing the objective seriousness of the murder.

"Let's not forget how horrific this murder was. The deceased was trapped in this room knowing she was going to die," counsel said.

Ms Ruddle said the court's assessment of objective seriousness was based on the actual features of the offending.

"That's what the court needs to look at: the actual features of the offence," she said.

Ms Ruddle also argued that even if Wijesinghe's mental illness reduced his moral culpability, the sentence still needed to reflect the seriousness of the offending and discourage similar crimes.

Ms Weston-Scheuber also argued Chief Justice McCallum erred by failing to reduce the head sentence to reflect Wijesinghe's guilty plea and that the overall sentence was manifestly excessive.

Ms Ruddle rejected both grounds, submitting it was open to the sentencing judge to recognise the guilty plea through the non-parole period and that the 30-year sentence remained within the available sentencing range.

The appeal sits before Justice Darryl Rangiah, Justice Andrew Muller, and Justice Jon White, with a decision to be handed down at a later date.

A large tree branch has fallen on a playground injuring a woman and child at a popular inner-city park in Brisbane. Emergency services rushed to Guyatt Park in St Lucia about 6pm on Wednesday when the tree branch – which Nine News described as running the length of the playground – struck an eight-year-old boy and a 29-year-old woman. A weekly community dinner run by Greens MPs Elizabeth Watson-Brown and Michael Berkman was taking place nearby. Neither was in attendance. The large branch, which extends the full length of the playground, which struck the woman and boy. Felicity Caldwell The boy suffered head injuries and the woman’s arm was injured by the falling tree.



Queensland Ambulance Service confirmed four crews attended the scene, and said the woman was taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, while the boy was taken to the Queensland Children’s Hospital. In a statement posted online, Berkman praised park goers and dinner attendees for providing prompt assistance to the pair. A witness described a huge police presence alongside fire and ambulance crews at the park. Felicity Caldwell “Around 5.45pm a large tree branch fell in the playground area at Guyatt Park, seriously injuring one woman and a young boy. My community meals team was there at the time for our regular dinner,” he wrote. “I hear that there was an incredible effort from everyone in the park to move the tree, get firies and ambos there, and help out wherever possible. I couldn’t be prouder of our community right now.



“Obviously medical professionals are still assessing the situation, but I understand the woman is receiving treatment for traumatic injuries to her arm. One of the Greens’ free community dinners, held weekly at Guyatt Park in St Lucia. World.title: Rinehart lobbied Bleijie on Rockhampton rowing. Then the LNP backed it
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Rinehart lobbied Bleijie on Rockhampton rowing. Then the LNP backed it Matt Dennien July 29, 2026 — 8:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland government went against the advice of its own Olympic venue review with a controversial decision to host rowing in Rockhampton after intervention from Australia’s richest person and conservative political patron Gina Rinehart. A letter obtained by this masthead under Right to Information laws reveals Rinehart personally wrote to Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie after the proposal came to her attention, extolling the virtues of the pitch across 283 words. “I hope that the Queensland government can well consider the Rockhampton proposal, and I wish you all the best in planning the best Olympic Games,” the billionaire businesswoman wrote on Hancock Prospecting letterhead. Hancock Prospecting chief Gina Rinehart highlighted Rockhampton’s status as a major mining town in her push for the Fitzroy River to host the 2032 Olympic rowing. Trevor Collens This masthead sought access to the letter via Bleijie’s office last month.



Within hours of a decision to grant full access to it on Wednesday afternoon, and questions from this masthead about when the undated letter was sent to Bleijie, the document appeared in News Corp reporting. While Bleijie’s office has not responded, News Corp reported the letter came before the government’s March 2025 announcement and “soon after the idea to host it in Rockhampton was floated by Queensland Nationals Senator Matt Canavan”. The letter from Rinehart, who is a patron of Rowing Australia, notes the proposal had “come to my attention” and that the Fitzroy River often hosts Australian team training and annually hosts the Queensland state school championships. “This rowing facility is world class and is already close to major infrastructure, so it offers the potential to save taxpayer money,” she wrote.



“Hosting a marquee Olympic event like rowing at Australia’s ‘Beef Capital’ in Rockhampton would enable Queensland to tell the iconic Australian story of our pastoralists and farmers, terrific Aussies. “As you would know too, Rockhampton has also always been a major mining town, the nearby Mt Morgan mine was once the biggest gold mine in the world. I am told that metals from this mine will produce the gold, silver, and bronze medals for the Olympics! “To marry showing where the Olympic medals come from and having Olympic events nearby sounds to me like a beautiful extra!” Rinehart also noted the “obvious plus” of showcasing more of the state beyond Brisbane, dispersing crowds and infrastructure stress in the capital, and enabling visitors to “take home with them warm positive memories of the friendly country people of rural Queensland”.





The Crisafulli LNP’s decision to pursue rowing on the central Queensland city’s Fitzroy River has sparked swift and sustained backlash over the fitness of that site for global competition, including from Rowing Australia, of which Rinehart is a patron. Instead, GIICA’s 100-day review of venues recommended rowing be held at the site of the Sydney 2000 Olympic competition in Penrith. World.title: No quick end to the war as US and Saudis strike Iran’s allies in Iraq
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war No quick end to the war as US and Saudis strike Iran’s allies in Iraq Parisa Hafezi , Ahmed Tolba and Ahmed Elimam July 29, 2026 — 8:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dubai/Cairo: The United States on Wednesday launched its first airstrikes in the Middle East since

suspending its bombing campaign last week, hitting Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq jointly with Saudi Arabia, while Tehran spurned an Omani plan to manage the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said it had fired on ships in the strait and at US bases in Jordan, and oil prices rose again as renewed combat and diplomatic setbacks signalled no quick end to the war the United States and Israel started in February. Black smoke rises following explosions near a military base hosting US forces in the northern Iraqi city of Irbil. AP Washington and Riyadh said they had jointly struck Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq in retaliation for drone attacks on Saudi oil targets. Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces, powerful Iran-backed paramilitary groups incorporated into the formal Iraqi security forces, said at least 20 members were killed and 32 wounded in US-Saudi strikes targeting several bases across Iraq.



It was the first major US military action in the Middle East since last Friday, when US President Donald Trump abruptly suspended an intensive bombing campaign after 13 days, having been advised by commanders that the strategy had run its course. An  for a smartphone stands in front of a billboard depicting US President Donald Trump being grabbed by the neck in Tehran, Iran. AP Photo/Vahid Salemi The joint strikes potentially widen the conflict by drawing Sunni Muslim Saudi Arabia into combat against Shiite proxies of Iran on a new front. It was the first time during the war that Saudi Arabia had publicly declared its participation in joint strikes alongside the US. Iraq’s Shiite-led government, one of the few in the world to maintain close military and diplomatic ties with both Iran and the US, called an emergency meeting. Washington has long called on the Baghdad government to crack down on Iran-backed paramilitaries, but efforts to do so in the past have provoked domestic unrest.



Saudi Arabia has also been drawn into the conflict on another front, with the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen announcing a blockade of Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea last week and firing on ships and oil facilities. Hours before launching the joint attacks with Saudi Arabia on Iraq, the US military said its air defences had averted a surprise Iranian attack on US troops in the region. Loading Jordan’s military said its air defences had intercepted and shot down five Iranian missiles. Three of the four US service members killed this month were killed in Jordan, where US bases have become primary Iranian targets.



Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had fired several ballistic missiles at US military installations in Jordan, and had struck three tankers that were attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz along an unauthorised route. World.title: Mother attended police station day before murder-suicide; Search for infant son called off
World.content:
NationalTragedy Mother attended police station day before murder-suicide; Search for infant son called off Isabel McMillan July 29, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the hours before Helena Wright’s body was pulled from the waters off South Australia’s Limestone Coast, police received a call from her friend. The details of that call are not publicly known, but it was enough to prompt a welfare check at the 36-year-old’s Compton home, on the outskirts of Mount Gambier. The call came at 9.28am on Monday, and when police knocked shortly after, no one answered the door. No one was home. Less than two hours later, reports from the public led police to find a vehicle parked on a clifftop at Cape Northumberland, near Port Macdonnell, a 30-minute drive from Wright’s home. The vehicle was empty, but its engine was still running.



Then, in the treacherous waters below South Australia’s southernmost point, police and local fishermen found Wright’s body, and the body of her 23-month-old daughter. Her three-month-old son could not be found. Loading As emergency services, community members, friends and family grapple with the tragic deaths and what led to them, police have confirmed Wright had visited a police station the day before, they believe she took her life, and the lives of her two young children. “South Australia Police can confirm Helena Wright attended the Mount Gambier Police Station on Sunday 26 July where she spoke with police,” a police spokesperson confirmed to this masthead on Wednesday night. “As this matter is now subject to a coronial investigation, SAPOL will provide all relevant information and evidence to the coroner. It is not appropriate to comment further while coronial proceedings are underway.”



Volunteers battled the harsh weather conditions for days, trying to find the body of Wright’s youngest child. On the water, on land and in the sky, help came from across the state and Victoria in the hopes of finding the baby. While Superintendent Trent Cox on Monday admitted it would be unlikely the infant would be found alive, he said he was holding out hope. The search near Port Macdonnell on South Australia’s south-east coast. 9News The last glimmer of that hope had faded when he again faced the waiting press pack on Wednesday, standing in the rain to announce the search would be unlikely to yield any positive result. Later, police confirmed they would cease searching altogether and, based on expert advice, declared the baby “could not have survived the period of time that has elapsed, either in the water or on land”. “Additionally, a range of factors, including the search environment and prevailing weather conditions, significantly reduce the likelihood of locating the infant in the immediate term. “The reality is, after three days, the chances of finding the baby alive are zero, sadly,” Cox said. “It’s a retrieval effort, but we don’t know where he is.”



Cox confirmed that, after days of investigation, the evidence police had gathered suggested no one else was believed to be involved in the deaths, and said the matter was now being handled as a murder-suicide. When asked if Wright had been turned away by police when she visited the Mount Gambier station on Sunday, and told to come back another day, Cox said he wouldn’t “confirm anything or deny anything”. “Any contact with police will form part of the brief that we provide the coroner,” he said. “I’m not aware of anything that I can release to you about the mother’s mental state or her personal medical issues. “The investigation of any death is very delicate, but when it involves children as young as 23 months and three months, it adds another layer of complexity, but also trauma for those who are involved. “It’s delicate in a number of ways. Obviously, the welfare aspect for my staff and for our volunteers. Also recognising it’s a local family.”



To those speculating on the tragedy without knowing the facts, Cox warned against adding to misinformed commentary. “Public commentary without the facts is always dangerous,” he said. “Misinformed commentary doesn’t help anyone.” To the wider community, who are struggling to come to terms with the circumstances of the deaths, Cox’s message was clear: “Wrap your arms around each other.” “Look after yourselves, look after your loved ones,” he said. “Give your kids an extra tight hug. “It will affect the community whether they have children or not because the deaths of such young children and a mother in these circumstances is tragic on so many levels.”



If you or anyone you know needs help, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 (see lifeline.org.au), Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 (see beyondblue.org.au) or 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732). Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

From enhanced lifestyle and comfort, quality materials and craftsmanship to greater environmental friendliness, renovated luxury homes can bring a host of benefits. Here are five of our favourite renovated luxury homes for sale right now. 71 North Road, Brighton, VIC Could it be your turn to own a piece of Bayside history?



John Knox House, a double-storey Gothic Victorian set on about 1647 square metres in one of Brighton’s most prestigious pockets, is on the market, with expressions of interest closing on September 15. Built in the 1880s, the home has been extensively renovated to balance the original heritage character with modern living. The original facade, open fireplaces and high ceilings pay homage to the history, while concrete walls and expansive windows showcase contemporary design. There are five bedrooms, four upstairs and a main suite on the ground floor, plus an additional wing with a showstopping kitchen featuring thick slab benchtops, Miele appliances and a walk-in pantry. A surround-sound system is fitted inside and out. The outside of the property also features a paved dining area with a built-in fridge, pizza oven, integrated seating, a retractable awning, a pool and a tennis court.



1/39 Arcadia Street, Coogee, NSW Located within a walk of Coogee Beach, this ground-floor luxury apartment, “Heritage Residence 1”, offers the epitome of beachside living. Developers Central Element have collaborated with a team of experts, including adaptive reuse specialists TZG Architects, interiors studio MIM Design and JILA Landscape Architects, to transform the 1860s heritage-listed property. The design style juxtaposes past and present.



The apartment features lofty ceilings, sandstone walls and sculptural archways, along with large windows that frame the sunlight and gardens. The apartment has three bedrooms and three bathrooms, and includes access to the building’s amenities, including an infrared sauna, a heated plunge pool and a gym. 90 Gipps Street, East Melbourne, VIC This Victorian terrace in East Melbourne was renovated for liveability by Carr Architecture.



The home has generous proportions, about 360 square metres of internal living space over two levels, and a climate-controlled basement wine cellar. Featuring quality craftsmanship, the home has floor-to-ceiling windows in the living room that look onto a central courtyard with a fully retractable roof, creating an all-year-round indoor-outdoor space. The chef’s kitchen, spanning more than 10 metres, is a standout, with Corian benchtops, integrated Gaggenau appliances, a commercial refrigerator, an ice maker, a concealed appliance cupboard and an oversized butler’s pantry. 14 Pymble Avenue, Pymble, NSW



Landmark property “The Knoll”, a home built about 1904 and measuring about1684 square metres, is on Pymble Avenue, a street of equal esteem. The arts and crafts Federation home has been renovated by heritage consultant Cubic, which has balanced historical integrity with modern appeal. Restored original features of the home include 3.3-metre-high ceilings, a chequered marble entry floor, and formal lounge and dining rooms with vintage stone-framed fireplaces. The home also features a rear studio with an en suite, a hidden sauna, home automation, designer lighting, a basement cellar and a pool. 1/131 Terrace Street, New Farm QLD



This renovated cottage offers heritage character and modern luxury. Original proportions are preserved across the home’s two levels, including high ceilings and an entry dome. From the sleek colour scheme to Japanese herringbone hardwood flooring, the updates create a sense of luxury, with carefully selected materials and technology, including a Sonos sound system and climate control, adding to this and bringing a sense of low-maintenance convenience. Other features include a vertical green wall, a custom bar, an al fresco courtyard and a media room.

A large tree branch has fallen on a playground injuring a woman and child at a popular inner-city park in Brisbane. Emergency services rushed to Guyatt Park in St Lucia about 6pm on Wednesday when the tree branch – which Nine News described as running the length of the playground – struck an eight-year-old boy and a 29-year-old woman. A weekly community dinner run by Greens MPs Elizabeth Watson-Brown and Michael Berkman was taking place nearby. Neither was in attendance. The large branch, which extends the full length of the playground, which struck the woman and boy. Felicity Caldwell The boy suffered head injuries and the woman’s arm was injured by the falling tree.



Queensland Ambulance Service confirmed four crews attended the scene, and said the woman was taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, while the boy was taken to the Queensland Children’s Hospital. In a statement posted online, Berkman praised park goers and dinner attendees for providing prompt assistance to the pair. A witness described a huge police presence alongside fire and ambulance crews at the park. Felicity Caldwell “Around 5.45pm a large tree branch fell in the playground area at Guyatt Park, seriously injuring one woman and a young boy. I couldn’t be prouder of our community right now.



“Obviously medical professionals are still assessing the situation, but I understand the woman is receiving treatment for traumatic injuries to her arm. World.title: Rinehart lobbied Bleijie on Rockhampton rowing. Then the LNP backed it
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Rinehart lobbied Bleijie on Rockhampton rowing. Then the LNP backed it Matt Dennien July 29, 2026 — 8:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland government went against the advice of its own Olympic venue review with a controversial decision to host rowing in Rockhampton after intervention from Australia’s richest person and conservative political patron Gina Rinehart. A letter obtained by this masthead under Right to Information laws reveals Rinehart personally wrote to Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie after the proposal came to her attention, extolling the virtues of the pitch across 283 words. “I hope that the Queensland government can well consider the Rockhampton proposal, and I wish you all the best in planning the best Olympic Games,” the billionaire businesswoman wrote on Hancock Prospecting letterhead. Hancock Prospecting chief Gina Rinehart highlighted Rockhampton’s status as a major mining town in her push for the Fitzroy River to host the 2032 Olympic rowing. Trevor Collens This masthead sought access to the letter via Bleijie’s office last month.



Within hours of a decision to grant full access to it on Wednesday afternoon, and questions from this masthead about when the undated letter was sent to Bleijie, the document appeared in News Corp reporting. While Bleijie’s office has not responded, News Corp reported the letter came before the government’s March 2025 announcement and “soon after the idea to host it in Rockhampton was floated by Queensland Nationals Senator Matt Canavan”. The letter from Rinehart, who is a patron of Rowing Australia, notes the proposal had “come to my attention” and that the Fitzroy River often hosts Australian team training and annually hosts the Queensland state school championships. “This rowing facility is world class and is already close to major infrastructure, so it offers the potential to save taxpayer money,” she wrote.



“Hosting a marquee Olympic event like rowing at Australia’s ‘Beef Capital’ in Rockhampton would enable Queensland to tell the iconic Australian story of our pastoralists and farmers, terrific Aussies. “As you would know too, Rockhampton has also always been a major mining town, the nearby Mt Morgan mine was once the biggest gold mine in the world. I am told that metals from this mine will produce the gold, silver, and bronze medals for the Olympics! “To marry showing where the Olympic medals come from and having Olympic events nearby sounds to me like a beautiful extra!” Rinehart also noted the “obvious plus” of showcasing more of the state beyond Brisbane, dispersing crowds and infrastructure stress in the capital, and enabling visitors to “take home with them warm positive memories of the friendly country people of rural Queensland”.





The Crisafulli LNP’s decision to pursue rowing on the central Queensland city’s Fitzroy River has sparked swift and sustained backlash over the fitness of that site for global competition, including from Rowing Australia, of which Rinehart is a patron. Instead, GIICA’s 100-day review of venues recommended rowing be held at the site of the Sydney 2000 Olympic competition in Penrith. World.title: After Allan, comes legacy and judgment
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters After Allan, comes legacy and judgment July 29, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. One has to acknowledge that the criminal connections around the Big Build have been an egregious blight on the Labor government. Jacinta Allan had to go. That said, seen from the perspective of one who has travelled regularly by train and car along the route of the Frankston railway line, the now reconfigured and modernised stations that have emerged from the level crossing removal program represent a testament to the aesthetic and quality of life changes wrought.

There was a time when Liberal Party state governments made an art form of inertia, especially in the era of Ted Baillieu’s leadership. By contrast, in 2026, due to Allan’s industriousness, suburbs like Carrum, Seaford, Aspendale, Mentone and Edithvale have been transformed with attractive shopping and landscaped precincts, ″⁣fly over″⁣ bay views, and, significantly, enhanced traffic flow. Once the ritual demonisation of what has been, for all its industrial relations missteps, an impressive innovative civic design policy achievement fades, history may deliver a kinder judgment.

Jon McMillan, Mornington Transport and education are positives

Now that we no longer need to distract ourselves, or let others distract us, by ALP state leadership issues, we can focus on some of the other issues – things that have been achieved. Top of the list for me would be the great work of Lily d’Ambrosio on the energy front. There has been a quiet revolution in the state’s energy system that recognises the immediacy of the current situation of old plant requiring replacement, and the challenge of rapidly bringing new renewable generation capacity online amid a political climate plagued by excessive venom and negativity.

We can also acknowledge and appreciate the public transport upgrades including the Metro Tunnel and numbers of level crossing removals. On the back of the fastest growing population of any state, we can see hospitals that have been built and others expanded, plus more than 100 new state schools being opened.

Robert Brown, Camberwell Royal commission is much needed

Nick McKenzie (Comment, 29/7) is right to call for a broad-based royal commission into the Big Build saga. If we are concerned about the waste of public money on poorly managed projects, then the commission must be allowed to look at the planning, or lack thereof, and selection of these projects in the first place.

The community is rightly concerned that the principles of good planning have been abandoned in favour of political expediency, thereby channelling vast amounts of money to a select few.

The West Gate Tunnel is a good example. Labor had an electoral mandate for a $1 billion project called the Western Distributor but instead delivered the more than $10 billion West Gate Tunnel project. This decision increased the cost of removing trucks from the streets of Footscray by more than $9 billion. And then there is the Suburban Rail Loop. The community deserves to know how our money is being spent.

Eric Keys, Flemington



Next on Carroll’s agenda . . .

I firmly endorse the change in leadership, however Labor needs to show leadership in these areas – a crackdown on corruption, divert resources from the SRL to completing the rail link to the airport, electrification of the rail line to Melton, repairing country road potholes and clamping down on criminal activities like the fire bombing of businesses. The SRL project needs to be placed on hold until a viable business case can justify its cost. I hope Ben Carroll puts the above actions on his agenda and proceeds with the above tasks; only then will people trust Labor to run Victoria.

David Orr, St Kilda In Allan’s debt, and not in a good way

Jacinta Allan in her resignation speech understandably hardly mentioned Victoria’s mountain of debt, which will prove to be her government’s principal enduring legacy to the state because of its profligate spending.

Dennis Walker, North Melbourne THE FORUM Rethink housing

We cannot build our way out of the housing crisis if population growth continually outpaces our capacity and resources for their supply (″⁣Three-storey homes: the radical plan to cut prices″⁣, 28/7). Insisting on high-density housing will not improve affordability because multi-level developments are far more expensive per square metre to build than single dwellings.

Furthermore, the resulting loss of tree canopies, gardens, and local character will erode the very qualities that draw people to these communities in the first place, as well as increasing urban temperatures.

Looking to our neighbours, a sharp decline in immigration in New Zealand has meant that new housing supply is finally outpacing population demand. As a result, house prices and rental costs have fallen significantly since 2021.

Jennie Epstein, Little River Who to trust?

Tony Wright’s fascinating historical recap on the ways of political demise (″⁣Allan exit follows familiar script″⁣, 29/7), can also be summed up with an excerpt from the 1950s sketch by Canadians Johnny Wayne and Frank Shuster. It’s a skit of an investigation by private detective Flavius Maximus into the death of Julius Caesar.

Maximus receives an agitated visitor with important information so (naturally) asks, “Are we alone?“, and the visitor replies in the affirmative. But twice more is the question asked with a final reply, “I’m positive we’re alone”.

Maximus then asks, “But who’s that standing beside you?” “That’s you!” “Yes, but can I be trusted?“

Jim Aylmer, Mt Waverley



Full exposure

Nick McKenzie (Comment, 29/7) is spot on. He rightly notes that the proposed royal commission must fully expose the actions of any CFMEU officials, any bureaucrats, and any politicians who have used the Big Build for corrupt purposes or for covering up political malfeasance.

The new Carroll government must ensure the commission’s terms of reference are comprehensive and transparent, while also ensuring that it investigates the extent to which corporate CEOs and senior managers in the construction industry have kowtowed to the alleged CFMEU thugs or who have knowingly co-operated with them.

Allan Patience, Newport Children’s needs

It is alarming to read that “one in three students are not engaged in their schooling during years 7-9” (“The multibillion-dollar cost of students who can’t – or won’t – engage with school”, 29/7). As the article mentions, it is the social costs which are most concerning and last the longest.

The transition to secondary school has always been difficult for many. These days, the picture is more complex: many students are on the ADHD spectrum and many struggle with their sexuality and gender identity.

Society is more complex as well, with both parents working and higher cost of living. It stands to reason then, that schools would optimally have more support staff to assist students, because teachers cannot do this on their own. I have worked in government and private schools and with youth in the community, and I know support staff can make a huge difference.

We need experienced and compassionate counsellors to work with students, and sometimes their parents, and expert educational support staff for one-on-one work with struggling students. These staff are most needed in government schools who have to enrol all students who apply from the school’s zone. Such schools are often underfunded and certainly cannot afford the useful year 9 camps that private schools run.

If we value our young people, this funding must be found.

Jan Marshall, Brighton Trump’s follies

Whether Donald Trump succumbs to the influence of Benjamin Netanyahu to escalate the war with Iran is uncertain (“Netanyahu lands with eyes on Iran”, 28/7). What we do know is the reckless and clueless way Trump miscalculated the war he started five months ago and was supposed to be finished in a few weeks. The US president went to war with no long-term strategy.

What is not surprising are the grandiose statements he makes that are fatally flawed. If he takes heed of Netanyahu, the unforeseen consequences will have an impact on the whole world.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading Workers, unite

As usual, Ross Gittins provides a succinct explanation of our cost-of-living and sluggish wages position (″⁣Bosses will hate this economic fix″⁣, 29/7).

Losing the effectiveness of collective bargaining has resulted in a substantial decline in wages and associated productivity. In an era when business profits have skyrocketed and union membership decreased to around 13 per cent, it’s indeed time that the workers again unite and we establish a renewed body like the Industrial Relations Commission to again set appropriate wages.

The decentralised wage-fixing model may have suited some industries, but not all workers have benefited, and in many cases, ″⁣real wages″⁣ have declined.

Time to fix this mess.

Denise Stevens, St Kilda Should be byelection

Moira Deeming was elected as a Liberal Party member (″⁣Deeming’s awkward exit″⁣, 29/7). As she is no longer a member, there should be a byelection to vote for her replacement.

The same should have applied to Lidia Thorpe, who was elected as a member of the Greens party.

Voters are not being represented properly when the person who has been voted in to parliament by them as a representative of a party continues to hold power, but who can use it according to their own wishes rather than by holding to the party line.

Marguerite Marshall, Eltham



Yawning gap

While sitting in a doctor’s waiting room on Tuesday, Jacinta Allan came on the TV to give her resignation speech. It seemed a kind and gracious speech.

But looking around the room of the dozen people waiting, I was the only person watching. Everyone else was staring at their phones. Maybe they were watching her online – but I doubt it.

I should not be surprised. This lack of interest in the politics that influences so many aspects of our lives is widespread. Recently, I had to explain to colleagues that it was the state government who built and ran schools, and removed level crossings. It was like these things just happen magically. But just as oddly, they happily offered negative opinions on politicians, sometimes without understanding which party they were from.

It feels that there is a very real disconnect between our political systems, the policies affecting our lives, and people’s interest . This gap may prove tough to close and lead to reactionary choices with long-term implications.

Clancy Briggs, Berwick Melbourne, wake up

I was a resident of Melbourne for many years during which time I was CEO of Tourism Victoria from 2001-06. Now living in my native Canada, I returned to Melbourne for a visit earlier this year.

Sadly, I was struck by the decline in Melbourne’s amenity and appearance.

Graceful Collins Street was no more. I had to navigate around homeless people to enter shops and use an ATM.

In addition, the homeless were many in number on the corner of Flinders Lane and Elizabeth Street. The junction of Elizabeth and Flinders streets was depressing, ugly and made me feel unsafe. Even allowing for the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, I sensed that the city had lost its famed friendliness and style. Melbourne always had style. I was really disappointed that downtown Melbourne looked the way it did.

Melbourne is too great a city to allow the loss of its well-earned appeal. The time for recognition of its decline and restoration of its faded glory has come. I hope the people of Melbourne rally to insist that local government takes action to clean the city up.

Lois Appleby, Calgary, Canada Interest owing

“It didn’t cost the taxpayer one cent for my trip overseas. Not one cent,” Pauline Hanson said (″⁣Rinehart paid for Hanson’s overseas flights″⁣, 29/7).

It seems that she doesn’t understand (or care?) that having her bills paid unavoidably compromises her independence as a politician, and that she will always be suspected of serving the interest of that benefactor,

quid pro quo, rather than the Australian people.

Anthony Hitchman, Eltham Subsidiary holding

World.title: Mother attended police station day before murder-suicide; Search for infant son called off
World.content:
NationalTragedy Mother attended police station day before murder-suicide; Search for infant son called off Isabel McMillan July 29, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the hours before Helena Wright’s body was pulled from the waters off South Australia’s Limestone Coast, police received a call from her friend. The details of that call are not publicly known, but it was enough to prompt a welfare check at the 36-year-old’s Compton home, on the outskirts of Mount Gambier. The call came at 9.28am on Monday, and when police knocked shortly after, no one answered the door. No one was home. Less than two hours later, reports from the public led police to find a vehicle parked on a clifftop at Cape Northumberland, near Port Macdonnell, a 30-minute drive from Wright’s home. The vehicle was empty, but its engine was still running.



Then, in the treacherous waters below South Australia’s southernmost point, police and local fishermen found Wright’s body, and the body of her 23-month-old daughter. Her three-month-old son could not be found. Loading As emergency services, community members, friends and family grapple with the tragic deaths and what led to them, police have confirmed Wright had visited a police station the day before, they believe she took her life, and the lives of her two young children. “South Australia Police can confirm Helena Wright attended the Mount Gambier Police Station on Sunday 26 July where she spoke with police,” a police spokesperson confirmed to this masthead on Wednesday night. “As this matter is now subject to a coronial investigation, SAPOL will provide all relevant information and evidence to the coroner. It is not appropriate to comment further while coronial proceedings are underway.”



Volunteers battled the harsh weather conditions for days, trying to find the body of Wright’s youngest child. On the water, on land and in the sky, help came from across the state and Victoria in the hopes of finding the baby. While Superintendent Trent Cox on Monday admitted it would be unlikely the infant would be found alive, he said he was holding out hope. The search near Port Macdonnell on South Australia’s south-east coast. 9News The last glimmer of that hope had faded when he again faced the waiting press pack on Wednesday, standing in the rain to announce the search would be unlikely to yield any positive result. Later, police confirmed they would cease searching altogether and, based on expert advice, declared the baby “could not have survived the period of time that has elapsed, either in the water or on land”. “Additionally, a range of factors, including the search environment and prevailing weather conditions, significantly reduce the likelihood of locating the infant in the immediate term. “The reality is, after three days, the chances of finding the baby alive are zero, sadly,” Cox said. “It’s a retrieval effort, but we don’t know where he is.”



Cox confirmed that, after days of investigation, the evidence police had gathered suggested no one else was believed to be involved in the deaths, and said the matter was now being handled as a murder-suicide. When asked if Wright had been turned away by police when she visited the Mount Gambier station on Sunday, and told to come back another day, Cox said he wouldn’t “confirm anything or deny anything”. “Any contact with police will form part of the brief that we provide the coroner,” he said. “I’m not aware of anything that I can release to you about the mother’s mental state or her personal medical issues. “The investigation of any death is very delicate, but when it involves children as young as 23 months and three months, it adds another layer of complexity, but also trauma for those who are involved. “It’s delicate in a number of ways. Obviously, the welfare aspect for my staff and for our volunteers. Also recognising it’s a local family.”



To those speculating on the tragedy without knowing the facts, Cox warned against adding to misinformed commentary. “Public commentary without the facts is always dangerous,” he said. “Misinformed commentary doesn’t help anyone.” To the wider community, who are struggling to come to terms with the circumstances of the deaths, Cox’s message was clear: “Wrap your arms around each other.” “Look after yourselves, look after your loved ones,” he said. “Give your kids an extra tight hug. “It will affect the community whether they have children or not because the deaths of such young children and a mother in these circumstances is tragic on so many levels.”



If you or anyone you know needs help, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 (see lifeline.org.au), Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 (see beyondblue.org.au) or 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732). Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Upper Hutt mayor: Don't force us to amalgamate with Wellington councils
World.content:
Upper Hutt's mayor is urging other Wellington councils not to force it into amalgamating against its will.

Councils across the motu have until August 9 to come up with plans to simplify local government, but in the capital there's still stark disagreement about the details.

The current proposal has Wellington, Upper Hutt, Lower Hutt, and Porirua city councils merging, as well as three Wairarapa councils and potentially Kāpiti District Council.

A layer of community councils would sit beneath that.

An email that Wellington Mayor Andrew Little sent last week to all councillors, which RNZ has seen, said Upper Hutt intended to vote against a plan to merge with the other Wellington councils.

The email said the city's mayor Peri Zee intended to ask councillors in each council to propose an amendment to have Upper Hutt excluded from any amalgamation proposal.

Zee told RNZ she was sceptical of amalgamation.

"I haven't yet heard anybody articulate the value proposition, or the outcomes we expect to get from this project.

"Our region already has strong regional governance in things like transport."

Upper Hutt mayor urging Wellington councils not to force amalgamation Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Analysis by consultants MartinJenkins showed a Wellington council made up of the city, Hutt Valley and Porirua councils could cost $290 million to set up and result in savings of $930 million over 25 years.

Zee said amalgamation would not deliver enough benefits for ratepayers.

She said she would ask elected members across the region to respect local decision-making if Upper Hutt votes against the idea next week.

"If a council votes no, that means no... and I would expect that they would respect that."

But that plea may be rejected.

Little said the proposal he would submit, if it was backed by his council, would include the region's four metro councils.

He said ministers had ultimately designed the process this way.

"Ministers can say it doesn't make sense for you not to be in it, therefore you're in it."

Little said he wants the Wellington region to decide its own fate, and not leave the plan up to the Government by missing a deadline.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He believed the benefits, including savings, from a larger council would be a win for ratepayers in the long run.

"We're not setting up for a few years, we're setting up an arrangement that is intended to last for two or three decades."

A majority of 3016 surveyed Wellington city residents said they wanted councillors to forge ahead with merger plans.

About 85 percent said they supported councillors putting forward plans, with 68 percent strongly supporting that and 17 percent somewhat supporting that.

Little said councillors were still debating amalgamation. He expected a decision next week.

What Wellingtonians think of amalgamation

Resident Ellen Blake believed forced amalgamation jeopardised Wellington city's special character.

"We have lots of council housing, we've got significant nature restoration programmes, those are all unique to Wellington - and not to the rest of the region. So we've got our own local identity, and we want to keep it."

Climate consultant Matt Raeburn was more positive about the idea. On Wednesday he told councillors in the capital that merging would help the region address climate change.

He said in his opinion, Wellington's voice was currently weaker than Auckland council's unified one when it came to climate.

"From central governments over the last few years, and frankly even before that, the message to councils has increasingly been you're on your own.

World.title: Government repeals Holidays Act, 'simpler' leave bill becomes law
World.content:
A major change to how leave is calculated in workplaces has become law.

The Employment Leave Bill passed its third and final reading in Parliament on Wednesday evening.

The legislation repeals the Holidays Act 2003, attempting to simplify the regime for both workers and employers.

Speaking at the third reading, Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden said the bill delivered long-overdue reform to "one of the most complex and problematic areas of our employment law".

It means annual and sick leave will now be accrued in hours, rather than days.

Additional and casual hours will not accrue annual or sick leave, with employers having to pay a 12.5 percent leave compensation payment for these hours instead.

All employers, including casuals, will be able to access annual, sick, bereavement, and family violence leave from the first day of work.

Workers will also be able to cash in up to 25 percent of their total annual leave balance every year.

Van Velden said the bill removed the need for "confusing conversions" between hours, days, and weeks, and its passing was an "important milestone" for New Zealand's workplaces.

"This bill delivers a simpler, fairer, and more workable system," she said.

All three opposition parties opposed the legislation, with Labour saying it would mean part-time workers would have to choose between going to work sick or losing pay, and people who worked extra hours would not have it reflected in the leave they earn.

In his contribution to the debate, Labour MP Phil Twyford said the legislation took from those who could least afford it.

"From all of the documents, from all of the debates we've had in the House, all the submissions we heard at Select Committee, all of the exchanges with the minister in the Committee Stage, it's clear that she and this government have chosen to prioritise administrative efficiency for employers at the expense of part-time and casual workers, who lose money and lose time off as a result of this law."

The Public Service Association had campaigned heavily against the bill, with national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons saying 200,000 workers faced a pay cut if the bill passed.

World.title: Biggest overhaul of gun regulations in decades passes into law
World.content:
The biggest overhaul of gun regulations in more than 40 years has passed into law.

Among the changes brought by the Arms Bill are a new firearms regulator removing police from oversight duties, restrictions for gang members and a host of new offences and penalties.

National and ACT agreed to rewrite the Arms Act - in place since the early 1980s - as part of its coalition arrangement.

The legislation has had many iterations, more recently a ban on semi-automatics and a new firearms regulator, introduced after the March 15 terror attacks in 2019.

Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee said the changes would improve public safety, keeping guns out of the hands of criminals while making it easier for licensed firearm owners to comply with the law, and be trusted and respected.

In her speech to Parliament on Wednesday during the third reading, McKee said opposition parties and the media had demonised gun owners and conflated them as criminals.

"The reality is the legislation that went through in 2019 and 2020, rushed as it was, without any consultation, without due select committee process, didn't address the issue of unlicensed criminal behaviour. Instead, it pointed the finger at those that conform and those that do behave," she said.

"These legislative changes that we're making will do some greatness, I think, towards being able to show and build trust and confidence in a regime again."

McKee referenced changes including separating the Firearms Safety Authority from Police, regulating large capacity pistol magazines, introducing infringement notices rather than revoking licenses, extending dealer license durations and banning gang members from having licenses.

For her speech she wore a korowai, gifted from the Council of Licensed Firearms Owners (COLFO).

"They placed it around my shoulders, and they told me that I had the weight of licensed firearm owners around my shoulders," she said.

"I have hung this korowai in my office for the last six years, and every time I've made a decision about firearms, I've looked at the wall and I've looked at that, and I've had the best intent for all firearm licence holders throughout New Zealand in every decision that we've made."

Labour's Duncan Webb told the House that McKee's claim that gun owners had been demonised was not accurate.

"The minister referred to the reforms that all but one member of this House, at the time, supported, which was to put an effective ban on semi-automatic weapons."

Labour supported responsible firearms regulation, and it had cooperated with other parties to make the bill more workable, said Webb.

But the party still disagreed with removing police as the regulator, he said, calling the move "strange".

"We think the police are the proper agency to supervise the use of firearms."

Webb said McKee had listened to COLFO, the lobby group that she was formerly closely involved with.

World.title: Police 'hold serious concerns' for missing 69-year-old in Auckland
World.content:
Police have serious concerns for a 69-year-old reported missing from a residential complex on Auckland's North Shore.

Maree Jennins was reported missing from the complex on Roseberry Rd in Birkenhead on Tuesday evening.

The last confirmed sighting of Jennins was on the afternoon of Friday, July 24.

She had no form of transport, but had been known to use taxis in the past, police said.

"We have made enquiries with taxi firms throughout the day, we know that Maree has recently avoided using her name when she has made taxi bookings. She may have caught a taxi from the Roseberry Rd or wider Birkenhead area," Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams, from Waitematā East CIB, said.

"Maree's family and police hold serious concerns for her following recent comments she has made. She stayed in a north Auckland motel recently and it is possible she has done the same again, but we continue to be worried for her wellbeing."

Police want any taxi drivers that might have picked her up on Friday afternoon to contact them. They have asked accommodation providers with information to get in touch as well.

Residents in the wider Birkenhead area that may have seen her should also contact police. Anyone who sees her should call 111 immediately.

World.title: Stillborn boy discovered on side of Marlborough road laid to rest
World.content:
A stillborn boy discovered on the side of the road in Marlborough has been laid to rest at a public funeral service.

About 30 people gathered this morning to mark the life of the boy, called Baby Doe, who was found by a mowing contractor on Wairau Bar Road on 19 May.

An investigation was launched, but police have not yet been able to identify the child or its family.

Funeral held for stillborn baby found on Marlborough roadside Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Baby Doe was laid to rest in a small white casket adorned with flowers, beneath an unnamed memorial plaque that read: "Every life that ever forms, touches the world in some small way, for all eternity."

The service was held at the children's memorial area at Fairhall Cemetery, near Blenheim.

The funeral service for Baby Doe at Fairhall Cemetery, near Blenheim, was attended by police, iwi and members of the public. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Police chaplain John Etheredge, who led the service, said while the circumstances were "tragic and traumatic", it was important to show love and respect for the young life.

"It will bring closure to those that are involved in it to a degree and it also puts it out there to hopefully to the mother and her family that people are caring about her."

He said many in the community had gone out of their way to show support for the baby and its family.

"We don't know what's happened with mum and how much agony it was to go through and to to lose the child, that must be terrible and quite traumatic," Etheredge said.

Wairau Bar Road, where the infant's body was found. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Iwi, police and members of the public were at the service, with some travelling from Nelson to mark their respects.

Ngāti Rārua representative Barney Thomas said a karakia and told those gathered: "This is our baby, belongs to all of us."

Detective Sergeant Jason Hillgrove said the baby was near full-term when he was stillborn, he appeared to have been cared for and was wrapped up when he was found.

"We've been endeavouring to try and identify who the mother is because our main concern through this investigation is to make sure that she's okay.

"We would really love to find out who she is so we can put a name to the baby, but also make sure that her welfare and mental health is looked after."

Detective Hannah McCabe and Detective Constable Paul Beckett, who were among the first on the scene, lower Baby Doe's casket at his funeral service. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Hillgrove said not knowing the boy's identity raised questions over how to appropriately lay him to rest.

"With the help of Sowman's [Funerals], the decision was made that we really need to have a service to allow the community to come together in grief for this little baby."

Two of the police officers first on the scene - Detective Hannah McCabe and Detective Constable Paul Beckett - also travelled with the baby to its post mortem in Christchurch, and Beckett read a poem at the service, before lowering the casket into the ground.

"Most of the police involved in this inquiry, we're parents too, so we've all been touched by this," Hillgrove said.

"This baby did belong to someone for nine months and that's the person we really want to find."

Iwi, police and members of the public at a funeral service for the stillborn baby found on Wairau Bar Road on 19 May, that has not yet been identified. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Marlborough mayor Nadine Taylor said it was important to honour Baby Doe in a proper memorial service.

"Somewhere there's a mother and a family, a whanau that's grieving for the loss of this baby and it was important that we came together as a community to be here on behalf of that family and to acknowledge Baby Doe."

Sowman's Funerals donated its time to make the service happen, with Mayflower Studio donating flowers and Artisan Memorials donating the plaque.

"Many parts of the community have contributed to this service, come together to make sure that the funeral is as it should be, is as it would be for any other much loved baby and that's been really important to the Marlborough community."

A plaque on the grave of Baby Doe, a stillborn boy discovered on the side of the Wairau Bar Road in Marlborough, on 19 May. RNZ / Samantha Gee

The plot at Fairhall Cemetery was donated by the Marlborough District Council, with Baby Doe buried among other children.

Sowman's Funerals manager Chelsea Brown said it was important that the baby had a final resting place, with a simple plaque, that people were able to visit.

"It's someone's baby and it's a life that needs to be represented."

Flowers from the Children's Commissioner on the grave of the stillborn baby found in Marlborough, named Baby Doe. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Flowers sent by the Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad were also placed on the grave.

"Tēnā koe pēpi, moe mai rā, moe mai rā, moe mai rā," the card attached to them read.

"Although you didn't have the chance to experience this world, we mourn for you, and will remember you, and we send our love to your māmā.

"Rest now, with the stars."

World.title: Overhauled Dog Control Act to be 'in place next year'
World.content:
An updated Dog Control Act should be in place by next year, Local Government Minister Simon Watts says.

On Wednesday he released guidelines which replace the guidance developed in 2009 and supplemented in 2015.

They were intended to help councils make full use of the tools currently available to them, promote responsible dog ownership and respond effectively when problems arose, Watts said,

Councils told to record more consistent data to tackle roaming dogs Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

He told Checkpoint it was the first phase of the comprehensive review of the Act ordered in March.

Too many Kiwis had been victims of dog attacks, "and we've even had loss of life", he said.

"We're aiming to have our recommendations to enable us to take steps to legislate by the end of this year, and have that law in place next year."

The guidelines also included standardised reporting across councils to "improve data collection", Watts added.

"Better information will help build a clearer picture of dog control issues across New Zealand and support better decision-making."

Local Government Minister Simon Watts RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Watts said standardised reporting was needed to guide the Dog Control Act, as it was difficult to review and change the legislation without it, but it was not yet mandatory.

"The consideration around the mandatory nature of whether this will be required formally will be something that we're considering through the legislation review that we're undertaking at the moment."

ACC recorded more than 14,000 claims related to dog bites and attacks in 2025.

World.title: Public service boss tells union to pull 'change the government' postcards from workplaces
World.content:
The country's top public servant has directed the Public Service Association (PSA) to stop handing out its "change the government" campaign material in departments and agencies, saying it breaches expectations of political neutrality.

But the union said that's an overreaction and is seeking an "urgent meeting" to make its case to the public service boss.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche wrote to the PSA on Wednesday that he had received "a number of queries" from public servants and union delegates about the campaign.

The country's top public servant has directed the Public Service Association to stop handing out its "change the government" campaign material. Supplied / PSA

He said the postcards were "clearly election advertising", noting they even included a promoter statement with the advertiser's name and contact details - a legal requirement for all election s.

Sir Brian said, as such, sharing or displaying them in public service workplaces breached the requirement for the sector to be politically neutral at all times.

"Public servants and the public service need to be kept safe from any accusations around political neutrality," he said.

"I am disappointed that public servants have been put in the unacceptable position where they have been asked to display and distribute material clearly inconsistent with our guidance."

In an email in response, PSA national secretaries Fleur Fitzsimons and Duane Leo said they disagreed that the postcards amounted to election advertising.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons disagreed that the union's postcards amounted to election advertising. Supplied

"It is important that public service agencies do not over-compensate during this time and unnecessarily restrict the right of public servants and their unions to express their views," they wrote.

The union asked Roche to refrain from briefing chief executives until the two sides had met and said it was seeking further legal advice.

RNZ, however, has seen an email already sent by Sir Brian to agencies notifying them of his decision and advising leaders to act in a "reasonable, fair and proportionate manner" if they needed to remove any advertising from their workplaces.

In his initial letter to the PSA, Roche said unions could still communicate with their members outside the workplace, including by email and at union meetings, for members to consider in their own time.

He said they were not, however, allowed to display union material in areas accessible to the public, nor election advertising anywhere on the premises.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders must be able to trust that the public service serves the government of the day with equal professionalism, regardless of political persuasion," Sir Brian wrote.

World.title: Government accepts all Covid-19 inquiry's recommendations 'in some form'
World.content:
Government to develop legislation to guide future pandemic responses Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

The government has accepted "in some form" all Covid-19 inquiry's recommendations, promising key advice will be made public within five working days in future pandemics.

The Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Covid 19 Response made 39 recommendations in its first "phase" and a further 24 recommendations in the second phase which focused primarily on how mandates were rolled out.

The final report was delivered in March, and the government has been considering its response since then.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said New Zealanders had placed enormous trust in the government and made real sacrifices to protect one another, and deserved "a clear account of what happened".

"This response is about learning from it."

Mixed reaction to government's response to Covid-19 inquiry Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

He said the government had accepted 21 recommendations in full, accepted 36 "in principle" and partially accepted the remaining six.

The resulting changes would be completed within 12 months where possible.

Cabinet had agreed to release advice behind any major decision affecting individuals' rights within five working days in future pandemics.

And while the government would not push ahead with standalone pandemic legislation, it would review the Health Act "to ensure any future response balances the protection of public health, the economy, and New Zealanders' rights".

Health Act review will take years - minister

Brown said the government's biggest undertaking now would be the Health Act review, which would go through a Select Committee process.

"We want to make sure that any legislation that is changed is done in a way that is transparent, that allows for people to make submissions," he said.

"Because we're balancing the economy with health and also people's rights and freedoms."

He expected the review would take several years.

Brow said he would be meeting with officials every three months to ensure they were acting on the inquiry's recommendations.

Labour's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall said the government needed to put money behind its response, to make any difference.

"It's incredibly disappointing to see that the recommendations to strengthen the health system are all unfunded," she said.

"We're not going to have a different pandemic experience in the future unless public health systems are strengthened."

Deputy Prime Minister and ACT party leader David Seymour said the government decided against pandemic legislation because it did not need any more power.

"We're actually here to stand up for the rights of people to go to school, run their businesses, and not inherit $100 billion worth of extra debt, which is what happened last time."

New Zealand First's leader and fellow coalition partner Winston Peters said the government's response to the inquiry was "pathetic".

"We're going to make sure there's going to be another inquiry, so people who were maltreated and abused, and not given the right advice, do get some justice."

Green Party co-leader Chloe Swarbrick said the government was not adequately funding front line health staff.

"You have a government right now that has actively undermined the health system's capacity to actually respond to the next pandemic, that's incredibly concerning," she said.

World.title: Rugby Australia tight-lipped on possible Cheika homecoming
World.content:
